section: 1. Definition of Insurance Contract
stem: X pays Y P10,000 so that Y will pay X P1M if a named ship, already lost at sea but unknown to both, failed to arrive. Is this a valid subject of insurance?
answer:
Yes. The undertaking is a valid subject of insurance because both parties were ignorant of the loss when the contract was perfected.
Under Section 2(a) of the Insurance Code, insurance is an undertaking for consideration to indemnify against loss from an unknown or contingent event, and under Section 3, insurance on a past event is allowed when the parties do not know whether it has already happened. Fortuity is therefore judged at perfection, and ignorance shared by both sides preserves it.
Here, each element is present on these facts. The P10,000 is the consideration. The P1,000,000 is the promised indemnity. The arrival or nonarrival of the named ship is the contingent event. Both X and Y were ignorant of the loss at perfection, so the counter-reading that an already lost ship cannot be insured fails under the Section 3 unknown-past rule.
The subject is therefore insurable. The contract is enforceable once insurable interest and the remaining requisites are shown, and the loss is payable within the agreed indemnity. Insurable interest remains the gatekeeper, as in La O v. Yek Tong Lin Fire and Marine (G.R. No. 33131, 1930), where recovery turned on identifying the holder of the damnifiable interest.
authorities: Part I-A General Concepts - Insurance Contract.md :: 1. Definition of Insurance Contract

section: 2. Principal Object and Purpose Test (HMO Product; Variable Contracts)
stem: An HMO sells cards guaranteeing doctor visits for a fixed fee, and it absorbs all costs even during epidemics. Is it doing an insurance business?
answer:
Yes. The HMO is doing an insurance business in substance and is answerable to regulation as an insurer.
Under Section 2(b)(1) of the Insurance Code, making insurance contracts as insurer is doing an insurance business, and under Section 2(b)(4), any business in substance equivalent to insurance that is designed to evade the Code is caught. The label on the card does not control. The principal object and purpose test decides. By contrast, a pre-need plan is held to its literal terms as the law between the parties rather than treated as Section 2(a) indemnity (Gaw v. CA, G.R. No. 147748, April 19, 2006).
Here, the HMO assumes risk for a price. The fixed fee is the consideration. Epidemic overuse is the contingent fortuitous cost. The guarantee of doctor visits is the undertaking to answer that contingency. The counter-reading that the HMO merely sells access to services fails because it absorbs cost variance instead of charging per visit.
The HMO is therefore transacting insurance business in substance. It needs a certificate of authority, and operating without one is punishable.
authorities: Part I-A General Concepts - Insurance Contract.md :: 2. Principal Object and Purpose Test (HMO Product; Variable Contracts)

section: 3. Doing an Insurance Business; Mutual Insurance Companies
stem: A civic club pools member contributions and pays fire losses of members, with no profit and no commission. Is it doing an insurance business?
answer:
Yes. The civic club is doing an insurance business even though it earns no profit and pays no commission.
Under Section 2(b)(1) of the Insurance Code, making or proposing to make any insurance contract as insurer is doing an insurance business, and under the no-profit sentence, the absence of profit and the absence of separate or direct consideration are not conclusive against doing an insurance business. Motive does not decide. The act decides. Substance controls over labels here, as the Court kept an insurer to obligations assumed in substance in Capital Insurance and Surety Co. v. Del Monte Motor Works, Inc. (G.R. No. 159979, 2015).
Here, the club performs the act. Member contributions are the consideration pooled from the many. Payment of members fire losses is indemnity on a contingency. Fire striking a member home is the fortuitous peril answered by the pool. The counter-readings that nonprofit pooling is mere mutual aid and that unpaid officers negate the business both fail under the no-profit sentence.
The club is therefore transacting an insurance business. It needs a certificate of authority like any insurer, and unlicensed operation is punishable.
authorities: Part I-A General Concepts - Insurance Contract.md :: 3. Doing an Insurance Business; Mutual Insurance Companies

section: 4. Applicable Laws (New Civil Code; Corporation Code)
stem: The policy is silent on when a mailed renewal binds. Which law answers?
answer:
The Civil Code answers through the cognition rule in Article 1319, applied suppletorily to the renewal.
Under Article 1319, paragraphs 1 and 2, of the Civil Code, consent is the meeting of offer and acceptance and a mailed acceptance binds the offeror only from knowledge, and under the suppletory-application rule, the Civil Code fills gaps the Insurance Code leaves open. The Code is primary on the contract and the business, while the Civil Code governs perfection timing. The cross-read illustration is Cebu Shipyard v. William Lines, where a Civil Code provision on subrogation was enforced alongside the policy (G.R. No. 132607, May 5, 1999).
Here, the renewal is a new contract on the old terms unless varied. The mailed renewal acceptance therefore binds only when the insurer as offeror knew of it. The counter-reading that mailing alone perfects the renewal fails under the cognition rule.
The renewal is therefore effective when the insurer knew of the acceptance, and rights under it are reckoned from that date.
authorities: Part I-A General Concepts - Insurance Contract.md :: 4. Applicable Laws (New Civil Code; Corporation Code)

section: 5. Importance of Insurance; Dealing with Risks
stem: Why can the insurer pay P45M on one fire (cf. Cebu Shipyard) and stay solvent?
answer:
The insurer stays solvent through pooling, which lets one large loss be paid from the contributions of the many.
Under the distribution-of-losses framework, fortuitous losses of the few are spread across homogeneous exposures, enforced through the Section 17 measure of damnification and the Section 77 earning of premium on exposure. The insurer prices fortuity across the pool and holds reserves from the common fund. The illustration is Cebu Shipyard v. William Lines, where the vessel insurer paid P45,000,000 on one fire and pursued the repairer by subrogation (G.R. No. 132607, May 5, 1999).
Here, the single fire loss is funded by the premiums of the many exposures, not by the premium on the burned property alone. The counter-reading that one large payment must exhaust the insurer fails because solvency rests on spread, pricing, and reserves rather than on any single risk.
The P45,000,000 payment is therefore consistent with solvency, and subrogation replenishes the fund where a third party caused the loss.
authorities: Part I-A General Concepts - Insurance Contract.md :: 5. Importance of Insurance; Dealing with Risks

section: 6. Characteristics (Indemnity; Not a Wagering Contract)
stem: A P5M building is insured for P3M and suffers a P1.5M partial fire loss under a 60 percent coinsurance clause. What is the recovery?
answer:
Recovery is scaled down to P900,000. The insured does not get the full P1,500,000.
Under Section 17 of the Insurance Code, the measure of property interest is capped at damnification, applied through the ratable-proportion rule, under which the insured is his own insurer for the uninsured excess (Galian v. State Assurance Co., G.R. No. L-8405, February 10, 1915). Partial loss therefore equals actual loss multiplied by insured value over value at fire. Coinsurance punishes underinsurance rather than rewarding it.
Here, the figures trigger the scale-down. The building is worth P5,000,000 but is insured for only P3,000,000, so the insured carried two-fifths of the risk. The P1,500,000 partial fire loss is multiplied by three-fifths, yielding P900,000. The counter-reading that any loss below the P3,000,000 face amount is paid in full fails because the 60 percent coinsurance clause makes the insured coinsure the uncovered portion.
The insurer therefore pays only P900,000, and the insured bears the P600,000 balance as his own insurer.
authorities: Part I-A General Concepts - Insurance Contract.md :: 6. Characteristics (Indemnity; Not a Wagering Contract)

section: 7. Perfection (Requisites, Cognition, Offer/Acceptance, Unaccepted Application, Stipulation, Tort Liability, Delivery)
stem: "Jason is the proud owner of a newly-built house worth PS million. As a protection against any possible loss or damage to his house, Jason applied for a fire insurance policy thereon with Shure Insurance Corporation (Shure) on October 11, 2016 and paid the premium in cash. It took the company a week to approve Jason's application. On October 18, 2016, Shure mailed the approved policy to Jason which the latter received five (5) days later. However, Jason's house had been razed by fire which transpired a day before his receipt of the approved policy. Jason filed a written claim with Shure under the insurance policy. Shure prays for the denial of the claim on the ground that the theory of cognition applies to contracts of insurance. Decide Jason's claim with reasons. (5%)"
answer:
Jason loses and Shure properly denies the claim because no insurance contract had yet been perfected when the fire occurred.
Under Article 1319, paragraph 2, of the Civil Code, a mailed acceptance binds the offeror only from knowledge, and under Sections 77 and 78 of the Insurance Code, premium is earned on exposure and cover attaches only upon a perfected contract plus exposure within the policy period. The application is the offer and the company approval is the acceptance, which must be absolute and known to the offeror. Delay alone is neither acceptance nor, without inexcusable neglect proved, a tort.
Here, the dates defeat the claim. Jason applied and paid in cash on October 11, 2016. Shure approved and mailed on October 18. Jason received the policy five days later. The fire came the day before receipt, while the approval was still in transit, so at loss no acceptance had reached Jason and no contract yet existed despite premium payment.
Shure is therefore correct to deny. The cash premium is returnable, and no tort liability arises on these facts without inexcusable delay proved.
authorities: Part I-A General Concepts - Insurance Contract.md :: 7. Perfection (Requisites, Cognition, Offer/Acceptance, Unaccepted Application, Stipulation, Tort Liability, Delivery)

section: 8. Kinds of Insurance; Kinds of Property Insurance Policy
stem: Two fire policies cover the same building, with the owner holding one and the lessee holding the other, and both are disclosed. Is there a forfeiture?
answer:
No. There is no forfeiture, and both policies stand in full force.
Under Sections 13 and 14 of the Insurance Code, any damnifiable relation to the thing is an insurable interest, applied through the triple-identity rule, under which forfeiture for other insurance needs the same subject, the same interest, and the same risk. Different interests defeat the clause even on the same building. The contracting insured sues on his own interest, and other policies on different interests are no breach (La O v. Yek Tong Lin Fire and Marine, G.R. No. 33131, December 30, 1930). Undisclosed coinsurance on the same interest forfeits all benefits, which confirms that identity of interest is the pivot (Multi-Ware Manufacturing Corp. v. Cibeles Insurance Corp., G.R. No. 230528, February 1, 2021).
Here, the required identity is lacking. The owner holds the ownership interest and the lessee holds the leasehold interest. Both policies are disclosed. The counter-reading that two policies on one building automatically forfeit fails for want of the same interest.
Both policies therefore stand, and each pays within its own measure without double recovery.
authorities: Part I-A General Concepts - Insurance Contract.md :: 8. Kinds of Insurance; Kinds of Property Insurance Policy

section: 10. The Policy (Form, Basic Provisions, Identification, Adhesion, Interpretation, Indivisibility, Proof, Riders, Cover Notes, Renewal, Reformation)
stem: A policy insures "Building A", and the insurer denies a claim on Building B by invoking an unsigned, unattached, and unreferred-to endorsement. Does that endorsement form part of the contract?
answer:
The endorsement forms no part of the contract, so the Building A claim stands on the policy as written.
Under Section 50 of the Insurance Code, the policy must carry the seven mandatory specifications, applied with Article 1377 of the Civil Code, under which obscurity is construed against the drafter, and with the adhesion rule, under which ambiguities are resolved against the insurer to avoid forfeiture (Qua Chee Gan v. Law Union and Rock Insurance Co., G.R. No. L-4611, December 17, 1955). Riders become part of the contract only when attached to the policy, referred to in it, and supported by premium.
Here, the endorsement fails every test. It is unsigned, unattached, and unreferred to in the policy. The counter-reading that the insurer may invoke an unattached paper to deny a Building B loss fails because an unmentioned endorsement binds no one.
The endorsement is therefore disregarded entirely, and the Building A fire loss is payable in full within the written terms and limits of the policy.
authorities: Part I-A General Concepts - Insurance Contract.md :: 10. The Policy (Form, Basic Provisions, Identification, Adhesion, Interpretation, Indivisibility, Proof, Riders, Cover Notes, Renewal, Reformation)

section: 11. Elements (Distribution of Losses; Risk; Insurable Interest)
stem: "(c) Insurable interest in property (2%)".
answer:
Insurable interest in property is every interest in property, whether real or personal, or any relation thereto, or liability in respect thereof, of such nature that a contemplated peril might directly damnify the insured.
Under Section 13 of the Insurance Code, insurable interest in property is every damnifiable relation to the thing. Under Section 18, a property policy is enforceable only for the benefit of one holding such interest. Under Section 19, the interest must exist both when the insurance takes effect and when the loss occurs. Under Section 17, the measure is the extent of damnification. The definition is therefore framed by an enforceability condition, a two-point timing rule, and a loss-based measure. Interest enforcement runs as in La O v. Yek Tong Lin Fire and Marine (G.R. No. 33131, 1930), where the Court first identified the holder of the damnifiable interest before sustaining recovery.
Here, only the bare definition is asked, and the Section 13 sentence supplies it word for word. The timing and measure provisions complete the answer by showing when the interest must exist and how far recovery reaches.
A complete answer therefore recites the Section 13 definition together with the Section 19 timing at effect and loss and the Section 17 measure of damnification.
authorities: Part I-A General Concepts - Insurance Contract.md :: 11. Elements (Distribution of Losses; Risk; Insurable Interest)

section: 11. Elements (Distribution of Losses; Risk; Insurable Interest)
stem: "Emilio owns a car which he purchased from Gregorio. Emilio agreed to pay Gregorio the balance of the purchase price in the amount of P500,000 within one year. To secure the payment of the balance, Emilio and Gregorio executed a security agreement that complies with the requirements of the Personal Property Security Act (PPSA). The security interest was also perfected in accordance with the PPSA. Who has insurable interest over the car? Explain your answer."
answer:
Both Emilio and Gregorio hold insurable interest over the car, and either or both of them may insure.
Under Sections 13 and 14 of the Insurance Code, any damnifiable relation to the thing is an insurable interest, including an existing interest and an expectancy coupled with an existing interest, measured by Section 17 at damnification. Separate interests on one thing support separate policies without breach (La O v. Yek Tong Lin Fire and Marine, G.R. No. 33131, December 30, 1930).
Here, Emilio as buyer-owner holds the existing ownership interest and is damnified by loss of the car beyond the unpaid balance. Gregorio as perfected secured creditor holds an interest to the extent of the P500,000 collectible from the car, because a perfected Personal Property Security Act interest is a damnifiable relation to the thing. The counter-reading that perfection merges the two interests into one fails because ownership and security interests remain distinct.
Either or both may therefore insure, each within his own measure, and the two policies are no double-insurance breach.
authorities: Part I-A General Concepts - Insurance Contract.md :: 11. Elements (Distribution of Losses; Risk; Insurable Interest)

section: 12. Premium (Accrual, Provision, Forms, Non-Payment, Check, Binding Despite Unpaid, Lapse Prevention, Return, Rebate)
stem: "Flavio obtained from Safe Assurance Corporation (SAC), through its agent Laureen, a fire insurance policy over his residential house for a period of one year from August 25, 2024 to August 24, 2025. Flavio delivered on August 26, 2024 a check representing premium payment to Laureen who then issued an acknowledgment receipt. On August 27, 2024, a fire completely razed Flavio's house. Oblivious of the incident, Laureen deposited the check on August 28, 2024 to SAC's bank account and was credited on the same day. Thereafter, Flavio filed against SAC an insurance claim. However, SAC denied the claim and argued that there was no payment of premium yet to make the insurance policy effective at the time of the loss. SAC explained that it received the premium payment only on August 28, 2024 or after the fire occurred on August 27, 2024. Is there a valid and binding insurance contract between SAC and Flavio? Explain."
answer:
Yes. A valid and binding insurance contract exists between SAC and Flavio, and SAC must pay for the razed house.
Under Sections 77 and 78 of the Insurance Code, premium is earned on exposure and cover attaches upon a perfected contract plus exposure within the policy period, applied with the agency rule, under which premium delivered to the authorized agent with an acknowledgment receipt is payment to the insurer itself. An insurer that collects premium through its agent is estopped from denying payment on internal-timing grounds, as in Qua Chee Gan v. Law Union and Rock Insurance Co. (G.R. No. L-4611, 1955).
Here, Flavio delivered his check to Laureen on August 26, 2024, inside the August 25, 2024 to August 24, 2025 term, and Laureen issued an acknowledgment receipt before the August 27 fire. The August 28 deposit and crediting are merely internal timing that does not move the payment date back. The counter-reading that payment happened only on August 28 fails because delivery to the authorized agent was complete on August 26.
The denial therefore fails. The contract is valid, the August 27 loss fell within cover, and SAC must pay.
authorities: Part I-A General Concepts - Insurance Contract.md :: 12. Premium (Accrual, Provision, Forms, Non-Payment, Check, Binding Despite Unpaid, Lapse Prevention, Return, Rebate)

section: 1. Cancellation; Rescission
stem: N, a non-life insurer, sent a cancellation notice for a fire policy five days before termination, citing a ground not listed in Sec. 64. The insured demanded the facts and received none. May the insurer treat the policy as cancelled?
answer:
No. The insurer may not treat the policy as cancelled. The five-day notice invoking a ground outside Sec. 64 is void for lack of a statutory ground and for defective notice, so the fire policy remains in force.
Under Secs. 64 and 65 of the Insurance Code, cancellation of a non-life policy after effectivity is allowed only on the seven exclusive statutory grounds, and only with prior written notice stating the ground relied upon, with the insured entitled to demand the supporting facts. Cancellation operates prospectively and strictly on its written basis, as Fieldmen's Insurance v. Asia Surety (G.R. No. L-23447, 1970) holds that cancellation does not reach accrued obligations and rescission needs a proved Code ground.
Here N cited a ground that Sec. 64 does not list, gave only five days, and refused the demand for the supporting facts. The counter-reading that any written notice suffices fails because Sec. 65 requires the notice to state a lawful ground and back it with facts on demand, and an unlisted ground is no ground at all.
The attempted cancellation is therefore ineffective. The policy stands, the insurer remains bound as if no notice had been sent, and any claim denial resting on that cancellation must be rejected.
authorities: Part I-B Grounds for Rescission.md :: 1. Cancellation; Rescission

section: 2. Ascertaining and Controlling Risks
stem: P applied for marine cargo cover and disclosed the voyage route but not the well-known port congestion surcharge practice. The insurer asked no question on surcharges, issued the policy, then sought rescission for concealment. Will rescission prosper?
answer:
No. Rescission will not prosper. The undisclosed port congestion surcharge practice was a general usage of trade equally open to the insurer, so there was no concealment of a material fact the insurer had no means of ascertaining.
Under Sec. 28 of the Insurance Code, each party must communicate in good faith all material facts within his knowledge which the other has no means of ascertaining. Under Sec. 32, each party is bound to know all general causes open to inquiry equally with the other and all general usages of trade. Under Sec. 33, the right to material information may be waived by neglect to inquire where the fact is distinctly implied in communicated facts.
Here P disclosed the voyage route, which distinctly implied exposure to port costs, while the surcharge practice was well known in the trade and equally accessible to the marine underwriter. The insurer asked no question on surcharges and issued the policy. The counter-reading that any undisclosed cost practice is concealment fails because Secs. 28 and 32 excuse what the other could ascertain and charge the insurer with usages of trade, and Sec. 33 treats the neglected inquiry as waiver.
There is therefore no concealment under Secs. 26 to 27. The policy stands, the insurer is deemed to have waived the information, and the rescission action must be dismissed.
authorities: Part I-B Grounds for Rescission.md :: 2. Ascertaining and Controlling Risks

section: 3. Concealment
stem: Diego, a cancer survivor, filed an application for a life insurance policy with Garantiya Insurance Company (GIC). He delivered his application and insurance premium to Gabriela, the officer of GIC in charge of approving life insurance policies. Gabriela then approved the application of Diego on June 1, 2020. On January 30, 2023, Diego died in a vehicular accident. When the heirs of Diego claimed the insurance proceeds, GIC denied the claim on the ground that Diego had concealed the fact of his illness. Moreover, Gabriela knew about the illness of Diego but also concealed it from GIC. Is the denial of the insurance claim by GIC proper? Discuss.
answer:
No. The denial is improper. GIC is deemed to have known of the cancer history through Gabriela, its approving officer, so there is no concealment against it, and the policy had already become incontestable months before Diego died.
Under Secs. 26 to 28 and 31 of the Insurance Code, concealment is the neglect to communicate a known material fact which the other has no means of ascertaining, with materiality judged by probable influence on underwriting and not by the event. Under Sec. 48, after a life policy payable on death has been in force during the insured's lifetime for two years from issue, the insurer cannot prove voidness ab initio or rescindibility for fraudulent concealment or misrepresentation, as Manila Bankers Life v. Aban (G.R. No. 175666, 2013) holds that styling the defense as nullity does not evade the bar.
Here Diego delivered his application and premium to Gabriela, the officer in charge of approving life policies, and Gabriela knew of the cancer yet approved the application on June 1, 2020. That knowledge is GIC's knowledge, so GIC had the means of ascertaining the illness and cannot plead concealment. The counter-reading that Gabriela concealed the illness from her own company fails because the officer's breach of duty to her principal is not concealment by the applicant, and the insurer's remedy was against its officer and not the heirs. Diego died on January 30, 2023 in a vehicular accident, about two years and eight months after approval, so the two-year bar had long run and the accidental death confirms materiality is never judged by the event.
GIC therefore holds no concealment defense and no timely fraud defense. The denial must be reversed, the proceeds must be paid to the heirs, and GIC's recourse, if any, lies against Gabriela.
authorities: Part I-B Grounds for Rescission.md :: 3. Concealment

section: 4. Representation
stem: A applied for fire insurance stating the warehouse was "concrete-walled" when it was half timber, but added "per my caretaker, who I have not verified." The policy as issued expressly describes the building as "concrete throughout." May the insurer rescind, and may A invoke the caretaker explanation?
answer:
Yes. The insurer may rescind if the concrete-wall statement is false in a material point, and A may not invoke the caretaker remark or use the representation to contradict the express policy term.
Under Secs. 44 to 46 of the Insurance Code, a representation is false when the facts fail to correspond with its assertions, and if false in a material point, whether affirmative or promissory, the injured party may rescind from the time the representation becomes false, with materiality tested as in concealment. Under Sec. 40, a representation cannot qualify an express provision of the policy, though it may qualify an implied warranty.
Here A stated the warehouse was concrete walled when it was half timber, so the facts fail to correspond with the assertion and the representation is false. Wall construction plainly bears on fire underwriting, so the falsity is material. The counter-readings fail one by one. The claim that the caretaker sourcing excuses the falsity fails because A adopted the statement as his own to obtain cover, and one who asserts as fact what he has not verified assumes the risk of falsity. The attempt to soften the expressly issued term fails because Sec. 40 gives the express description of concrete throughout priority over the collateral remark.
The insurer is therefore entitled to rescind from the time the representation became false upon proving materiality at trial. The policy cannot be read down by the caretaker remark, and indemnity need not be paid under the avoided contract.
authorities: Part I-B Grounds for Rescission.md :: 4. Representation

section: 5. Warranties
stem: A fire policy warrants "two 2.5-inch hydrants with 100 psi at all times." At issuance the insurer inspects, sees one weak hydrant, issues anyway, and collects premiums for two years. After a fire, may it avoid solely for breach of that warranty with no fraud shown?
answer:
No. The insurer may not avoid the policy on the hydrant warranty alone. Its prior inspection with knowledge, followed by two years of premium collection, estops the defense, and without fraud Sec. 76 gives only exoneration while breached rather than avoidance.
Under Secs. 74 to 76 of the Insurance Code, violation of a material warranty entitles the other party to rescind, but breach of an immaterial provision does not avoid the policy unless so declared, and breach of warranty without fraud merely exonerates the insurer from the time breach occurs or prevents attachment if broken in inception. As Qua Chee Gan v. Law Union and Rock Insurance (G.R. No. L-4611, 1955) holds, an insurer that inspects, knows the premises lack the warranted appliances, yet issues the policy and keeps collecting premiums is estopped from invoking the warranties, with ambiguities construed against it.
Here the warranty called for two 2.5-inch hydrants at 100 psi at all times, yet the insurer saw one weak hydrant at issuance, issued anyway, and collected premiums for two years. The counter-reading that any paper breach voids the policy fails twice. It fails on estoppel because knowing issuance plus continued collection is waiver by conduct under Qua Chee Gan. It fails on remedy because with no fraud shown, Sec. 76 does not convert a supervening shortfall into voidness from the beginning.
The warranty defense therefore fails. The insurer remains liable on the fire loss, subject only to proving some other valid defense, and it cannot treat the whole policy as void from the beginning.
authorities: Part I-B Grounds for Rescission.md :: 5. Warranties

section: 6. Conditions; Other Insurance Clause
stem: A insures factory machines with X containing an other-insurance clause, then secretly insures the same machines with Y against the same fire risk for an overlapping period. Separately, the X policy says suit must be filed within 6 months of loss. After fire, X invokes both defenses. Decide each defense.
answer:
On the first defense X wins and the claim is forfeited for breach of the other-insurance clause, but on the second defense X loses because the six-month suit limit is void. The insured keeps the lawful period to sue, though the forfeiture stands.
Under the other-insurance clause law, undisclosed co-insurance forfeits where the same subject matter, the same interest, and the same risk concur with non-disclosure, as Multi-Ware Manufacturing v. Cibeles Insurance (G.R. No. 230528, 2021) holds, while La O v. Yek Tong Lin Fire and Marine (G.R. No. 33131, 1930) requires all three identities and recognizes waiver by knowledge plus premium collection. Under Sec. 63 of the Insurance Code, any policy condition limiting suit to less than one year from accrual is void.
Here the Y policy covers the same factory machines, the same ownership interest, and the same fire peril for an overlapping period, secretly taken, so all three identities concur with non-disclosure and no waiver is shown. The counter-reading that any second policy is automatically a breach fails as a general proposition under La O, but it fails in the other direction here because difference of interest is absent. On suit time, six months falls below the one-year floor, so the limit is void and the lawful period governs.
X therefore prevails on forfeiture for the undisclosed concurring cover, but its time-bar defense must be denied. The suit proceeds under the lawful period, with the claim already defeated on the co-insurance breach.
authorities: Part I-B Grounds for Rescission.md :: 6. Conditions; Other Insurance Clause

section: 7. Exclusion/Exception; Burden of Proof
stem: In January 2016, Mr. H was issued a life insurance policy by XYZ Insurance Co., wherein his wife, Mrs. W, was designated as the sole beneficiary. Unbeknownst to XYZ Insurance Co., however, Mr. H had been previously diagnosed with colon cancer, the fact of which Mr. H had concealed during the entire time his insurance policy was being processed. In January 2019, Mr. H unfortunately committed suicide. Due to her husband's death, Mrs. W, as beneficiary, filed a claim with XYZ Insurance Co. to recover the proceeds of the late Mr. H's life insurance policy. However, XYZ Insurance Co. resisted the claim, contending that: 1. the policy is void ab initio because Mr. H fraudulently concealed or misrepresented his medical condition, i.e., his colon cancer; and 2. as an insurer in a life insurance policy, it cannot be held liable in case of suicide. Rule on each of XYZ Insurance Co.'s contentions. (5%)
answer:
Contention 2 fails. The January 2019 suicide, about three years after the January 2016 issue, falls outside the suicide exclusion, so XYZ remains liable on this ground.
Under Sec. 183 of the Insurance Code, the insurer in a life contract is liable for suicide committed after the policy has been in force for two years from issue or last reinstatement, with insanity suicide always compensable and shorter policy periods measured accordingly. Under Secs. 86 to 89, exclusions are strictly construed against the insurer, which carries the burden of proving the exception after the beneficiary's prima facie case, as United Merchants v. Country Bankers (G.R. No. 198588, 2012) holds on the burden sequence.
Here the policy ran from January 2016 to January 2019, about three years of continuous force, so the two-year suicide threshold is passed. XYZ proved no insanity question and no shorter policy period, and its blanket invocation of suicide cites no clause language. The counter-reading that suicide is never compensable in life insurance fails because Sec. 183 draws the line at two years precisely to cover this case, and an unproved exclusion construed against the insurer cannot carry the defense.
Contention 2 is therefore denied. XYZ is liable on the suicide ground, subject only to the Sec. 48 incontestability analysis that independently defeats contention 1.
authorities: Part I-B Grounds for Rescission.md :: 7. Exclusion/Exception; Burden of Proof

section: 8. Incontestable Clause
stem: In January 2016, Mr. H was issued a life insurance policy by XYZ Insurance Co., wherein his wife, Mrs. W, was designated as the sole beneficiary. Unbeknownst to XYZ Insurance Co., however, Mr. H had been previously diagnosed with colon cancer, the fact of which Mr. H had concealed during the entire time his insurance policy was being processed. In January 2019, Mr. H unfortunately committed suicide. Due to her husband's death, Mrs. W, as beneficiary, filed a claim with XYZ Insurance Co. to recover the proceeds of the late Mr. H's life insurance policy. However, XYZ Insurance Co. resisted the claim, contending that: 1. the policy is void ab initio because Mr. H fraudulently concealed or misrepresented his medical condition, i.e., his colon cancer; and 2. as an insurer in a life insurance policy, it cannot be held liable in case of suicide. Rule on each of XYZ Insurance Co.'s contentions. (5%)
answer:
Contention 1 is barred. XYZ can no longer prove the policy void from the beginning or rescindible for the colon-cancer concealment, the policy having been in force for about three years during Mr. H's lifetime.
Under Sec. 48 of the Insurance Code, after a life policy payable on death has been in force during the insured's lifetime for two years from issue or last reinstatement, the insurer cannot prove voidness from the beginning or rescindibility by reason of fraudulent concealment or misrepresentation, and the right to rescind must in any case be exercised before action on the contract. As Manila Bankers Life v. Aban (G.R. No. 175666, 2013) holds, styling the suit as a nullity action does not evade the bar, and the insured's own insurable interest in his own life suffices.
Here the policy was issued in January 2016 with Mrs. W as beneficiary and remained in force until Mr. H's death in January 2019, about three years during his lifetime. The concealed colon cancer is exactly the fraud defense Sec. 48 cuts off after two years. The counter-reading that fraud voids from the beginning regardless of time fails because Sec. 48 deliberately trades perpetual contestability for repose, forcing the insurer to investigate promptly and rescind within the period.
XYZ must therefore pay as to contention 1. Its remedy was timely investigation with pre-action rescission inside two years, and that window has closed.

section: 9. War Limitation Rider / War Clause
stem: Cargo insured under marine policy with F.C. and S. clause deleted and Institute War Clauses attached is seized by civil authority. Insurer denies, citing the war exclusion in the printed form. Rule on the denial.
answer:
The denial is improper. The insurer is liable because civil arrest is covered under the policy as rewritten, and the printed war exclusion it cites no longer exists.
Under Secs. 86 and 88 of the Insurance Code, liability turns on proximate cause and on perils especially excepted as written, with deleted exclusions read as deleted. As Malayan Insurance v. CA (G.R. No. 119599, 1997) holds, deletion of the free of capture and seizure clause removes the war exclusion and the added Institute War Clauses affirmatively restore risks such as civil arrest, so war allocation follows the policy as rewritten, strictly construed against the insurer.
Here the marine policy carries a deleted free of capture and seizure clause with Institute War Clauses attached, and the cargo was seized by civil authority, the very risk the rider restores. The counter-reading that the printed exclusion survives fails because deletion erased it and the rider affirmatively covered the peril. The insurer has proved no surviving exception under the rewritten text.
The war defense therefore fails. The insurer must pay the civil-arrest loss under the rider, with causation still governed by Secs. 86 and 88 on these facts.

section: 10. Defenses of Insured against Revocation
stem: Insurer learns of concealment in Year 1, keeps collecting premiums for a year, then after loss and after beneficiary sues, declares rescission. The insured pleads waiver, estoppel, and timeliness. Rule on the defenses.
answer:
All three defenses succeed. The rescission declared after loss and after suit is barred by waiver, by estoppel, and by untimeliness, so the insurer must pay.
Under Sec. 48 of the Insurance Code, a right to rescind given by the chapter must be exercised before commencement of action on the contract. Under the waiver and estoppel doctrines, an insurer that collects premiums with knowledge of the ground for forfeiture waives it, as La O v. Yek Tong Lin Fire and Marine (G.R. No. 33131, 1930) holds, and an insurer that by conduct recognizes the policy with knowledge is estopped from contradicting that position, as Qua Chee Gan v. Law Union and Rock Insurance (G.R. No. L-4611, 1955) holds. After two years of a life policy in force, fraud defenses are further barred under Sec. 48, as Manila Bankers Life v. Aban (G.R. No. 175666, 2013) holds.
Here the insurer learned of the concealment in Year 1, kept collecting premiums for a full year, then waited until after loss and after the beneficiary sued before declaring rescission. The year of post-knowledge collection shows intentional relinquishment and induced reliance, satisfying both waiver and estoppel. The post-suit declaration violates the previous-to-action rule on its face. The counter-reading that a real concealment survives any delay fails because Sec. 48 makes timeliness a separate procedural bar and knowledge plus collection independently relinquish the right.
Rescission is therefore ineffective on three independent grounds. The insurer is barred by waiver, estoppel, and timeliness, with incontestability as an added bar where its requisites are met, and the claim must be paid.

section: 1. Loss
stem: Absolute Timber Co. (ATC) has been engaged in the logging business in Isabela. To secure one of its shipments of logs to be transported by Andok Shipping Co., ATC purchased a marine policy with an "all risks" provision. Because of a strong typhoon then hitting Northern Luzon, the vessel sank and the shipment of logs was totally lost. ATC filed its claim, but the insurer denied the claim on several grounds, namely: (1) the vessel had not been seaworthy; (2) the vessel's crew had lacked sufficient training; (3) the improper loading of the logs on only one side of the vessel had led to the tilting of the ship to that side during the stormy voyage; and (4) the extremely bad weather had been a fortuitous event. ATC now seeks your legal advice to know if its claim was sustainable. What is your advice. Explain your answer. (3 percent)
answer:
The claim is sustainable and every one of the four denial grounds fails, so the insurer must pay the full value of the totally lost log shipment.
Under Sec. 86 of the Insurance Code, the insurer is liable where the insured peril was the proximate cause of the loss even if an uncontemplated peril was a remote cause, and under Sec. 89 negligence of the insured or its agents never exonerates while only a willful act or connivance bars recovery, which is why a sunken cargo rendered valueless to its owner is an actual total loss payable in full without notice of abandonment (Pan Malayan Insurance Corp. v. CA (FAO), G.R. No. 95070, 1991).
Here, ATC bought an all-risks marine policy for logs carried by Andok Shipping, and the vessel sank in a strong typhoon so the shipment was totally lost, which makes the typhoon peril of the sea the proximate cause of the loss. The first three grounds go to an unseaworthy vessel, an untrained crew, and one-sided loading, and each sounds in negligence that Sec. 89 keeps inside coverage rather than in a willful act that would bar it. The fourth ground concedes fortuity because extremely bad weather proves the loss was fortuitous, and no specially excepted peril was invoked under the Sec. 88 but-for test.
The denial is therefore improper and the insurer is liable for the total loss, with ATC recovering the full insured value of the shipment.

section: 2. Notice of Loss
stem: A fire policy requires written notice within 15 days. The insured notifies on day 40 without justification, then cures a defective proof after the insurer specifies the defect late. Run Secs. 90, 92, and 93 and conclude which omission exonerates the insurer and which omission it waived.
answer:
The forty-day delay in fire notice exonerates the insurer under Sec. 90 unless a Sec. 93 waiver is proved, while the late-specified proof defect is waived under Sec. 92 and cannot defeat the claim.
Under Sec. 90 of the Insurance Code, a fire insurer is exonerated unless written notice is given by the insured or a person entitled to the benefit of the insurance without unnecessary delay, while under Sec. 92 a remediable defect in notice or proof is waived unless the insurer specifies it without unnecessary delay as a ground of objection, and under Sec. 93 delay itself is waived only where the insurer caused it or failed to object promptly and specifically on the delay ground.
Here, the policy required written notice within fifteen days and the insured gave notice only on day forty without justification, which exceeds without unnecessary delay and triggers exoneration. The counter-reading that the cured proof saves the claim fails on the notice limb because notice and proof are separate requisites, although it succeeds on the defect limb since the insurer specified the proof defect late and therefore waived it.
The insurer is therefore exonerated for the late notice unless the insured proves a Sec. 93 waiver, but it can no longer rely on the waived proof defect, so the notice delay bars recovery while the defect does not.

section: 3. Collateral Source Rule
stem: The insured's employer pays sick-leave benefits for the same confinement the health insurer covers. The insurer deducts the sick-leave amount. Decide, then explain where the insurer's real recourse lies.
answer:
The deduction is improper and the health insurer must pay the policy benefits in full without subtracting the sick-leave pay.
Under the collateral source rule of the chapter, benefits received from a source independent of the insurer and the wrongdoer do not reduce the liability of the insurer on its own contract promise, and no double recovery results because total recovery stays capped at the loss. Under Secs. 95 and 96 of the Insurance Code, deduction and ratable contribution apply only between co-insurers of the same person covering the same subject and the same interest.
Here, the sick-leave benefits come from the employer under the employment relation while the health benefits answer the separate insurance contract, so the employer is an independent source and not a co-insurer of the same interest. The counter-reading that any overlapping payment reduces the policy fails because the two benefits answer different promises, and the insurer cannot borrow Secs. 95 and 96 for a same-person co-insurance adjustment that does not exist.
The insurer must therefore pay the health policy in full with aggregate recovery capped at the confinement loss, and any recourse runs through subrogation against the party liable for the loss rather than by deduction from the insured.

section: 4. Claims Settlement
stem: A non-life insurer receives complete proof of loss on March 1, neither agrees on the amount nor arbitrates within 60 days, and pays on day 120, blaming heavy volume. The insured sues for the proceeds plus damages. Decide interest and damages.
answer:
The insurer is liable for the proceeds plus double-ceiling interest running from May 31 until full satisfaction, together with attorney's fees and proven expenses.
Under Sec. 249 of the Insurance Code, a non-life insurer must pay within thirty days after receipt of proof of loss plus ascertainment by agreement or arbitration, or within ninety days of receipt where no ascertainment is made within sixty days, with delay interest at twice the Monetary Board ceiling unless the claim is fraudulent. Under Sec. 250, missing the statutory deadline is prima facie unreasonable delay once the Commissioner or the court makes the finding in enforcement litigation, and the award carries attorney's fees and expenses plus running double-ceiling interest.
Here, complete proof of loss was received on March 1 and neither agreement nor arbitration fixed the amount within sixty days, so the ninety-day default fixed the deadline at May 30 and payment on day 120 came thirty days late. The counter-reading that heavy volume excuses the lapse fails because volume is not just cause, and no fraud defense was pleaded that could stop the clocks under the rule in United Merchants Corp. v. Country Bankers Insurance Corp. (G.R. No. 198588, 2012).
The insured therefore recovers the proceeds with double-ceiling interest from May 31 until full satisfaction plus attorney's fees and proven expenses, with the delay deemed prima facie unreasonable under Sec. 250.
authorities: Part I-C Loss Settlement Subrogation.md :: 4. Claims Settlement

section: 5. Prescriptive Period
stem: A fire policy requires suit within six months of the fire. The insured sues in month eight after a denied claim. The insurer pleads the six-month clause. Decide.
answer:
The six-month suit clause is void and the plea of the insurer fails, so the suit filed in month eight stands and the insurer must defend on the merits.
Under Sec. 63 of the Insurance Code, any policy condition limiting the time for commencing an action to less than one year from accrual of the cause of action is void. A stipulation of one year or longer is enforced as written, and where no valid stipulation exists the general law on prescription governs. Accrual for an enforcement suit is reckoned from when the cause of action accrued rather than from the bare date of loss.
Here, the fire policy required suit within six months of the fire, which falls below the one-year-from-accrual floor and is therefore void. The counter-reading that time runs from the fire itself fails because accrual here postdated the fire through the denied claim, and the suit in month eight falls within the lawful minimum in any event.
The six-month clause is struck and the month-eight suit proceeds, with prescription measured from accrual under the lawful period.

section: 6. Subrogation
stem: X obtained an insurance policy for her Porsche Carrera GT from XYZ Insurance Company. The same car was insured by her creditor-mortgagee, Y, with ABC Insurance Company. When the car was damaged because of an accident, X filed a claim with XYZ Insurance Company. The latter denied the claim since it discovered that the car was also insured with ABC Insurance Company. According to XYZ Insurance Company, double insurance is prohibited by law. Decide with reason(s).
answer:
XYZ Insurance Company must pay the claim of X in full because there is no double insurance, and the other-insurance clause cannot defeat the ownership cover of X.
Under Sec. 95 of the Insurance Code, double insurance exists only where the same person is insured by several insurers separately for the same subject and the same interest. Under Malayan Insurance Co. v. Philippines First Insurance and Reputable Forwarder (G.R. No. 184300, 2012), the same goods exposed to the same peril for two different persons with distinct insurable interests is not double insurance, so the other-insurance and ratable-contribution clauses do not apply and each policy answers its own interest in full.
Here, X insured her Porsche Carrera GT with XYZ as owner while creditor-mortgagee Y insured the same car with ABC to secure the mortgage credit, so the persons and the interests differ as ownership against mortgage credit. The counter-reading that any overlap of car and accident triggers the clause fails because identity of person and interest is missing, and the accident damage is exactly the insured risk rather than an excluded peril.
XYZ is therefore liable on the policy of X in full, with any over-indemnity adjusted only under Sec. 96 among true co-insurers, and XYZ after payment is subrogated under Art. 2207 of the Civil Code against the party at fault for the accident.

section: 1. Reinsurance
stem: X obtained an insurance policy for her Porsche Carrera GT from XYZ Insurance Company. The same car was insured by her creditor-mortgagee, Y, with ABC Insurance Company. When the car was damaged because of an accident, X filed a claim with XYZ Insurance Company. The latter denied the claim since it discovered that the car was also insured with ABC Insurance Company. According to XYZ Insurance Company, double insurance is prohibited by law. Decide with reason(s).
answer:
No. XYZ must honor the claim because X and Y hold distinct insurable interests in the same car, so the two policies are not double insurance, and double insurance is in any event regulated rather than prohibited.
Under Sec. 95 of the Insurance Code, double insurance exists only where the same person is insured by several insurers separately for the same subject and interest, with Sec. 96 then ordering claiming, deduction, and ratable contribution. The Supreme Court applied this identity test in Malayan Insurance v. Philippines First Insurance (G.R. No. 184300, 2012), holding that two policies on the same goods for different persons with distinct interests are not double insurance.
Here, X insured her ownership interest with XYZ while Y, her creditor-mortgagee, insured its mortgage-credit interest with ABC, so the same-person and same-interest identities fail and each insurer answers on its own contract. The counter-reading that any overlap of cover voids the claim mistakes regulation for prohibition, since Sec. 96 preserves recovery through contribution rather than forfeiture.
XYZ is therefore liable on the claim and may neither deny outright nor invoke an other-insurance forfeiture, because each policy pays its own distinct interest without deduction from the other.
authorities: Part I-D Classes of Insurance.md :: 1. Reinsurance

section: 2. Fire Insurance
stem: Flavio obtained from Safe Assurance Corporation (SAC), through its agent Laureen, a fire insurance policy over his residential house for a period of one year from August 25, 2024 to August 24, 2025. Flavio delivered on August 26, 2024 a check representing premium payment to Laureen who then issued an acknowledgment receipt. On August 27, 2024, a fire completely razed Flavio's house. Oblivious of the incident, Laureen deposited the check on August 28, 2024 to SAC's bank account and was credited on the same day. Thereafter, Flavio filed against SAC an insurance claim. However, SAC denied the claim and argued that there was no payment of premium yet to make the insurance policy effective at the time of the loss. SAC explained that it received the premium payment only on August 28, 2024 or after the fire occurred on August 27, 2024. Is there a valid and binding insurance contract between SAC and Flavio? Explain.
answer:
Yes. A valid and binding fire insurance contract existed at the August 27 fire because Flavio paid the premium to the authorized agent of SAC on August 26, and payment to the agent binds the insurer from receipt.
Under the Insurance Code, premium payment through the authorized agent of the insurer is payment to the insurer itself, so the August 26 delivery of the check with the acknowledgment receipt of Laureen perfected payment even though the bank credited SAC only on August 28. Sec. 173 then measures the razed house at the replacement expense at the commencement of the fire in the condition it was in at injury, as applied in La O v. Yek Tong Lin Fire and Marine (G.R. No. 33131, 1930) and Galian v. State Assurance (G.R. No. L-8405, 1915).
Here, Laureen was the agent of SAC, Flavio delivered the check on August 26 within the August 25, 2024 to August 24, 2025 cover period, and the August 27 fire fell inside that period, so the August 28 bank-credit date is a mere internal clearing matter that does not move the payment date. The counter-reading that only bank credit counts would let the collection delay of the insurer defeat cover already paid for through its agent.
SAC is therefore liable for the fire loss measured under Sec. 173, because premium was paid before the loss and the policy was in force when the house burned.

section: 2. Fire Insurance
stem: Jason pays in cash Oct. 11. The insurer mails the approved policy Oct. 18. Fire razes the house before receipt. Decide under perfection and assumption-of-risk rules and state the measure under Sec. 173.
answer:
The insurer is liable because the contract was perfected on approval after the October 11 cash payment of Jason, so the risk had already attached before the fire and the October 18 mailing did not defer cover.
Under the Insurance Code, a fire policy is perfected upon approval of the application by the insurer with premium paid, and assumption of risk follows perfection rather than physical delivery of the policy. Sec. 173 measures an unvalued fire loss at the expense it would be to the insured at the commencement of the fire to replace the thing lost in its condition at injury.
Here, Jason paid in cash on October 11 and the insurer approved the risk before the fire razed the house, so the later mailing of the policy on October 18 is a mere formality that cannot postpone attachment. The counter-reading that cover begins only on receipt confuses evidence of the contract with perfection of the contract itself.
The insurer must therefore pay the Sec. 173 replacement measure, because a perfected policy with paid premium was already in force when the loss occurred.
authorities: Part I-D Classes of Insurance.md :: 2. Fire Insurance

section: 3. Life Insurance
stem: In January 2016, Mr. H was issued a life insurance policy by XYZ Insurance Co., wherein his wife, Mrs. W, was designated as the sole beneficiary. Unbeknownst to XYZ Insurance Co., however, Mr. H had been previously diagnosed with colon cancer, the fact of which Mr. H had concealed during the entire time his insurance policy was being processed. In January 2019, Mr. H unfortunately committed suicide. Due to her husband's death, Mrs. W, as beneficiary, filed a claim with XYZ Insurance Co. to recover the proceeds of the late Mr. H's life insurance policy. However, XYZ Insurance Co. resisted the claim, contending that: 1. the policy is void ab initio because Mr. H fraudulently concealed or misrepresented his medical condition, i.e., his colon cancer; and 2. as an insurer in a life insurance policy, it cannot be held liable in case of suicide. Rule on each of XYZ Insurance Co.'s contentions. (5%)
answer:
Both contentions of XYZ fail because the policy had been in force three years, so the concealment defense is barred by incontestability and the suicide falls outside the exclusion window.
Under Sec. 48 of the Insurance Code, the insurer is barred after two years from proving the policy void from the beginning or rescindable for fraud or concealment, a rule the Supreme Court sustained even against void-ab-initio recasts in Manila Bankers Life v. Aban (G.R. No. 175666, 2013). Under Sec. 183, the insurer is liable for suicide committed after the policy has been in force two years from issue or last reinstatement.
Here, the January 2016 to January 2019 period exceeds both two-year clocks, so the concealed colon cancer can no longer be proved to avoid the policy and the sane suicide after the period is a covered risk. The counter-reading that fraud preserves the defense indefinitely collapses against the very purpose of incontestability, which forces the insurer to investigate within two years rather than after the claim.
XYZ must therefore pay Mrs. W the proceeds, because both the concealment and the suicide defenses expired before the January 2019 death.
authorities: Part I-D Classes of Insurance.md :: 3. Life Insurance

section: 3. Life Insurance
stem: On June 21, 2008, Yate took out a life insurance policy on her life in the amount of PhP 10 million and named her husband Vandy and daughter as joint irrevocable beneficiaries. Before the policy was issued and the premiums were paid, Yate underwent a medical checkup with a physician accredited by the insurer, and the only result found was that she was suffering from high blood pressure. Yate was previously diagnosed by a private physician of having breast cancer which she did not disclose to the insurer in her application, nor to the insurer's accredited physician because by then, she was told that she was already cancer-free after undergoing surgery which removed both her breasts. She was later diagnosed with psychotic tendency that graduated into extreme despondency. She was found dead hanging in her closet 36 months after the issuance of the policy. The police authorities declared it to be a case of suicide. The policy did not include suicide as an excepted risk. (a) Can the insurer raise the issue of failure to disclose that she had cancer as a cause for denying the claim of the beneficiaries? (2.5%) (b) Are the beneficiaries entitled to receive the proceeds of the life insurance notwithstanding the fact that the cause of death was suicide? (2.5%)
answer:
(a) No. The insurer cannot raise the cancer non-disclosure because thirty-six months in force exceeds the two-year contestable period. (b) Yes. Vandy and the daughter recover the full P10 million because suicide at thirty-six months is compensable and they stand as joint irrevocable beneficiaries.
Under Sec. 48 as construed in Manila Bankers Life v. Aban (G.R. No. 175666, 2013), the insurer loses after two years the right to prove fraud or concealment to defeat the policy. Under Sec. 183, suicide after two years from issue is compensable, and insanity-graded despondency reinforces compensability at any date.
Here, the accredited physician of the insurer found only hypertension at underwriting, so the undisclosed cancer history, even if material, is time-barred at thirty-six months, and the hanging at thirty-six months falls outside any suicide exclusion window while the policy named no suicide exception. The counter-reading that an undisclosed cancer history survives indefinitely would nullify the incontestability bar the law imposes to close underwriting disputes.
The insurer must therefore pay Vandy and the daughter the P10 million as joint irrevocable beneficiaries, because both defenses expired and the designation was never revoked.

section: 3. Life Insurance
stem: Shortly after Yin and Yang were wed, they each took out separate life insurance policies on their lives, and mutually designated one another as sole beneficiary. Both life insurance policies provided for a double indemnity clause, the cost for which was added to the premium rate. During the last 10 years of their marriage, the spouses had faithfully paid for the annual premiums over the life policies from both their salaries. Unfortunately, Yin fell in love with his officemate, Vessel, and they carried on an affair. After two years, their relationship bore them a daughter named Vinsel. Without the knowledge of Yang, Yin changed the designation of the beneficiary to an "irrevocable designation" of Vinsel and Vessel jointly. When Yang learned of the affair, she was so despondent that, having chanced upon Yin and Vessel on a date, she rammed them down with the car she was driving, resulting in Vin's death and Vessel's complete loss of mobilization. Yang was sued for parricide, and while the case was pending, she filed a claim on the proceeds of the life insurance of Yin as irrevocable beneficiary, or at least his legal heir, and opposed the claims on behalf of Vessel and her daughter Vinsel. Yang claimed that her designation as beneficiary in Vin's life insurance policy was irrevocable, in the nature of one "coupled with interest," since it was made in accordance with their mutual agreement to designate one another as sole beneficiary in their respective life policies. She also claimed that the beneficiary designation of Vessel and the illegitimate minor child Vinsel was void being the product of an illicit relationship, and therefore without "insurable interest." (a) Is Yang correct in saying that her designation as beneficiary was irrevocable? (2.5%) (b) Do Vessel and Vinsel have "insurable interest" on the life of Yin? (2.5%)
answer:
(a) No. The designation of Yang was revocable and the later express irrevocable designation by Yin of Vinsel and Vessel displaced her, and her killing of Yin disqualifies her in any event. (b) Vessel and Vinsel need no insurable interest of their own because Yin had insurable interest in his own life and Sec. 184 lets the proceeds pass to any person.
Under Secs. 184 and 185 of the Insurance Code, a life policy may pass by transfer, will, or succession to any person whether or not he has an insurable interest, and notice to the insurer is unnecessary unless expressly required. A beneficiary designation is revocable unless expressly made irrevocable in the policy, and a private mutual agreement does not create irrevocability coupled with interest, while one who kills the insured cannot take as beneficiary.
Here, ten years of faithful premium payment created no vested irrevocability for Yang, so the written irrevocable change of Yin to Vinsel and Vessel controls, and the ramming by Yang that killed Yin and crippled Vessel bars her own recovery. The counter-reading that the mutual designation of the spouses froze both policies mistakes a private promise for a policy term, and the counter-reading that illicit origin voids the gift imports property-insurance interest rules that Sec. 184 expressly rejects for life cover.
The irrevocability and heir claims of Yang therefore fail while Vinsel and Vessel recover as designated irrevocable beneficiaries, subject to the parricide consequence that forfeits the own taking of Yang.
authorities: Part I-D Classes of Insurance.md :: 3. Life Insurance

section: 3. Life Insurance
stem: X insured his life for P20 million. X, plays golf and regularly exercises everyday, hence is considered in good health. He did not know, however, that his frequent headache is really caused by his being hypertensive. In his application form for a life insurance for himself, he did not put a check to the question if he is suffering from hypertension, believing that because of his active lifestyle, being hypertensive is a remote possibility. While playing golf one day, X collapsed at the fairway a [question continues in the official release on hypertension concealment and materiality]. [a] Will the beneficiary of X be entitled to the proceeds of the life insurance under the circumstances, despite the non-disclosure that he is hypertensive at the time of application? (2.5%) [b] If X died in an accident instead of a heart attack, would the fact of X's failure to disclose that he is hypertensive be considered as material information? (2.5%)
answer:
[a] The beneficiary recovers if the omission was an honest unknowing non-disclosure, but the insurer may deny if it proves X fraudulently concealed hypertension that caused the very death. [b] If X died by accident instead, the undisclosed hypertension is immaterial and cannot defeat the claim.
Under the Insurance Code, concealment avoids the policy only when fraudulent and material to the risk, and Sec. 48 through Manila Bankers Life v. Aban (G.R. No. 175666, 2013) bars late proof of fraud after two years in force. Accidental death is tested from the standpoint of the victim under Biagtan v. Insular Life (G.R. No. L-25579, 1972), so an unrelated undisclosed ailment does not touch an accidental cause.
Here, the genuine belief of X that his active lifestyle ruled out hypertension points to good faith and no fraudulent intent, yet hypertension that produced the fatal collapse would be material because it bore directly on the risk assumed. The counter-reading that any undisclosed condition voids cover regardless of knowledge or causal link would convert honest omission into fraud and let an immaterial ailment defeat an accidental death far removed from it.
The beneficiary therefore takes where the omission was innocent or time-barred, and takes in full on accidental death, while the insurer prevails only on proved fraudulent material concealment within the contestable period.
authorities: Part I-D Classes of Insurance.md :: 3. Life Insurance

section: 3. Life Insurance
stem: The insured names his business partner, who has no insurable interest, as irrevocable beneficiary, then outlives two years. Decide on the partner's right and the insurer's late fraud defense.
answer:
The business partner recovers the full proceeds because Sec. 184 lets a life policy pass to any person without insurable interest and the two-year incontestability bar has closed the late fraud suit of the insurer.
Under Sec. 184 of the Insurance Code, a life policy may pass by transfer, will, or succession to any person whether or not he has an insurable interest, and the transferee recovers whatever the insured could have recovered. Under Sec. 48 as construed in Manila Bankers Life v. Aban (G.R. No. 175666, 2013), the insurer is barred after two years from proving voidness or rescission for fraud or concealment.
Here, the lack of insurable interest of the partner is immaterial to a life designation, and the irrevocable form locks in his taking, while the fraud action of the insurer filed after two years in force arrives too late. The counter-reading that only interested takers may recover confuses life cover with property cover, where interest of the assignee matters, and the counter-reading that fraud is always provable ignores the two-year repose the law deliberately imposes.
The partner therefore takes the proceeds and the late fraud defense fails, because designation without interest is valid and time has barred avoidance.
authorities: Part I-D Classes of Insurance.md :: 3. Life Insurance

section: 3. Life Insurance
stem: An insured with two successive marriages names both wives as beneficiaries. State who takes and why, running Secs. 184-185 and the revocability default.
answer:
The widow named in the last valid written designation takes the proceeds because designations are revocable by default so the later one displaces the earlier, and neither widow needs insurable interest.
Under Secs. 184 and 185 of the Insurance Code, a life policy passes by transfer, will, or succession to any person with or without insurable interest, and notice to the insurer is unnecessary unless expressly required. The standing rule is revocability, so each new designation supersedes the last unless the policy expressly makes an earlier one irrevocable.
Here, the designation of the first wife fell when the insured validly named the second, since the succession of marriages itself neither supplies nor defeats a designation and each taker qualifies under Sec. 184 regardless of interest. The counter-reading that the first marriage freezes the first designation mistakes status for a policy term, and the counter-reading that a wife without interest cannot take repeats the property-insurance error Sec. 184 rejects.
The last designated widow therefore recovers in full, because revocability let the later designation control and interest was never required.
