section: 4. Annuity
stem: X transfers P1,000,000 to Y in exchange for a yearly pension during the life of Z, who dies of a pre-existing illness ten days after the contract. X demands the capital back. Decide under Arts. 2021-2024.
answer:
The constitution is void and X recovers the P1,000,000 capital because Z died within twenty days from an illness suffered at contracting, so no valid measuring life ever attached.
Under Art. 2023 of the Civil Code, a life annuity constituted upon one already dead or then suffering from an illness that causes death within twenty days is void. Under Art. 2021 the debtor pays the annual pension during the life of determinate living persons for capital transferred at once, and under Art. 2024 arrears for a valid annuity yield only a claim for unpaid income plus security, never reimbursement of capital.
Here, the death of Z on the tenth day from a pre-existing illness triggers Art. 2023 squarely, which voids the constitution from the start rather than merely ending future pensions. The counter-reading that X is confined to the Art. 2024 arrears remedy fails because that remedy presupposes a valid annuity with a living measuring life, which never existed.
X therefore takes back his capital in full, because voidness under Art. 2023 restores what a valid annuity under Art. 2024 would have kept transferred.
authorities: Part I-D Classes of Insurance.md :: 4. Annuity

section: 5. Casualty Insurance
stem: A personal accident policy excludes ten listed causes. The insured dies in a stabbing by strangers, with no provocation. The insurer denies the claim. It cites an unlisted peace-and-order exclusion it says is implied. Decide whether the insurer must pay.
answer:
The insurer must pay the face amount because the stabbing death is accidental as to the insured and murder falls outside the ten enumerated exclusions, which close the list against implied additions.
Under Sec. 176 of the Insurance Code, casualty covers loss from accident or mishap, and death by third-party violence unforeseen by the insured is accident judged from the standpoint of the victim. The Supreme Court so held in Finman General Assurance v. CA (G.R. No. 100970, 1992), where violent death by stabbing fell within personal-accident cover, and in Sun Insurance v. CA (G.R. No. 92383, 1992), which tested accident by fortuity rather than design.
Here, the insured died without provocation at the hands of strangers, so the death is fortuitous as to him, and the ten listed causes exclude murder and assault by omission, which under expressio unius keeps the insurer liable. The counter-reading that a peace-and-order exclusion is implied collapses because enumerated exclusions are exclusive and ambiguities construe against the insurer.
The insurer is therefore liable for the face amount, because the loss is accidental and no listed exclusion defeats it.
authorities: Part I-D Classes of Insurance.md :: 5. Casualty Insurance

section: 6. Compulsory Motor Vehicle Liability Insurance (CMVLI)
stem: A pedestrian is hit by a private car. Sworn police report and hospital receipts for P40,000 are filed with the offending car's insurer. The insurer refuses any payment until fault is proved and demands a full quitclaim for P15,000. The victim sues eight months after denial. Decide liability, amount floor, quitclaim, and prescription.
answer:
The insurer must pay no-fault indemnity of at least P15,000.00 on the sworn papers without proof of fault, it may not exact a full quitclaim for that payment, and the suit filed eight months after denial is timely.
Under Sec. 391 of the Insurance Code, death or injury claims pay without proof of fault on sworn police report plus death or medical proofs, with total indemnity of at least P15,000.00 per person and the occupant claim lying against the ridden vehicle and other claims against the directly offending vehicle. Under Sec. 398 the insurer ascertains and pays promptly without compelling a quitclaim for the no-fault balance, and under Sec. 397 the claim requires written notice within six months while suit prescribes one year from denial.
Here, the sworn police report plus P40,000 hospital receipts satisfy Sec. 391, so the fault-first refusal and the full-quitclaim demand both violate the no-fault track, while eight months from denial sits inside the one-year suit period. The counter-reading that no-fault needs negligence proof or buys total peace mistakes the P15,000.00 floor for a ceiling and the prompt-payment duty for a settlement.
The insurer must therefore pay no-fault now, litigate any excess on fault without a forced quitclaim, and face a timely action, because the papers, floor, and calendar all favor the victim.
authorities: Part I-D Classes of Insurance.md :: 6. Compulsory Motor Vehicle Liability Insurance (CMVLI)

section: 7. Marine Insurance
stem: A time-policy hull insurer denies a mid-period voyage loss because the ship, seaworthy at inception of the period, developed unseaworthiness during an earlier voyage that the master unreasonably delayed repairing. The cargo owner separately claims although the hull was sound for hull purposes. Decide both claims.
answer:
The hull claim fails for losses flowing from the unrepaired defect because seaworthiness is reckoned at every voyage and unreasonable delay in repair exonerates the insurer, while the cargo claim is tested separately on cargo fitness.
Under Sec. 117(a) of the Insurance Code, a time policy demands seaworthiness at the commencement of every voyage undertaken during the period, and under Sec. 120 unreasonable delay in repairing unseaworthiness exonerates the insurer on resulting loss. Under Sec. 121 a ship seaworthy for hull purposes may be unseaworthy for cargo purposes, a divide the Supreme Court enforced in Go Tiaoco v. Union Insurance Society of Canton (G.R. No. 13983, 1919), where a pre-voyage defect and slovenly repair made seawater entry a peril of the ship rather than of the sea.
Here, the unreasonable delay of the master in repairing the known defect triggers Sec. 120 on the resulting hull loss, so inception-period seaworthiness cannot save the mid-period voyage, while the recovery of the cargo owner turns on whether the vessel was fit for that cargo at the inception of the risk. The counter-reading that one seaworthiness finding covers both hull and cargo collapses against Sec. 121, which measures them independently.
The denial is therefore proper on the resulting hull loss and cargo recovery stands or falls on cargo-specific unseaworthiness, because voyage-stage fitness and subject-specific fitness each failed or must each be proved.
authorities: Part I-D Classes of Insurance.md :: 7. Marine Insurance

section: 8. Suretyship
stem: EFG, Inc. is indebted to Bank Y in the amount of P50,000,000.00. The loan was secured by a suretyship agreement issued by Z Insurance Co. Due to EFG, Inc's default, Bank Y filed a case against Z Insurance Co. as surety. There is also a pending criminal case for violation of the Bouncing Checks Law against the President of EFG, Inc., Mr. P, who signed the check as signatory for the company. Unable to meet its obligations as they fell due, EFG, Inc. filed a petition for rehabilitation. Finding the petition sufficient in form and substance, the court issued a Commencement Order, which was thereafter published. (a) Should the case filed against Z Insurance Co. be suspended in light of the Commencement Order? Explain. (2.5%) (b) Should the criminal case filed against Mr. P be suspended in light of the Commencement Order? Explain. (2.5%)
answer:
(a) No. The suit against Z Insurance as surety is not suspended because solidary surety liability is independent of the stayed principal obligation. (b) No. The criminal case against Mr. P proceeds because rehabilitation stays only civil enforcement against the debtor while his personal criminal liability stands apart.
Under Sec. 178 of the Insurance Code, the liability of the surety is joint and several with the obligor within the bond amount and fixed strictly by the bond terms, and under Art. 2047 of the Civil Code one who binds himself solidarily is a surety whom the creditor may pursue directly without exhaustion under Art. 2059. The Supreme Court confirmed this independence for continuing sureties in Stronghold Insurance v. Tokyu Construction (G.R. No. 158820, 2009) and for bond enforcement in Capital Insurance v. Del Monte Motor Works (G.R. No. 159979, 2015).
Here, Bank Y sues on the own solidary promise of Z rather than on the stayed debt of EFG, so the Commencement Order that halts enforcement against EFG leaves the surety suable up to the bond amount, and Mr. P faces prosecution for his own act of signing the worthless check rather than for the obligation of EFG. The counter-reading that the stay radiates to every related suit mistakes a debtor-protection device for a discharge of independent solidary and criminal liability.
Neither case is therefore suspended, so Bank Y collects from Z within the bond and the State prosecutes Mr. P, because suretyship and criminal responsibility each answer on their own footing.
authorities: Part I-D Classes of Insurance.md :: 8. Suretyship

section: 8. Suretyship
stem: Yellow Fin Tuna Corporation (Yellow Fin), a domestic corporation, applied for a credit facility in the amount of PhP 50 million with Yengzi Financial Corporation (YFC). The application was approved and the Credit Agreement was signed and took effect. Ysko and Yuan, Yellow Fin Chairman and President, respectively, executed a Continuing Suretyship Agreement in favor of YFC wherein they guaranteed the due and full payment and performance of Yellow Fin's guarantee obligations under the credit facility. YFC soon discovered material inconsistencies in the financial statements given by Yellow Fin, drawing YFC to conclude that Yellow Fin committed misrepresentation. Under the Credit Agreement, any misrepresentation by Yellow Fin or its sureties will constitute an event of default. YFC thus called an event of default and filed a complaint for sum of money against Yellow Fin, Ysko, and Yuan. Immediately thereafter, Yellow Fin filed a petition for rehabilitation. The court suspended the proceedings in YFC's complaint until the rehabilitation court disposed of the petition for rehabilitation. YFC posits that the suspension of the proceedings should only be with respect to Yellow Fin but not with respect to Ysko and Yuan. Is YFC correct? (2.5%)
answer:
Yes. YFC is correct because Ysko and Yuan bound themselves as continuing solidary sureties for the whole facility, so the stay that halts the case against Yellow Fin leaves the complaint against them fully alive.
Under Art. 2053 of the Civil Code, a guaranty may secure future debts even unliquidated, which is the office of a continuing suretyship over a running credit line. Under Sec. 178 of the Insurance Code and Art. 2047 of the Civil Code, sureties bind themselves jointly, severally, and solidarily with the principal, so the creditor proceeds directly against them without exhaustion, as the Supreme Court sustained in Stronghold Insurance v. Tokyu Construction (G.R. No. 158820, 2009).
Here, Ysko and Yuan guaranteed due and full payment and performance of the obligations of Yellow Fin under the P50 million facility, and the declaration of default by YFC on misrepresentation triggered their independent solidary liability before any rehabilitation order issued. The counter-reading that suspension against the principal suspends the sureties confuses a procedural stay of the case of the debtor with extinction of the own promise of the sureties, which survives with later reimbursement against the debtor under Arts. 2066 to 2067.
The complaint therefore proceeds against Ysko and Yuan while Yellow Fin alone rests under the stay, because continuing solidary suretyship answers for the facility on its own terms.
authorities: Part I-D Classes of Insurance.md :: 8. Suretyship

section: 1. Insurance Commissioner
stem: Villacorta leaves her insured car with a repair shop for check-up and repairs. A shop employee drives it to Montalban without her consent, crashes it into a parked truck, and the car is extensively damaged. The insurer invokes the authorized-driver clause and denies theft, and the Insurance Commission dismisses her complaint on those grounds. Decide whether recovery lies and state the appeal route.
answer:
Villacorta recovers on both the own-damage and theft covers, so the Insurance Commission dismissal must be set aside and the remedy from the adverse ruling is a Sec. 439 appeal to the Court of Appeals.
Under Sec. 439 of the Insurance Code, the Commissioner adjudicates an insured claim against the insurer up to P5,000,000.00 per single claim with a notice of appeal to the Court of Appeals filed with the Commissioner within thirty (30) days from receipt. Under the adhesion-construction doctrine applied in Jewel Villacorta v. Insurance Commission (G.R. No. L-54171, 1980), policy ambiguity is resolved strictly against the insurer. Under Art. 308 of the Revised Penal Code, unlawful taking without consent is theft because use itself is gain.
Here, Villacorta entrusted her Colt Lancer key to Sunday Machine Works for check-up and repairs and shop employee Benito Mabasa drove it to Montalban without consent before crashing it into a parked truck. The entrustment presumptively authorized legitimate driving by a licensed driver so the diversion to an illicit purpose did not breach the authorized-driver clause. The taking without consent was theft even if first framed as a temporary joy ride, and the extensive damage proved a lasting deprivation beyond mere use.
Villacorta therefore recovers P35,000.00 with legal interest from filing until full payment plus costs, with subrogation against Sunday Machine Works preserved, and the dismissal is corrected by a timely Sec. 439 notice of appeal to the Court of Appeals.
authorities: Part I-E Regulation of Insurance Business.md :: 1. Insurance Commissioner

section: 2. Regulations Imposed on Insurance Business
stem: A new domestic non-life insurer with P800,000,000.00 paid-up capital and facially complete papers applies for a certificate of authority, and the Commissioner considers refusing it. Decide whether the certificate may issue and state the refusal ground.
answer:
No certificate of authority may issue to the new domestic non-life insurer on these papers, and the Commissioner may lawfully refuse the application on the capital defect alone and on an adverse best-interest finding.
Under Sec. 194 of the Insurance Code, a new domestic stock life or non-life company must possess paid-up capital of at least P1,000,000,000.00 kept unimpaired for continuance. Under Sec. 193, no certificate issues until the Commissioner is satisfied on Philippine-law qualification and local economic justification and sound direction and administration with integrity and financial organization and capital reasonably assuring the safety of policyholders and the public, and refusal is allowed where refusal best promotes the interest of the people of the country.
Here, the applicant holds only P800,000,000.00 in paid-up capital and therefore falls P200,000,000.00 short of the P1,000,000,000.00 floor regardless of facially complete papers. Even with full capital, the four Sec. 193 satisfaction requisites of qualification and economic justification and management integrity and policyholder safety must each still be met. Complete papers answer form but never cure a capital shortfall.
The application must therefore be denied for failure to meet the Sec. 194 floor, and refusal remains lawful on an adverse Sec. 193 best-interest judgment with no new business until authority is restored on compliance.
authorities: Part I-E Regulation of Insurance Business.md :: 2. Regulations Imposed on Insurance Business

section: 3. Regulation of Persons Involved in the Business
stem: A non-life insurer controlled by H Corp. proposes to sell to H Corp. an asset worth 6 percent of its admitted assets as of Dec. 31 last year without asking anyone. H Corp. separately buys 45 percent of the insurer's voting stock without notice. Decide whether either transaction may proceed under Secs. 290, 299, and 302.
answer:
Neither the six percent asset sale nor the forty-five percent stock purchase may proceed as proposed because each crosses a control-line threshold that requires prior clearance.
Under Sec. 290(b) of the Insurance Code, control is presumed where a person directly or indirectly owns or holds forty percent or more of voting securities. Under Sec. 299, a controlled insurer transaction with its holding-company system involving five percent or more of admitted assets as of December 31 next preceding needs prior written approval. Under Sec. 302(a), a non-insurer acquisition of control of a domestic insurer needs twenty (20) days written notice plus prior written approval.
Here, H Corp. already controls the non-life insurer and the proposed sale of an asset worth six percent of admitted assets exceeds the five percent line so it needs prior written approval and cannot ride the thirty (30)-day notice band for smaller transactions. The separate purchase of forty-five percent of voting stock exceeds the forty percent presumption and is an acquisition of control by a non-insurer without the required notice and approval.
Neither transaction may therefore proceed without clearance, so the sale needs prior written approval and the stock purchase needs twenty (20) days written notice plus prior written approval before closing.
authorities: Part I-E Regulation of Insurance Business.md :: 3. Regulation of Persons Involved in the Business

section: 4. Insurers in Financial Distress
stem: The Commissioner places troubled insurer X under conservatorship. X argues the Commissioner should have gone straight to liquidation because its books look insolvent. State the correct sequencing answer with reasons.
answer:
The conservatorship of troubled insurer X was the correct first step, so the plea to go straight to liquidation on books that merely look insolvent must be rejected.
Under Sec. 254 of the Insurance Code, suspension or revocation answers unsound condition and legal noncompliance and hazardous method and impaired net worth and deficient solvency margin. Under Sec. 255, a conservator takes assets and liabilities and management on continuing inability or unwillingness to maintain adequate solvency or liquidity and overrules prior management to preserve assets and reorganize and restore viability. Under Sec. 256, receivership with forthwith cease-and-desist answers disclosed insolvency or hazardous continuance, and liquidation follows only on the ninety (90)-day determination that the insurer is insolvent or cannot safely resume with public interest requiring it.
Here, books that look insolvent establish only a trigger for examination with suspension or conservation rather than proof of inability to pay lawful obligations as they fall due under Sec. 200. The receiver gathers and administers assets for policyholders and creditors during the ninety (90)-day reorganization inquiry before any winding up is ordered.
Conservatorship therefore stands and receivership and liquidation follow only as the escalation matures, while a liquidated life or non-life insurer or professional reinsurer is never rehabilitated or reauthorized.
authorities: Part I-E Regulation of Insurance Business.md :: 4. Insurers in Financial Distress

section: 5. Rate Regulation
stem: Insurer Y charges a favored client 20 percent below its last-filed rate and pays the client's manager an unstated cash inducement. Y then seeks to charge a hazardous risk 30 percent above file without asking. Decide which acts violate Secs. 365, 366, and 370 and which can still be cured.
answer:
All three acts of insurer Y were unlawful as done, and only the proposed hazardous-risk surcharge can still be cured by prior approval.
Under Sec. 365 of the Insurance Code, no member or subscriber or company or agent or broker may charge or demand or receive a rate deviating from the rates last filed. Under Sec. 370, no off-policy rebate or special favor or unstated inducement may be paid or offered to the insured or its employee as inducement or after effectivity. Under Sec. 366, a higher-than-filed rate on a specific risk may be used only on written application stating reasons filed with and approved by the Commissioner.
Here, the twenty percent discount below the last filing is deviation regardless of client favor and the unstated cash to the client manager is a rebate to an employee of the insured. The thirty percent surcharge for the hazardous risk was charged without the required reasoned written approval, and hazard alone never excuses prior clearance.
The discount and the inducement therefore stand as violations priced at a fine up to P25,000.00 per policy with suspension or revocation, while only the surcharge is curable through a Sec. 366 application filed and approved before use.
authorities: Part I-E Regulation of Insurance Business.md :: 5. Rate Regulation

section: 1. Defined; Governing Law and State Policy; Insurance Commission
stem: A hospital gives subscribers, their spouses, and dependents free or discounted board, procedures, and drugs as subscriber incentives. Decide whether these perks are pre-need plans or HMO contracts.
answer:
The hospital perks are neither pre-need plans under Sec. 4(b) nor HMO contracts under EO 192 s. 2015, so they fall outside pre-need regulation and stand as mere shareholder incentives.
Under Sec. 4(b) of RA 9829, a pre-need plan is a contract for the benefit of planholders providing future service or money or other benefit at actual need or agreed maturity as specified therein in exchange for cash or installment amounts. Under EO 192 s. 2015 as applied in IC Letter Opinion 2022-01, an HMO contract delivers pre-agreed health care for a fixed prepaid fee over a period through a provider network. Under Gaw v. CA (G.R. No. 147748, 2006), the written plan terms control the classification because the plan is the law between the parties.
Here, the free and discounted board and procedures and drugs go to subscribers and their spouses and dependents as incentives for stock subscription rather than as specified benefits at actual need or agreed maturity paid for with plan consideration. The arrangement likewise collects no fixed prepaid membership fee over a period and operates no provider network, so the HMO definition fails on both price and structure. Treating share incentives as plan benefits would rewrite the Sec. 4(b) exchange element that Gaw enforces literally.
The perks are therefore neither pre-need plans nor HMO contracts, and no pre-need license or registration or brochure duty attaches to them as such.
authorities: Part I-F Pre-Need Plans.md :: 1. Defined; Governing Law and State Policy; Insurance Commission

section: 2. Parties; Other Regulated Persons; Suspension/Revocation
stem: A company offers pension plans online with bank-deposit payment instructions but holds no license. Decide whether the offer is actionable.
answer:
The unlicensed online pension-plan offer is unlawful on both the licensing and advertising gates, so the Insurance Commission may issue a cease-and-desist order against it and the sellers face fines and criminal exposure.
Under Sec. 10 of RA 9829, no person may operate as a pre-need company without a Commission license. Under Sec. 14, every plan intended for public sale needs a registration statement filed within forty-five days of licensing. Under Sec. 18, no pre-need advertising may run without prior Commission approval. Under Primamanila Plans v. SEC (G.R. No. 193791, 2014), a website offer of pension plans with bank-deposit payment instructions and no license sustains a cease-and-desist order. Under Secs. 53(c) and 54, unauthorized selling draws fines on a thirty-percent and forty-percent and license-loss ladder plus one year of imprisonment and triple-price fines.
Here, the company holds no license yet offers pension plans to the public online and collects through bank deposits. The missing license breaches Sec. 10 and the missing registration breaches Sec. 14 while the unapproved website solicitation breaches Sec. 18. That the payments look like ordinary bank deposits changes nothing because plan consideration paid through a bank remains plan consideration. The Primamanila pattern is matched element for element.
The Commission may therefore shut the offer down by cease-and-desist order, and the sellers answer for administrative fines and criminal liability for unregistered selling.
authorities: Part I-F Pre-Need Plans.md :: 2. Parties; Other Regulated Persons; Suspension/Revocation

section: 3. Kinds of Plans; Pre-need Contract and Interpretation
stem: After a planholder's mother dies, the family at once engages an outside funeral home that embalms the body and supplies a casket, notifies the provider only that evening, and later substitutes a different casket. Decide whether the provider owes memorial services.
answer:
The provider owes no memorial services on these facts, so the dismissal of the planholder claim stands and the family bears the outside funeral and replacement-casket costs alone.
Under RA 9829 and the plan-is-law rule of Gaw v. CA (G.R. No. 147748, 2006), the clear stipulations of the pre-need plan control literally between the parties. Under Gaw, the provider holding the sole and exclusive right to arrange services with a mortuary of its choice requires notice directly to and acknowledged by the provider before the family acts, with time of the essence. Under Sec. 3, doubts favor the planholder, but liberality never rewrites a clear term. Under Dio v. St. Ferdinand Memorial Park (G.R. No. 169578, 2006), an adhesion contract binds as written because the adherer was free to reject it entirely.
Here, the family engaged an outside funeral home at once upon the death of the mother and let it embalm the body and supply a casket before notifying the provider only that evening. The evening notice after embalming and casketing preempted the sole arrangement right and breached the imperative acknowledged-notice term. The later substitution of a different casket breached the pre-selected-casket term whose upgrade cost Gaw assigns to the family alone. That the plan is an adhesion contract avails nothing because Dio enforces clear adhesion terms literally.
The provider therefore properly refused the memorial services, and the dismissal stands with the family absorbing the outside expenses.
authorities: Part I-F Pre-Need Plans.md :: 3. Kinds of Plans; Pre-need Contract and Interpretation

section: 4. Registration/Disclosure; Consideration
stem: A planholder misses six months of installments after receiving only one notice, and the company cancels the plan. Decide whether the cancellation is valid.
answer:
The cancellation is invalid, so the company must treat the plan as merely lapsed and either accept reinstatement within the window or reimburse the late payments.
Under Sec. 23 of RA 9829, every contract carries a grace period of at least sixty days from the due date of the first unpaid installment, and nonpayment within that period renders the plan only lapsed. Under the same section, the planholder may reinstate within not less than two years from grace lapse, and no cancellation may be made inside that window. Under Sec. 23 paragraph 2, the company must give two written notices, one within thirty days after grace expiry and another within thirty days after reinstatement-period expiry warning of cancellation, and failure to give either notice precludes cancelled treatment. Under Sec. 23, payments made after grace must be reimbursed forthwith unless the planholder duly reinstates.
Here, six months of missed installments sits well inside the two-year reinstatement window that opened after the sixty-day grace lapsed. The single notice satisfies neither the two-notice rule nor the timing of the second notice, which can only follow the two-year expiry. That the planholder is deeply delinquent changes nothing because delinquency past grace produces lapsed status only and never cancelled status inside the window.
The company therefore cannot cancel yet, and it must accept a timely reinstatement or return the late payments.
authorities: Part I-F Pre-Need Plans.md :: 4. Registration/Disclosure; Consideration

section: 5. Termination (by Planholder; by Company)
stem: A pre-need company offers to buy out plans at 120 percent of termination value without Commission approval, and some planholders object. Decide whether the offer may proceed.
answer:
The buyout offer cannot proceed as to the objecting planholders without prior Commission approval, so the company must either secure that approval or limit any deal to consenting planholders within reserves and without prejudice to the rest.
Under Sec. 24 of RA 9829, a planholder may terminate at any time by written notice and collect the termination value from the schedule predetermined by the company actuary at registration and disclosed in the contract, which must be fair and equitable and Commission-compliant. Under the Sec. 24 regulatory backdrop, a company offer above termination value needs no prior Commission approval only where three conditions concur, namely consideration below the plan pre-need reserves and planholder acceptance and no prejudice to non-availing planholders. Under Sec. 30, reserves and trust assets answer solely to planholders and cannot fund prejudice to the remaining pool.
Here, the one hundred twenty percent of termination value exceeds the scheduled value, so the three-condition gate governs rather than the planholder termination right. The objections defeat the acceptance condition for the objectors and raise the non-prejudice condition for everyone else. That the premium looks generous changes nothing because generosity above reserves without clearance still raids the actuarial base that protects the remaining planholders. Below-reserves proof alone cannot cure a missing acceptance.
The offer therefore stalls as to objectors until the Commission approves it, and any consenting-only buyout must stay below reserves and leave non-availing planholders unprejudiced.
authorities: Part I-F Pre-Need Plans.md :: 5. Termination (by Planholder; by Company)

section: 6. Claims Settlement; Unfair Claims Settlement
stem: A matured education plan pays 60 days late without any fraud. State what the beneficiary collects.
answer:
The beneficiary of the matured education plan collects delay interest at twice the legal rate for the forty-five-day delay plus Sec. 28 litigation damages on a successful enforcement suit.
Under Sec. 26 paragraph 1 of RA 9829, scheduled benefit plans such as education plans pay immediately upon maturity, with installments or annuities as they fall due, and refusal or failure to pay within fifteen days from maturity entitles the beneficiary to interest at twice the legal rate for the delay unless the claim is fraudulent and the planholder complied with the documentary requirements. Under Sec. 28, the Commission determines in any enforcement litigation whether denial or withholding was unreasonable, and unreasonable delay draws actual damages plus attorney fees and legal interest from claim date to full satisfaction. Under Sec. 28, failure to pay within the Sec. 26 time is prima facie evidence of unreasonable delay.
Here, the education plan matured on a date fixed at purchase, which makes it a scheduled benefit plan under Sec. 4(q) rather than a contingent plan. The sixty-day payment delay with no fraud leaves forty-five compensable days from day sixteen to day sixty at twice the legal rate. That no fraud tainted the claim removes only the Sec. 26 fraud defense and never the delay price, while the missed fifteen-day clock supplies the prima facie unreasonableness case for Sec. 28 damages. Documentary compliance is assumed on the stated facts, so the interest entitlement stands.
The beneficiary therefore recovers twice-legal-interest for the delay period, and a court finding of unreasonableness adds actual damages with attorney fees and running legal interest.
authorities: Part I-F Pre-Need Plans.md :: 6. Claims Settlement; Unfair Claims Settlement

section: 7. Trust Fund; Regulation of Companies; Companies in Distress
stem: General creditors of an insolvent pre-need company seek to attach the trust fund. Decide whether attachment lies.
answer:
The attachment does not lie against the trust fund, so the general creditors are confined to the company non-fund assets while the fund answers exclusively to the planholders.
Under Sec. 30 paragraph 1 of RA 9829, each plan category carries a trust fund whose assets remain at all times for the sole benefit of the planholders and may never be diverted, and no part of the fund may satisfy other creditors of the company notwithstanding any contrary law. Under Sec. 30 paragraph 2, the fund is immune from attachment and garnishment and levy and seizure except for the planholder plan debt or criminal liability. Under Sec. 52, court insolvency proceedings reach company assets excluding the fund, and creditors have no personality in Commission fund proceedings. Under SEC v. Laigo (G.R. No. 188689, 2015), beneficial ownership of the fund lies in the planholders with legal title in the trustee and none in the company.
Here, the insolvent company creditors target the trust fund itself, which is the precise object of the statutory shield. That the company is insolvent changes nothing because Sec. 30 expressly extends the shield to insolvency and Sec. 52 removes the fund from the court insolvency estate. The creditors cannot recharacterize fund assets as company assets because Laigo places beneficial ownership in the planholders. Only trustee fees and trust taxes share the fund with planholders on distribution.
The attachment therefore fails, and the Commission may take custody of the fund to satisfy planholder obligations pro rata to termination values.
authorities: Part I-F Pre-Need Plans.md :: 7. Trust Fund; Regulation of Companies; Companies in Distress

section: 1. Definition; Parties; Elements; Perfection
stem: Wisconsin Transportation Co., Inc. (WTC) owned and operated an inter-island de luxe bus service plying the Manila-Batangas-Mindoro route. Three friends, namely: Aurelio, Jerome and Florencio rode on the same WTC bus from Manila bound for Mindoro. Aurelio purchased a ticket for himself. Jerome, being a boyhood friend of the bus driver, was allowed a free ride by agreeing to sit during the trip on a stool placed in the aisle. Florencio, already penniless after spending all of his money on beer the night before, just stole a ride in the bus by hiding in the on-board toilet of the bus. During the trip, the bus collided with another bus coming from the opposite direction. The three friends all suffered serious physical injuries. What are WTC's liabilities, if any, in favor of Aurelio, Jerome and Florencio? Explain your answer. (4%)
answer:
WTC answers as common carrier to Aurelio the ticketed passenger and to Jerome the free rider, while it owes Florencio the hidden stowaway no carrier duty and answers to him only on proved ordinary fault.
Under Art. 1732 of the Civil Code, a common carrier is one who offers carriage to the public for compensation, and the contract is perfected by consent once passage is accepted. Under Arts. 1755 and 1756, the carrier owes passengers the utmost diligence of a very cautious person, and injury raises the presumption of fault that yields only to proof of extraordinary diligence. Under British Airways v. Court of Appeals (G.R. No. 92288, 1993), acceptance of fare with confirmed carriage perfects the contract even before any ticket is issued. Under LRTA v. Navidad (G.R. No. 145804, 2003), that safety duty is nondelegable and runs over the whole carrier operation.
Here, Aurelio purchased a ticket and boarded the Manila to Mindoro bus, which perfected his passenger carriage. Jerome boarded with the permission of the bus driver and rode inside the vehicle on an aisle stool, so the carrier accepted him as a rider although he paid no separate fare. Florencio stole his ride by hiding in the on board toilet without the knowledge or acceptance of the carrier, so no meeting of minds ever bound him to WTC. Reading a driver allowed free ride as noncarriage would mistake liberality for lack of consent, while reading stealth boarding as carriage would dispense with the acceptance that perfection demands.
WTC therefore answers to Aurelio and Jerome under presumed fault unless it proves extraordinary diligence against the collision, while Florencio recovers only upon proof of ordinary negligence.
authorities: Part II-A Contract of Common Carriage.md :: 1. Definition; Parties; Elements; Perfection

section: 2. Common Carriers: Tests, Characteristics, Ancillary Business, Exclusions
stem: LMN, Inc. operates a beach resort in a secluded island off the coast of Puerto Princesa City, Palawan. It operates three (3) motorized boats to ferry its guests from the city proper to the island resort and vice-versa. During one rainy morning, the guests were informed that the ferry services for that day were cancelled due to a storm forecast. In order to appease the apparent dismay of most of the guests who will miss their flight back to Manila, the boat captain of one of LMN, Inc.'s motorized boats decided to push through with its trip back to the city. Shortly after the boat sailed, the storm hit and the winds and waves became stronger, causing engine trouble to the boat. Unfortunately, the boat capsized and sank, resulting in the death of one of the passengers, Mr. X. This prompted Mr. X's heirs to file a complaint for damages against LMN, Inc., which they alleged to be a common carrier. In its defense, LMN, Inc. maintained that it is not a common carrier because its boats are not available to the general public but only ferry resort guests and employees. (a) May LMN, Inc. be considered a common carrier? Explain. (3%) (b) Assuming LMN, Inc. is a common carrier, may it be absolved from liability on the ground of fortuitous event? Explain. (2%)
answer:
LMN Inc. is a common carrier of its resort guests, and it is not absolved from liability for the death of Mr. X because the storm it braved was forecasted and its fault concurred with the waves.
Under Art. 1732 of the Civil Code, anyone who offers carriage by water for compensation to the public is a common carrier, and neither an ancillary purpose nor a narrow clientele takes the operator out. Under Sps. Cruz v. Sun Holidays Inc. (G.R. No. 186312, 2010), a resort ferrying package tour guests without a separate boat charge is a common carrier because the package price carries the imputed fare. Under Arts. 1734 and 1735, a storm excuses only as a fortuitous event that was unforeseeable and unavoidable with no concurrent carrier fault, and death of a passenger otherwise raises the presumption of fault.
Here, LMN Inc. ferries whoever books its secluded island resort across by its three motorized boats, and the fare lives inside the resort package although no separate boat charge is collected. That the boats serve only resort guests and employees changes nothing because the character follows the nature held out and not the headcount served. The ferry services for that rainy morning had already been cancelled on a storm forecast, yet the boat captain pushed through with the trip back to the city to appease guests who feared missing their Manila flights. Sailing into a known storm is concurrent fault that keeps the waves from standing alone as fortuity.
LMN Inc. is therefore a common carrier that answers for the death of Mr. X under the presumption of fault, which a voluntary voyage into a forecasted storm cannot rebut.
authorities: Part II-A Contract of Common Carriage.md :: 2. Common Carriers: Tests, Characteristics, Ancillary Business, Exclusions

section: 3. Effect of Charter Party
stem: Onassis Shipping, Inc. (Onassis) operated passenger vessels and cargo trucks, and offered its services to the general public. In line with its vision and mission to protect the environment, Go-Green Asia (Go-Green), an NGO affiliated with Greenpeace, entered into a contract with Onassis whereby Go-Green would operate with its own crew the MN Dolphin, an ocean-going passenger vessel of Onassis. While on its way to Palawan carrying Go-Green's invited guests who were international and local observers desirous of checking certain environmental concerns in the area, the MN Dolphin encountered high waves and strong winds caused by a typhoon in the West Philippine Sea. The rough seas led to serious physical injuries to some of the guests. Discuss the liabilities of Onassis and Go-Green to the passengers of the M/V Dolphin. Explain briefly your answer. (3%)
answer:
Go Green answers as the carrier for the MN Dolphin voyage while Onassis keeps registered owner and franchise exposure, because the contract placed vessel crew and command in Go Green and made the charter a demise in substance.
Under the charter rule applied in Planters Products v. Court of Appeals (G.R. No. 101503, 1993), a time or voyage charter that leaves vessel crew and command with the owner keeps the owner common, while only a bareboat or demise charter that transfers possession and command makes the charterer the carrier. Under National Steel v. Court of Appeals (G.R. No. 112287, 1997), a vessel serving only select charterers without a public holding out is a private carrier governed by the charter and the Code of Commerce. Under Art. 1734 of the Civil Code, a typhoon excuses only where it stood alone without concurrent fault in braving known rough seas.
Here, Onassis offered passenger and cargo service to the general public, but it turned the MN Dolphin over to Go Green to operate with its own crew on the Palawan voyage. That transfer of manning and command marks a demise in substance even if the papers call it an operating contract, so Go Green became the carrier for the invited international and local observers aboard. The rough seas came from a typhoon in the West Philippine Sea, yet the voyage proceeded into high waves and strong winds, which raises the question of fault in sailing on that the fortuity defense must survive.
Go Green therefore carries the primary voyage liability to the injured guests unless it proves the typhoon alone caused the injuries despite due care, while Onassis remains reachable on registered ownership and its public franchise.
authorities: Part II-A Contract of Common Carriage.md :: 3. Effect of Charter Party

section: 4. Common vs Private Carrier; vs Towage, Arrastre, Stevedoring, Travel Agency
stem: To celebrate her 70th birthday, A hired F Travel & Tours to arrange and facilitate her booking, ticketing, and accommodation for a two-week foreign tour, which included visits to Italy and Greece, for the total amount of PHP 145,000.00. On Wednesday, August 14, 2024, B, an employee of F Travel & Tours, went to A's house to deliver the travel documents and plane ticket. She told A to be at the Ninoy Aquino International Airport (NAIA) on Saturday, August 17, 2024 two hours before her flight schedule. Without checking her travel documents, A went to NAIA on Saturday, August 17, 2024. When she got there, she was informed that the flight she was supposed to take had already left the previous day. A demanded that F Travel & Tours refund her payment. She claimed that F Travel & Tours did not observe the standard of care required of a common carrier when its employee, B, informed her of the wrong flight schedule. Is F Travel & Tours liable as a common carrier? Reason(s).
answer:
F Travel and Tours is not liable as a common carrier, although it may answer as an agent for the fault of its employee B in giving A the wrong flight date.
Under Art. 1732 of the Civil Code, only one who undertakes carriage of passengers or goods for compensation as a business offered to the public is a common carrier. Under Unsworth Transport v. Court of Appeals (G.R. No. 166250, 2010), a forwarder that merely arranges transport answers for its own negligence only, and it binds itself as carrier only when it undertakes delivery or issues its own bill of lading. The extraordinary diligence of Art. 1733 and the presumed fault of Arts. 1735 and 1756 therefore follow the carriage undertaking and never the arranging work.
Here, A hired F Travel and Tours to arrange and facilitate booking ticketing and accommodation for a two week Italy and Greece tour for PHP 145000, and no route was ever operated by F itself. Employee B went to the house of A to deliver the travel documents and plane ticket and told her to be at NAIA on Saturday August 17 2024, while the flight had already left the previous day. That mistaken advice is agency fault in the arranging task and not carrier breach, because F never held itself out as transporting the public over any route. Treating a booking error as carrier breach would attach the presumed fault rule to work the rule was never written for.
F Travel and Tours therefore escapes carrier liability, and A recovers if at all by proving the agency fault behind the wrong date advice with the refund as the operative relief.
authorities: Part II-A Contract of Common Carriage.md :: 4. Common vs Private Carrier; vs Towage, Arrastre, Stevedoring, Travel Agency

section: 5. Tramp vs Line Service; Governing Laws; Nature of Business
stem: A liner keeps a fixed Manila-Cebu schedule for whoever books, while a tramp takes whatever bulk cargo offers under voyage charters to chosen charterers. A shipper asks which vessel answers as a common carrier if its cargo is lost. How do you advise?
answer:
The liner answers as the common carrier while the tramp on these facts answers as a private carrier, so the shipper sues the liner under presumed fault and sues the tramp on proved fault.
Under Art. 1732 of the Civil Code, the decisive test is whether carriage for pay is held out to the public as a business, with regularity purpose means and clientele all immaterial. Under National Steel v. Court of Appeals (G.R. No. 112287, 1997), a vessel serving only select charterers without a public holding out is a private carrier governed by the charter and the Code of Commerce. Under Planters Products v. Court of Appeals (G.R. No. 101503, 1993), owner retention of vessel crew and command keeps the common character, while only a demise transfer changes it.
Here, the liner keeps a fixed Manila Cebu schedule open to whoever books, which is a public holding out for pay that meets Art. 1732 without further proof. The tramp takes whatever bulk cargo offers under voyage charters to chosen charterers by special contract without a public offer, which places it under charter and Code of Commerce rules with willful negligence to be proved. Reading the timetable alone as decisive would mistake evidence for the test, because schedules only evidence and never replace the holding out inquiry.
The shipper therefore holds the liner to extraordinary diligence with fault presumed from loss, while against the tramp the shipper carries the burden of proving the charter breach or negligence that caused the loss.

section: 6. Registered Owner Rule and Kabit System; Boundary System
stem: A bus is sold but the sale is never registered, and the buyer ties the unit to the seller franchise under a kabit arrangement with the driver on boundary. A passenger is hurt when the bus collides with a truck. From whom may the passenger recover?
answer:
The injured passenger may recover from the registered franchise holder, who cannot hide behind the unregistered sale the kabit tie up or the boundary arrangement.
Under the registered owner doctrine applied under C.A. No. 146, the owner on record answers to third persons for vehicles operated under his franchise even where beneficial ownership has passed or the transfer was never registered. Under that same policy, a kabit tie up is void between the operators yet the franchise holder still answers the victim, because the pari delicto bar runs only between the wrongdoers and never against the injured third person. Under LRTA v. Navidad (G.R. No. 145804, 2003), the carrier safety duty is nondelegable, and a boundary remittance that leaves routes schedules and discipline with the operator keeps the driver and conductor within employment.
Here, the bus was sold yet the sale stayed off the registry, so the seller on record remains the public face of operation that the passenger properly sues. The buyer tied the unit to the seller franchise without transfer or approval, and that illegal pact binds no victim although it voids the operators recourse against each other. The driver ran on a fixed daily boundary and kept the excess, yet the operator kept control of the service, so the driver fault in the collision with the truck is the operator fault for which the carrier presumption provisionally answers.
The passenger therefore recovers from the registered franchise holder, with reimbursement and employment blame to be sorted between the operators and crew afterward.
authorities: Part II-A Contract of Common Carriage.md :: 6. Registered Owner Rule and Kabit System; Boundary System

section: 7. Formalities: Bill of Lading
stem: A carrier issues a clean bill of lading for bagged fertilizer in apparent good order, and the consignee receives short and hardened bags at discharge. The carrier points to a printed clause exempting it from all liability for any loss. Is the bill conclusive and is the clause valid?
answer:
The clean bill makes a prima facie case of carrier fault for the shortage and deterioration, and the printed clause exempting the carrier from all liability is void so the carrier answers unless it proves an excepted cause with extraordinary care.
Under Art. 350 of the Code of Commerce, the bill of lading admits receipt of the goods as described and embodies the voyage terms, and a clean bill acknowledges apparent good order at loading. Under Art. 1735 of the Civil Code, good order receipt followed by short or bad order delivery raises prima facie carrier fault. Under Westwind Shipping v. UCPB General Insurance (G.R. No. 200289, 2013), that sequence lays the prima facie case on the carrier with reimbursement against the actual wrongdoer preserved. Under Art. 1745 of the Civil Code, stipulations that erase carrier responsibility or cut diligence below extraordinary fall as contrary to public policy.
Here, the carrier issued a clean bill for bagged fertilizer in apparent good order, and the consignee received short and hardened bags at discharge, which completes the prima facie sequence. The printed total exemption asks less than the diligence the law commands, so it contributes nothing to the defense although the shipper accepted the adhesion bill. Reading acceptance of a preprinted bill as consent to total exemption would enforce the very stipulation Art. 1745 voids.
The carrier therefore answers for the shortage and deterioration unless it proves one of the excepted causes with extraordinary care, with the clean bill fixing the case the carrier must defeat.
authorities: Part II-A Contract of Common Carriage.md :: 7. Formalities: Bill of Lading

section: 1. Duty to Accept Goods; Grounds for Refusal; Animals
stem: A shipper tenders drums of nitric acid in brittle crates for a Friday sailing, plus fighting cocks in flimsy coops. The carrier refuses both. A second shipper tenders bagged fertilizer in sound sacks for the same sailing and is also refused for lack of space though room can be made. Which refusals stand?
answer:
Both refusals of the acid drums and the fighting cocks stand, while the refusal of the bagged fertilizer fails and exposes the carrier to damages for refusal to carry.
Under Art. 1732 of the Civil Code, a common carrier that holds itself out to the public must accept all goods duly tendered within its route and means, and it may refuse only on lawful ground such as danger, illegality, unfitness, or want of capacity or route. Under Art. 1734 of the Civil Code, the character of the goods and defects in packing count among the causes that excuse the carrier, and concealment of danger is the fault of the shipper. The private carrier under special contract, such as the time-chartered vessel serving select charterers in National Steel Corporation v. Court of Appeals (G.R. No. 112287, 1997), takes only what its contract names, while the common carrier takes all fit and lawful tender.
Here, the shipper tendered drums of nitric acid in brittle crates for the Friday sailing with fighting cocks in flimsy coops, and both tenders were unfit because the acid threatened the voyage without disclosure and safeguards and the coops could not contain live carriage. The second shipper tendered bagged fertilizer in sound sacks for the same sailing within the advertised run, and the carrier refused only for lack of space though room could be made. Tight space from ordinary demand is inconvenience rather than want of means, so the fertilizer tender was due tender and the acid and bird tenders were not until disclosure, safeguards, and fit containers cured them.
The carrier therefore keeps its refusal of the acid drums and the fighting cocks until proper tender is made, and it answers in damages for refusing the bagged fertilizer that it was bound to accept.

section: 2. Timely Delivery; Place of Delivery; To Whom Delivered
stem: A consignee lost the original bills and presents certified copies, then signs delivery receipts for each lot through his clerks. Months later the shipper sues the carrier for non-delivery, blaming the missing originals. Is the carrier discharged?
answer:
The carrier is discharged from the non-delivery claim, because signed delivery receipts by the entitled recipient produce the same discharging effect as return of the original bills.
Under Art. 1736 of the Civil Code, extraordinary responsibility lasts from unconditional receipt until delivery actually or constructively to the consignee or to the person with the right to receive them. Under Art. 353 of the Code of Commerce, discharge follows surrender of the bill or equivalent acknowledgment of delivery by the entitled person. In Republic v. Lorenzo Shipping Corporation (G.R. No. 153563, 2005), the Court discharged the carrier that demanded the bills, followed standard procedure, and took signed receipts from the entitled recipient though the originals were never surrendered.
Here, the consignee lost the original bills and presented certified copies, then signed delivery receipts for each lot through his clerks upon turnover. The agents demanded the bills and documented each delivery, which proves the extraordinary diligence that rebuts the fault presumption. The shipper blames the missing originals months later yet left its own supervisor unpursued until resignation, so it cannot pass to the carrier what may have been its own employee faithlessness.
The non-delivery claim therefore fails, and the carrier keeps no liability for the lots duly covered by the signed receipts.

section: 2. Timely Delivery; Place of Delivery; To Whom Delivered
stem: Hari and Reyna booked a honeymoon package at Anya Resort (AR) in Palawan which included transportation from Batangas to Palawan, and vice versa, via M/B Prinsesa owned and operated by AR. Despite PAGASA storm warning bulletins, M/B Prinsesa proceeded to ferry Hari and Reyna from the port of Batangas to Palawan. While in open seas, the boat was hit by big waves and eventually capsized, drowning Hari and Reyna. When sued by the heirs of the couple, AR denied liability on the ground that it is not a common carrier, as M/B Prinsesa is not available to the general public or other tourists, and exclusively ferries resort guests and crew members. AR further argued that they did not charge Hari and Reyna separate fees to board M/B Prinsesa. Are the arguments of AR correct? Discuss your answer.
answer:
The arguments of Anya Resort are incorrect. The resort boat is a common carrier, the imputed fare binds the package, and sailing into the published storm breached utmost diligence, so the resort answers for the deaths.
Under Art. 1732 of the Civil Code, a person that carries guests by water for compensation as part of its regular resort undertaking offers carriage to whoever books the resort, and narrow clientele does not make the service private. Under Arts. 1755 and 1756 of the Civil Code, the carrier owes the utmost diligence of very cautious persons with due regard for all the circumstances, and death of a passenger presumes fault unless extraordinary diligence is proved. In Sps. Cruz v. Sun Holidays (G.R. No. 186312, 2010), the Court treated an ancillary resort ferry with imputed fare as common carriage.
Here, Hari and Reyna booked a honeymoon package at Anya Resort that included transportation from Batangas to Palawan and back via M/B Prinsesa owned and operated by the resort, so the boat fare lived inside the package price though no separate boarding fee was charged. PAGASA storm warning bulletins preceded the sailing, yet M/B Prinsesa proceeded from Batangas, and big waves in open seas capsized the boat and drowned the couple. Braving a forecasted storm is human fault concurrent with the waves, which defeats the fortuity claim and cannot supply the extraordinary diligence needed to rebut the presumption.
The resort therefore answers as a common carrier for the deaths of Hari and Reyna, and neither the closed clientele nor the absence of a separate fare excuses the voluntary voyage into a known peril.

section: 4. Extraordinary Diligence: Rationale, Meaning, Presumption, Duration, and Stipulations
stem: Ysidro, a paying passenger, was on board Bus No. 904 owned and operated by Yatco Transportation Company (Yatco). He boarded the bus at Munoz, Nueva Ecija with Manila as his final destination. He was seated on the first row, window seat on the left side of the bus. As the bus was negotiating the national highway in front of the public market of Gerona, Tarlac, the bus came to a full stop because of the traffic. The driver of the bus took this opportunity to check on the tires of the bus and to relieve himself. As he was alighting from the bus to do these, an unidentified man standing along the highway hurled a huge rock at the left side of the bus and hit Ysidro between his eyes. He lost consciousness and immediately the driver, with the conductor, drove the bus to bring him to the nearest hospital. He expired before the bus could reach the hospital. Ysidro's wife and children brought a civil action to collect damages from Yatco, alleging that as a common carrier, it was required to exercise extraordinary diligence in ensuring the safety of its passengers. They contended that, in case of injuries and/or death on the part of any of its passengers, the common carrier is presumed to be at fault. In its defense, Yatco alleged that it is not an absolute insurer of its passengers and that Ysidro's death was not due to any defect in the means of transport or method of transporting passengers, or the negligent acts of its employees. Since the accident was due to the fault of a stranger over whom the common carrier had no control, or of which it did not have any prior knowledge to be able to prevent it, the cause of Ysidro's death should be considered a fortuitous event and not the liability of the common carrier. (a) Is a common carrier presumed to be at fault whenever there is death or injury to its passengers, regardless of the cause of death or injury? (2.5%) (b) What kind of diligence is required of common carriers like Yatco for the protection of its passengers? (2.5%) (c) Will your answer be the same as your answer in (b) above, if the assailant was another paying passenger who boarded the bus and deliberately stabbed Ysidro to death? (2.5%)
answer:
(a) Yes, the carrier is presumed at fault upon death or injury of a passenger. (b) It owes the utmost diligence of very cautious persons with due regard for all the circumstances. (c) The same test governs a fellow-passenger stabbing, since liability turns on what diligence could have prevented.
Under Art. 1756 of the Civil Code, death of or injury to a passenger presumes the carrier at fault unless it proves the extraordinary diligence of Arts. 1733 and 1755. Under Art. 1755, the carrier must carry passengers safely as far as human care and foresight can provide using the utmost diligence of very cautious persons. Under Art. 1759, the carrier answers for assaults by strangers and fellow passengers only where good-family diligence could have prevented or stopped the attack, so it is no absolute insurer. In LRTA v. Navidad (G.R. No. 145804, 2003), the Court held the safety duty non-delegable and measured it by utmost diligence.
Here, Ysidro was a paying passenger of Yatco aboard Bus No. 904 from Munoz, Nueva Ecija to Manila when the bus stopped in traffic before the Gerona, Tarlac market. The driver had alighted to check tires and relieve himself when an unidentified man hurled a huge rock through the left window and struck Ysidro between the eyes, and the crew drove him toward the hospital where he expired on the way. The presumption therefore applies on every limb, and Yatco must prove precautions rather than point to sound tires or to the stranger hand. The fellow-passenger stabbing is judged the same way, since the carrier answers only where its crew could have prevented or stopped the assault.
Yatco therefore carries the burden on all three limbs and escapes only by proving that utmost diligence could neither have foreseen nor stopped the fatal attack.
authorities: Part II-B Obligations of the Parties.md :: 4. Extraordinary Diligence: Rationale, Meaning, Presumption, Duration, and Stipulations

section: 5. Extraordinary Diligence by Sea
stem: Nautica Shipping Lines (Nautica) bought a second hand passenger ship from Japan. It modified the design of the bulkhead of the deck of the ship to accommodate more passengers. The ship sunk with its passengers in Tablas Strait due to heavy rains brought by the monsoon. The heirs of the passengers sued Nautica for its liability as a common carrier based on the reconfiguration of the bulkhead which may have compromised the stability of the ship. Nautica raised the defense that the monsoon is a fortuitous event and, at most, its liability is prescribed by the Limited Liability Rule. Decide with reasons. (5%)
answer:
Nautica answers as a common carrier for the deaths, and it keeps neither the fortuitous-event defense nor the limited-liability cap on these facts.
Under Art. 1734 of the Civil Code, flood, storm, and like calamity excuse only when the carrier proves the excepted cause stood alone and that it observed extraordinary diligence. Under the seaworthiness rule applied in Philippine American General Insurance Co. v. Court of Appeals (G.R. No. 116940, 1997), unfit hull conditions presume unseaworthiness, and ordinary voyage vicissitudes never excuse a ship that sailed unfit. Under Art. 587 of the Code of Commerce, abandonment of vessel and freight caps only the blameless owner whose captain alone was at fault, never the owner whose own negligence concurred.
Here, Nautica bought a second-hand passenger ship from Japan and modified the bulkhead design of the deck to accommodate more passengers, and the ship sank with its passengers in Tablas Strait during heavy monsoon rains. The bulkhead reconfiguration that may have compromised stability puts sailing fitness in issue, and ordinary monsoon rains are voyage vicissitudes rather than an irresistible calamity standing alone. Sailing a possibly unstable rebuilt ship with passengers aboard proves the opposite of the diligence the law demands, so the storm defense fails at its first element.
Nautica therefore pays in full under the Civil Code without the Art. 587 cap, because the owner fault that concurred in the casualty defeats both fortuity and limitation.

section: 5. Extraordinary Diligence by Sea
stem: A railroad track of the Philippine National Railway (PNR) is located near a busy intersection of Puyat Avenue and Osmeña Highway. One afternoon, the intersection was heavily congested, as usual. Juan, the driver of a public utility jeepney (PUJ), drove onto the railroad tracks but could go no farther because of the heavy traffic at the intersection. After the jeepney stopped right on the railroad track, it was hit and overturned by a PNR train, resulting in the death of Kim, a passenger of the PUJ, and injuries to Juan and his other passengers. Juan, the injured passengers and Kim's family sued the PNR for damages for its negligence. It was established that the steel pole barrier before the track was broken, and that the PNR had the last clear chance of avoiding the accident. On the other hand, the PNR raised the defense that the track is for the exclusive use of the train and that motorists are aware that it is negligence per se to stop their vehicles on the tracks. Decide the case and explain. (5%)
answer:
The PNR answers to the family of Kim and to the injured passengers, though Juan personal recovery suffers his own contributory fault, because the broken barrier and the last clear chance keep the operator liable while driver fault never travels to the riders.
Under Art. 1756 of the Civil Code, death of or injury to passengers presumes the carrier at fault unless it proves the extraordinary diligence of Arts. 1733 and 1755. Under the crossing-diligence rule, the rail operator must keep bells, lights, barriers, and watchmen working at known congested crossings, and the train with the final opportunity to stop must use it. In LRTA v. Navidad (G.R. No. 145804, 2003), the Court measured train and station safety by utmost diligence and held the duty non-delegable. Driver negligence is never imputed to the riding passenger, so the passenger claim survives though the jeepney driver shared blame.
Here, the PNR track lay near the busy intersection of Puyat Avenue and Osmena Highway where congestion was usual, and Juan drove his public utility jeepney onto the rails but could go no farther because of heavy traffic. The jeepney stopped on the track and the PNR train hit and overturned it, killing passenger Kim and injuring Juan and the other passengers. The steel pole barrier before the track was broken, and the PNR had the last clear chance of avoiding the accident. The exclusive-track argument cannot excuse a broken warning device at a known choke point, and Juan breached his own motorist duty by entering rails he could not clear.
Kim family and the riding passengers therefore recover in full from the PNR, while Juan personal claim is reduced by his contributory fault under the last-clear-chance sorting.
authorities: Part II-B Obligations of the Parties.md :: 5. Extraordinary Diligence by Sea

section: 5. Extraordinary Diligence by Sea
stem: A bus company hires an unlicensed driver without road test, skips brake inspection for a month, and the bus with worn pads rams a truck. The company blames the truck driver. Who answers the injured bus passengers?
answer:
The bus company answers the injured passengers in full, since its own want of diligence keeps the presumption unrebutted regardless of what the truck driver did.
Under Art. 1756 of the Civil Code, injury to passengers presumes the carrier at fault unless it proves the extraordinary diligence of Arts. 1733 and 1755. Under that diligence, the operator must hire licensed and tested drivers, supervise them in service, and inspect brakes and gear before and during the run. In LRTA v. Navidad (G.R. No. 145804, 2003), the Court held carrier safety duty non-delegable and measured crew and equipment fitness by utmost diligence.
Here, the company hired an unlicensed driver without road test and skipped brake inspection for a month, and the bus with worn pads rammed a truck. Hiring without license or test breaches selection diligence and running a month without brake checks breaches inspection diligence, so no concrete precaution rebuts the presumption. The truck fault, if proved, divides the ultimate loss between the operators through contribution, yet division never delays or defeats the passenger recovery.
The passengers therefore collect from their carrier upon the presumption, and the company pursues the truck operator separately for its share.
authorities: Part II-B Obligations of the Parties.md :: 5. Extraordinary Diligence by Sea

section: 7. Passenger Baggage
stem: A tagged suitcase checked into the hold vanishes before arrival, while a laptop kept in the overhead bin is snatched when the passenger leaves it to use the lavatory. What must each claimant prove?
answer:
The suitcase claimant recovers on proof of turnover with loss at arrival, while the laptop claimant recovers only on proof of carrier fault, because custody fixes the burden for each piece.
Under Art. 1733 of the Civil Code, extraordinary diligence governs goods in carrier custody, and loss outside the five Art. 1734 causes presumes fault unless extraordinary diligence is proved. Under the baggage rule, a tagged piece handed to the carrier for the hold rides under the goods rules, while a hand-carried piece kept by the passenger stays under proved-fault rules. In Regional Container Lines of Singapore v. The Netherlands Insurance Co. (Phils.), Inc. (G.R. No. 168151, 2009), the Court kept custody and the fault presumption alive through unloading and required proof of diligence rather than mere pointing at another handler.
Here, the tagged suitcase was checked into the hold and vanished before arrival, so it rode in carrier custody and its disappearance raises the presumption unless the carrier proves an Art. 1734 excuse or extraordinary diligence. The laptop stayed in the overhead bin in passenger custody, and the passenger left it to use the lavatory before the snatching, so no presumption runs and the passenger must show the loss came through employee fault or want of due precautions.
The first claim therefore succeeds on custody and loss alone unless rebutted, while the second needs specific carrier fault proved against the operator.
authorities: Part II-B Obligations of the Parties.md :: 7. Passenger Baggage

section: 8. Obligations of the Passenger and Shipper
stem: A shipper declares general merchandise but hides drums of calcium carbide that explode on contact with seawater, damaging fellow cargo. He then refuses freight, claiming the carrier failed to deliver. Who pays for the damage and the freight?
answer:
The shipper answers for the explosion damage to fellow cargo and still owes the freight, because concealment caused the casualty while the carriage was duly performed.
Under Art. 1734 of the Civil Code, the act or omission of the shipper excuses the carrier, and undisclosed dangerous character is shipper fault that breaks the carrier chain. Under the freight and lien rules of the contract and the Code of Commerce, the price of carriage is earned by receiving, stowing, and sailing the goods with the diligence the known facts demanded, and unpaid charges hold a lien on goods in carrier hands. In Planters Products v. Court of Appeals (G.R. No. 101503, 1993), the Court gave effect to agreed handling allocations between ship and shore and defeated claims laid outside the allocation.
Here, the shipper declared general merchandise but hid drums of calcium carbide that explode on contact with seawater, and the explosion damaged fellow cargo on the voyage. The carrier stowed and sailed on the declared character without the safeguards disclosure would have triggered, so the concealed danger caused the casualty rather than any want of carrier diligence. Refusal to pay freight has no basis in a failed-delivery claim where the carrier performed its part and the shipper caused the loss.
The shipper therefore pays the explosion damage with recourse from him by the fellow cargo owners, and the carrier keeps its lien on surviving goods for the unpaid freight.

section: 8. Obligations of the Passenger and Shipper
stem: A passenger boards without a visa for the destination state and is refused onward carriage at the transit stop. He demands a full refund and damages for delay. Does he collect?
answer:
The passenger collects no damages for the refusal, though the tariff decides any refund for the unflown portion, because travel papers are his own duty and want of them lawfully excuses onward carriage.
Under Art. 1761 of the Civil Code, the passenger must observe the diligence of a good father of a family to avoid injury to himself, which includes carrying the passports, visas, and health papers the destination requires and obeying lawful crew orders. Under the ticket and contract terms of passage, as in British Airways v. Court of Appeals (G.R. No. 92288, 1993) where confirmed booking with paid fare perfected the terms of carriage, the carrier may refuse carriage without required documents and without breach. Delay flowing from that lawful refusal is the passenger own making rather than carrier fault.
Here, the passenger boarded without a visa for the destination state and was refused onward carriage at the transit stop under immigration and contract rules. The carrier performed the flown legs and stopped only where the law required it to stop, so no delay damages run. The demand for full refund plus delay damages mistakes a self-caused interruption for a carrier breach.
The carrier therefore keeps the flown legs earned and refunds only what its tariff promises for the unflown portion, with no damages for the interrupted journey.

section: 1. Kinds of Defenses; Proximate Causation
stem: LMN, Inc. operates a beach resort in a secluded island off the coast of Puerto Princesa City, Palawan. It operates three (3) motorized boats to ferry its guests from the city proper to the island resort and vice-versa. During one rainy morning, the guests were informed that the ferry services for that day were cancelled due to a storm forecast. In order to appease the apparent dismay of most of the guests who will miss their flight back to Manila, the boat captain of one of LMN, Inc.'s motorized boats decided to push through with its trip back to the city. Shortly after the boat sailed, the storm hit and the winds and waves became stronger, causing engine trouble to the boat. Unfortunately, the boat capsized and sank, resulting in the death of one of the passengers, Mr. X. This prompted Mr. X's heirs to file a complaint for damages against LMN, Inc., which they alleged to be a common carrier. In its defense, LMN, Inc. maintained that it is not a common carrier because its boats are not available to the general public but only ferry resort guests and employees. (a) May LMN, Inc. be considered a common carrier? Explain. (3%) (b) Assuming LMN, Inc. is a common carrier, may it be absolved from liability on the ground of fortuitous event? Explain. (2%)
answer:
Yes, LMN, Inc. is a common carrier, but it is not absolved because its voluntary sailing into a forecasted storm concurs with the waves and defeats fortuity.
Under Art. 1732 of the Civil Code, one who offers carriage by water to the public for compensation is a common carrier, and an ancillary resort ferry with an imputed fare inside the package price satisfies the test even for a narrow clientele as Sps. Cruz v. Sun Holidays (G.R. No. 186312, 2010) holds. Under Art. 1739 of the Civil Code, a natural disaster excuses only where it stood as the proximate and only cause with due diligence before and during and after the occurrence, and eleven-mile winds meeting a cracked lighter prove unseaworthiness rather than calamity under Compañia Maritima v. Insurance Company of North America (G.R. No. L-18965, 1964).
Here, LMN operated three motorized boats that ferried guests between the city proper and its island resort with the fare carried inside the package price. The trips for that rainy morning stood cancelled because of a storm forecast, yet the captain pushed through with the return trip to appease guests who would miss their Manila flights. Shortly after sailing the forecasted storm struck with stronger winds and waves, the boat developed engine trouble mid-voyage, and it capsized and sank with the death of Mr. X. Reading narrow clientele as private carriage mistakes headcount for holding out, while reading a forecasted blow met by voluntary sailing as fortuity ignores the concurring fault that breaks the proximate and only cause.
LMN therefore answers as a common carrier under the Art. 1756 presumption of fault for the death of Mr. X, and the fortuity defense fails, so the heirs recover unless LMN proves utmost diligence no voyage into a forecasted storm can supply.

section: 2. Defenses in Carriage of Goods in Their Exclusivity and in Carriage of Passengers
stem: A vessel loses bagged coffee to warehouse rats during a tariff stop while a passenger on the same voyage is hurt by a falling hatch cover. The carrier pleads unlisted vermin for the coffee and talks of open rebuttal for the passenger. Which plea follows the correct structure?
answer:
The carrier likely pays for the coffee lost to vermin while it keeps a fighting chance on the passenger fall, because rats fit no closed goods excuse and the hatch injury turns on utmost diligence.
Under Art. 1734 of the Civil Code, the carrier answers for goods loss unless it fits one of the five exclusive causes, and unlisted vermin or pilferage triggers the Art. 1735 presumption of fault that yields only to proof of extraordinary diligence. Under Art. 1756 of the Civil Code, death or injury of a passenger is presumed to be carrier fault, yet the passenger carrier may rebut with any convincing proof of the utmost diligence of Arts. 1733 and 1755. Under Planters Products v. Court of Appeals (G.R. No. 101503, 1993), the goods carrier escapes only by proving an actual listed cause with extraordinary care over the cargo.
Here, the vessel lost bagged coffee to warehouse rats during a tariff stop, which names no flood or storm or public enemy or shipper act or goods character or authority order and therefore leaves the Art. 1735 presumption standing. The same voyage hurt a passenger with a falling hatch cover, which is open rebuttal territory where inspection records and maintenance logs can show the utmost care. Reading vermin as goods character mistakes a preventable custody failure for inherent vice, while reading every falling object as automatic liability mistakes a rebuttable presumption for absolute insurance.
The carrier therefore answers for the coffee unless it proves extraordinary diligence over the stored bags, while it defeats the passenger claim where it proves utmost diligence over the hatch, so the coffee claim likely succeeds and the fall turns on the maintenance proof.
