section: 3. Fortuitous Event with Carrier Participation, Rationale, Fire, Storm, Hijacking, Mechanical Defects, Tire Blowouts, and Other Invalid Defenses
stem: A warehouse holding consigned sugar burns from an unknown origin at night while a bus with bald tires blows one on the highway and topples. The warehouseman pleads fire and the bus line pleads blowout. Which plea has a path and what must each prove?
answer:
The warehouseman keeps a narrow path on the fire where it proves extraordinary diligence, while the bus line keeps almost none on the blowout because bald treads prove want of roadworthiness.
Under Art. 1735 of the Civil Code, loss outside the five Art. 1734 causes is presumed to be carrier fault, and fire appears in none of those causes, so the carrier must prove extraordinary diligence with the origin and spread of the fire fully accounted for. Under Art. 1739 of the Civil Code, a calamity excuses only as the proximate and only cause with diligence before and during and after, and carrier-side unfitness concurring with the event keeps liability alive. Under Compañia Maritima v. Insurance Company of North America (G.R. No. L-18965, 1964), a cracked hull meeting ordinary winds proves unseaworthiness rather than fortuity.
Here, the warehouse holding consigned sugar burned from an unknown origin at night, so the warehouseman carrier must show watchmen and wiring and extinguishers and segregation of the stored sugar. The bus ran on bald treads with skipped inspection, blew one tire on the highway, and toppled, so the blowout grew out of want of roadworthiness rather than out of an extraneous road hazard. Reading an unaccounted fire as automatic fortuity ignores the unlisted-cause rule, while reading a blowout on worn treads as calamity mistakes carrier-side unfitness for an inevitable event.
The sugar claim therefore turns on whether the warehouseman proves extraordinary diligence over custody, while the bus claim fails on the treads alone, so the bus line answers under the presumption and the sugar carrier survives only on full diligence proof.

section: 3. Fortuitous Event with Carrier Participation, Rationale, Fire, Storm, Hijacking, Mechanical Defects, Tire Blowouts, and Other Invalid Defenses
stem: Scrap iron rides a carrier lighter when an acting mayor with armed men orders the crew to dump it into the sea as part of a shakedown of the shipper. The carrier obeys and pleads competent authority. Does the excuse stand?
answer:
No, the excuse fails, because a shakedown order from an acting mayor without power over the goods is no competent authority and obedience to it is carrier fault.
Under Art. 1743 of the Civil Code, seizure or destruction by order excuses only where the public authority had power to issue the order. Under Ganzon v. Court of Appeals (G.R. No. L-48757, 1988), the carrier must prove official power with a lawful order issued under legal process, and an acting mayor with armed men pressing a money demand over goods the town never owned supplies none of the three. The same decision bars switching from authority below to fortuity on appeal.
Here, scrap iron rode a carrier lighter when an acting mayor with armed men ordered the crew to dump it into the sea as part of a shakedown of the shipper. The mayor held no power over the scrap, the order carried no lawful process, and the scraps could have been unloaded ashore and delivered after the dispute instead of dumped. Reading obedience to armed coercion as obedience to law confuses submission with authority, while reading difficulty in the dispute as fortuity ignores that possible performance with unloading ashore defeats impossibility.
The line therefore answers under the Art. 1735 presumption with no diligence proved, and it bears the actual with exemplary exposure that Ganzon imposes, so the authority defense fails and the carrier pays for the dumped scrap.

section: 3. Fortuitous Event with Carrier Participation, Rationale, Fire, Storm, Hijacking, Mechanical Defects, Tire Blowouts, and Other Invalid Defenses
stem: Bulk urea sails in sealed holds with intact seals and arrives short with part contaminated by sand after eleven days of rainy unloading by consignee labor under free-in-and-out terms. The consignee sues for shortage and pollution. Who bears the loss?
answer:
The consignee bears the loss, because inherent urea solubility with shipper-side unloading under free-in-and-out terms caused the shortage despite a diligent voyage.
Under Art. 1734 of the Civil Code, the character of the goods excuses the carrier where the inherent vice truly caused the loss. Under Art. 1742 of the Civil Code, even where goods character caused the loss, the carrier must still exercise due diligence to forestall or lessen it. Under Planters Products v. Court of Appeals (G.R. No. 101503, 1993), sealed hatches with intact seals and clean holds prove the extraordinary care the voyage demanded, and loss in consignee-side unloading under free-in-and-out terms stays a shipper-side risk.
Here, bulk urea sailed in sealed holds with intact seals, arrived short with part polluted by sand, and spent eleven days in rainy unloading handled by consignee labor under free-in-and-out terms. The sealed voyage shows the forestalling care, while the rainy open-air handling with sandy hauling sits inside the cargo interests stevedoring rather than inside carrier custody. Reading soluble cargo handled in rain by the consignee as carrier fault mistakes agreed allocation for breach, while reading shortage alone as breach ignores the proven inherent vice.
The Art. 1735 presumption therefore stands rebutted and the claim fails, so the consignee absorbs the shortage and the pollution that its own unloading produced.

section: 5. Defenses in Carriage of Passengers; Acts of Employees, of Other Passengers and Third Persons, and of Shipper or Passenger
stem: A conductor pockets a sleeping passenger watch while a stranger at a traffic stop hurls a rock through the window and blinds another rider. The line pleads stranger fortuity for both losses. How does liability divide?
answer:
The line pays for the pocketed watch as of course, while the rock blinding turns on whether good-family crew vigilance could have prevented or stopped the attack.
Under Art. 1759 of the Civil Code, the carrier answers for the negligence and wilful acts of its employees though they acted beyond scope or against orders, and diligence in selection and supervision is no defense. Under Art. 1760 of the Civil Code, that employee responsibility cannot be eliminated or limited by stipulation or ticket statement. Under Art. 1763 of the Civil Code, the carrier answers for injuries from fellow passengers or strangers only where its employees through the diligence of a good father of a family could have prevented or stopped the act. Under LRTA v. Navidad (G.R. No. 145804, 2003), the safety duty behind these articles is non-delegable from fare payment with entry.
Here, a conductor pocketed a sleeping passenger watch, which is a wilful employee act inside Art. 1759 though done against orders, so no hiring care or ticket term escapes it. A stranger at a traffic stop hurled a rock through the window and blinded another rider, which is stranger harm inside Art. 1763 where closed windows and guards and route care decide the outcome. Reading the theft as outside scope mistakes the very channel Art. 1759 closes, while reading every thrown rock as automatic liability mistakes preventability for insurance.
Theft therefore pays as of course with no diligence defense available, while the blinding pays only where the prevention proof fails, so the line answers for the watch and reaches the merits on the rock.

section: 6. Notice of Claim and Prescription in Overland and Coastwise Shipping, in International Carriage by Sea, and in Subrogation
stem: A consignee receives crates by truck with intact exteriors, opens them after three days to find water damage, and complains on the fifth day. A second consignee receives container cargo by foreign vessel, joins the survey at receipt, then sues ten months after discharge. Which claims live?
answer:
The truck claim dies on late notice under Art. 366, while the vessel claim reaches the merits because joint survey excused the writing and suit came inside the one-year period.
Under Art. 366 of the Code of Commerce, concealed damage found on opening must be claimed within twenty-four hours from receipt, apparent damage at receipt itself, and lapse of the period or payment of freight without protest bars the condition claim. Under New Zealand Insurance Co. v. Choa Joy (G.R. No. L-7311, 1955), Art. 366 applies only where goods were actually received, so total non-delivery needs no such notice. Under Sec. 3(6) of COGSA, concealed sea loss needs written notice within three days from delivery, joint survey at receipt excuses the writing, and suit must come within one year after delivery or the due date, which late notice never shortens, as Belgian Overseas Chartering v. Philippine First Insurance (G.R. No. 143133, 2002) holds.
Here, the consignee received crates by truck with intact exteriors, opened them after three days to find water damage, and complained on the fifth day, which is concealed damage notified beyond twenty-four hours. The second consignee received container cargo by foreign vessel, joined the survey at receipt, and sued ten months after discharge, which excuses the COGSA writing and sits inside the one-year suit period. Reading a fifth-day truck complaint as timely mistakes days for hours, while reading want of earlier shipper notice as fatal to the sea suit mistakes notice for prescription.
The first consignee therefore loses procedurally without reaching fault, while the second reaches the merits on loss with the carrier fault presumption, so only the vessel claim survives the bars.

section: 6. Notice of Claim and Prescription in Overland and Coastwise Shipping, in International Carriage by Sea, and in Subrogation
stem: An insurer pays the shipper in full eleven months after discharge, takes a subrogation receipt, and sues the foreign line in the twelfth month without any prior shipper notice. The line pleads prescription and want of notice. Does the suit prosper?
answer:
Yes, the suit prospers past both bars, because the subrogated insurer inherits the shipper clock and files inside the one-year sea period that want of notice never shortens.
Under Compañia Maritima v. Insurance Company of North America (G.R. No. L-18965, 1964), the insurer that pays the shipper steps into the shipper shoes and sues the carrier as assignee by subrogation. Under Sec. 3(6) of COGSA, the international sea suit must be brought within one year after delivery or the date delivery was due, the one-year period binds shipper with consignee with bill holder with insurer alike, and failure to give notice of loss never affects the right to sue within that year, as Belgian Overseas Chartering v. Philippine First Insurance (G.R. No. 143133, 2002) holds.
Here, the insurer paid the shipper in full eleven months after discharge, took a subrogation receipt, and sued the foreign line in the twelfth month without any prior shipper notice. Payment with assignment puts the insurer in the shipper shoes rather than in the place of a stranger, and filing in the twelfth month satisfies the one-year period. Reading the insurer as a new claimant with its own clock mistakes subrogation for assignment of a fresh right, while reading want of notice as prescription mistakes a procedural aid for the suit period itself.
Prescription and want of notice therefore both fail as bars, so the suit reaches the merits where the insurer must still prove the loss with the carrier fault presumption behind it.

section: 7. Prohibited and Limiting Stipulations with Purpose, Presumption, Reduced Diligence, Fixed Recovery, Riots and Strikes, and COGSA with Its Limits
stem: A shipper signs a bill limiting recovery to invoice value for lower freight, then a strike delays the voyage for a week and the line deviates to an unscheduled port where theft guts the container. The line invokes the invoice cap and the strike clause. What survives?
answer:
The strike clause stays valid for the week of stoppage delay, but the invoice cap cannot shelter the theft after the deviation, so the post-deviation loss recovers outside the limit.
Under Art. 1744 of the Civil Code, a limit below extraordinary diligence stands only with signed writing and separate valuable consideration and reasonableness, and a signed invoice-value limit for lower freight satisfies those requisites on its face. Under Art. 1747 of the Civil Code, unjust delay or route change forfeits the limiting contract for the ensuing loss. Under Art. 1748 of the Civil Code, delay limits on account of strikes or riots are valid, though only delay caused by the stoppage sits inside them, and valid bill terms bind only inside their own terms as Lu Do and Lu Ym Corporation v. Binamira (G.R. No. L-9840, 1957) shows.
Here, the shipper signed a bill limiting recovery to invoice value for lower freight, then a strike delayed the voyage for a week and the line deviated to an unscheduled port where theft gutted the container. The signed invoice limit with lower freight met the Art. 1744 face test for ordinary voyage loss, and the strike clause covers the week the stoppage itself delayed. Reading deviation as covered delay mistakes carrier-created routing for stoppage time, while reading the theft at the off-route port as stoppage loss ignores that the deviation forfeited the limit for what followed.
The line therefore keeps the strike-delay shelter for the week of stoppage but pays the theft after deviation outside the invoice cap, so the cap survives only for loss the deviation did not produce.

section: 7. Prohibited and Limiting Stipulations with Purpose, Presumption, Reduced Diligence, Fixed Recovery, Riots and Strikes, and COGSA with Its Limits
stem: A foreign-going bill carries no package-limit term and the shipper declares no higher value, then ten packages land short by twenty thousand dollars. The line invokes the five-hundred-dollar cap per package. Does it hold?
answer:
Yes, the cap holds and cuts recovery to five thousand dollars, because COGSA supplies the five-hundred-dollar package limit where the bill carries no term and the shipper declared no higher value.
Under Sec. 4(5) of COGSA, neither the carrier nor the ship shall be liable beyond five hundred dollars per package or customary freight unit unless the nature and value of the goods were declared by the shipper and inserted in the bill of lading. Under Belgian Overseas Chartering v. Philippine First Insurance (G.R. No. 143133, 2002), the limitation rides inside every foreign sea bill as though written there, binding accepting shippers and consignees to the declared maximum, while a letter of credit alone declares nothing. The section never pays beyond damage actually sustained, and knowing fraudulent overstatement forfeits all.
Here, the foreign-going bill carried no package-limit term, the shipper declared no higher value, and ten packages landed short by twenty thousand dollars. No higher declaration in the bill means no higher valuation binds, and no deviation or coercion attends the invocation on these facts. Reading silence in the bill as no limit mistakes omission for freedom, while reading actual loss above the cap as recoverable mistakes ceiling for floor.
The line therefore pays five hundred dollars per lost package with interest and costs as the law allows, so ten packages yield five thousand dollars and the excess above the cap goes unrecovered.

section: 1. Contract vs Other Sources; Culpa Contractual vs Culpa Aquiliana; Concurrent Causes
stem: Ysidro, a paying passenger, was on board Bus No. 904 owned and operated by Yatco Transportation Company (Yatco). He boarded the bus at Munoz, Nueva Ecija with Manila as his final destination. He was seated on the first row, window seat on the left side of the bus. As the bus was negotiating the national highway in front of the public market of Gerona, Tarlac, the bus came to a full stop because of the traffic. The driver of the bus took this opportunity to check on the tires of the bus and to relieve himself. As he was alighting from the bus to do these, an unidentified man standing along the highway hurled a huge rock at the left side of the bus and hit Ysidro between his eyes. He lost consciousness and immediately the driver, with the conductor, drove the bus to bring him to the nearest hospital. He expired before the bus could reach the hospital. Ysidro's wife and children brought a civil action to collect damages from Yatco, alleging that as a common carrier, it was required to exercise extraordinary diligence in ensuring the safety of its passengers. They contended that, in case of injuries and/or death on the part of any of its passengers, the common carrier is presumed to be at fault. In its defense, Yatco alleged that it is not an absolute insurer of its passengers and that Ysidro's death was not due to any defect in the means of transport or method of transporting passengers, or the negligent acts of its employees. Since the accident was due to the fault of a stranger over whom the common carrier had no control, or of which it did not have any prior knowledge to be able to prevent it, the cause of Ysidro's death should be considered a fortuitous event and not the liability of the common carrier. (a) Is a common carrier presumed to be at fault whenever there is death or injury to its passengers, regardless of the cause of death or injury? (2.5%) (b) What kind of diligence is required of common carriers like Yatco for the protection of its passengers? (2.5%) (c) Will your answer be the same as your answer in (b) above, if the assailant was another paying passenger who boarded the bus and deliberately stabbed Ysidro to death? (2.5%)
answer:
(a) Yes, the carrier is presumed at fault once the heirs prove carriage plus death, though the presumption is rebuttable and never absolute. (b) Yatco owes the utmost diligence of very cautious persons with due regard for all the circumstances. (c) The same prevention test governs the fellow-passenger stabbing, so liability still turns on what the crew could have prevented or stopped.
Under Art. 1756 of the Civil Code, death or injury of a passenger during carriage presumes the carrier at fault unless extraordinary diligence is proved. Under Arts. 1733 and 1755 of the Civil Code, that diligence is the utmost diligence of very cautious persons with due regard for all the circumstances. Under Art. 1763 of the Civil Code, the carrier answers for harm from strangers and fellow riders where its servants could have prevented or stopped it, as the train death in LRTA v. Navidad (G.R. No. 145804, 2003) holds.
Here, Ysidro boarded Bus No. 904 as a paying passenger from Munoz bound for Manila, and the bus halted on the Gerona highway while the driver stepped out. An unidentified man hurled a huge rock that struck Ysidro between the eyes and killed him before the hospital run ended, so carriage plus death engages the presumption. The prompt hospital run mitigates but never proves prior diligence, and the fortuitous-event reading fails unless the rock was truly unforeseeable and unpreventable. The knife variant keeps the same test because a fellow-passenger stabbing is measured by what the conductor saw and could have stopped.
Yatco therefore escapes the rock only by proving utmost diligence with true non-preventability, and it answers the stabbing where the crew could have prevented or stopped the attack.

section: 1. Contract vs Other Sources; Culpa Contractual vs Culpa Aquiliana; Concurrent Causes
stem: A stowaway hiding in a bus toilet and a fare-paying rider beside him are both hurt when a stranger smashes a window with a bottle. The line answers the rider but disowns the stowaway. Which answers stand?
answer:
Both answers stand, because the fare-paying rider holds a contract claim tested by prevention while the stowaway holds no contract claim at all.
Under Art. 1756 of the Civil Code, injury to a passenger presumes the carrier at fault once carriage plus harm is shown, and the carrier rebuts only with extraordinary diligence. Under Art. 1763 of the Civil Code, stranger harm is tested by what the crew could have prevented or stopped. Under Art. 2176 of the Civil Code, fault without a pre-existing contractual relation is quasi-delict, so a traveler without carriage must prove fault with causation, as the careful gratuitous host in Lara v. Valencia (G.R. No. L-9907, 1958) shows at the relation line.
Here, the fare-paying rider beside the toilet proves his ticket with his injury, so the presumption runs and the line must show utmost diligence with nothing preventable left undone around the smashed window and the bottle attack. The stowaway hiding in the toilet proves no carriage, so no contract presumption ever arises for him and only a tort claim with fault proof could even begin. The counter-reading that one bottle treats both victims alike fails because the source of duty differs even though the glass is the same.
The line therefore pays or rebuts on the rider under the contract presumption while meeting the stowaway purely on proved fault if sued at all.

section: 1. Contract vs Other Sources; Culpa Contractual vs Culpa Aquiliana; Concurrent Causes
stem: A consignee proves the bill with short delivery of ten crates but brings no purchase invoices, then claims the highest price the goods ever fetched that year. What does the claim still lack?
answer:
The consignee keeps liability established but recovers only the peso value its own evidence sustains, because carriage plus shortage states breach while money still needs proof.
Under Arts. 1735 and 1756 of the Civil Code, loss in transit presumes carrier fault, so the bill with the short delivery of ten crates fixes breach. Under Art. 2199 of the Civil Code, actual damages pay only pecuniary loss duly proved as adequate compensation once. Under the proof rule in British Airways v. Court of Appeals (G.R. No. 92288, 1993), sums never documented or already satisfied recover nothing as actual damages.
Here, the consignee proves the bill with the short delivery of ten crates, so breach is fixed and the carrier must pay whatever loss the papers prove. The consignee brings no purchase invoices and claims only the highest price the goods ever fetched that year, which proves no value actually lost at the time and place of shipment. The counter-reading that shortage alone liquidates the peak price fails because speculation never substitutes for receipts and market papers.
The claim therefore succeeds on liability but collects only the invoice or market value duly proved, never the peak-year price.

section: 1. Contract vs Other Sources; Culpa Contractual vs Culpa Aquiliana; Concurrent Causes
stem: A line in good faith misroutes a crate of ordinary spare parts, while a second line spitefully strands a migrant worker who then loses an abroad job. How does extent differ between the two?
answer:
The parts owner recovers only the foreseeable natural and probable value of the misrouted crate, while the stranded worker recovers the lost placement with its reasonably attributed consequences because spite widens extent.
Under Art. 2201 of the Civil Code, a good-faith obligor pays the natural and probable consequences foreseen or reasonably foreseeable at constitution. Under the second rule of the same article, fraud, bad faith, malice, or wanton attitude makes the obligor answer for all damages reasonably attributed to non-performance. Under the bad-faith awards in British Airways v. Court of Appeals (G.R. No. 92288, 1993), spiteful cancellations drew moral with exemplary correction on top of whatever actual loss survived proof.
Here, the first line in good faith misroutes a crate of ordinary spare parts whose ordinary value any carrier foresees at booking, so only that value with its foreseeable market consequence is due. The second line spitefully strands a migrant worker who then loses an abroad job, and the lost placement flows reasonably from stranding a worker known to travel for employment. The counter-reading that both breaches pay alike fails because state of mind sets the measure even though both sue in contract.
The parts owner therefore collects the foreseeable crate value while the worker collects the wider placement loss with its consequences.

section: 3. Actual/Compensatory Damages; Attorney's Fees; Interests
stem: A shipper claims twenty thousand dollars for ten missing crates but its own manager admits the foreign principal already reimbursed the full invoice value. The bill carries no declared higher value. What survives of the money claim?
answer:
The money claim for the ten missing crates fails entirely, though moral with exemplary correction could still live on separate fraud or bad-faith proof.
Under Art. 2199 of the Civil Code, actual damages pay only pecuniary loss duly proved as adequate compensation once, so reimbursement quenches the award to the extent paid. Under British Airways v. Court of Appeals (G.R. No. 92288, 1993), ticket expense reimbursed in full recovered nothing as actual damages though spite still drew moral with exemplary sums. Under the package discipline in Unsworth Transport International (Phils.), Inc. v. Court of Appeals (G.R. No. 166250, 2010), a bill with no declared higher value caps any surviving cargo value in any event.
Here, the shipper claims twenty thousand dollars for ten missing crates while its own manager admits the foreign principal already reimbursed the full invoice value. The bill carries no declared higher value, so no higher surviving value exists even apart from payment. The counter-reading that the carrier still owes the invoice to the shipper fails because single satisfaction bars the second payment of one loss.
The shipper therefore keeps at most moral with exemplary damages on fraud or bad-faith proof, never the reimbursed sum again.

section: 3. Actual/Compensatory Damages; Attorney's Fees; Interests
stem: A bus line kills a thirty-year-old father earning thirty thousand pesos a month. The heirs prove the payroll with the birth record. Walk the award from indemnity to interest.
answer:
The heirs collect the fifty thousand pesos death indemnity with six million pesos loss of earning capacity with moral damages, and exemplary with fees where proved, all earning six percent legal interest until full payment.
Under Art. 2206 of the Civil Code, death draws indemnity with earning capacity with moral damages for the anguish of close kin. Under the formula applied in Sps. Cruz v. Sun Holidays, Inc. (G.R. No. 186312, 2010), net capacity equals life expectancy times net annual income, with life expectancy at two thirds of eighty minus age and living expenses halved from gross. Under Nacar v. Gallery Frames (G.R. No. 189871, 2013), the prevailing legal interest since July 1, 2013 is six percent.
Here, the bus line killed a thirty-year-old father earning thirty thousand pesos a month, and the heirs prove the payroll with the birth record. Life expectancy is two thirds of fifty years or thirty-three and one third years, and net yearly income is one hundred eighty thousand pesos after halving the three hundred sixty thousand pesos gross. The product is six million pesos on full proof, and the indemnity follows on the death alone. The counter-reading that gross income times full life expectancy applies fails because the formula deducts living expenses the deceased would have spent.
The award therefore stacks the fifty thousand pesos indemnity with the six million pesos capacity with moral and further relief on its own proof, all at six percent legal interest.
## 4. Moral; Nominal; Temperate or Moderate; Liquidated; Exemplary or Corrective Damages

section: 3. Actual/Compensatory Damages; Attorney's Fees; Interests
stem: A line delays a bride three hours through plain mismanagement, apologizes at once, and refunds the fare in full. She sues for moral damages over ruined photographs. Does she collect?
answer:
She collects no moral damages, because a clean delay with prompt apology and full refund draws only actual loss and the refund already quenches it.
Under Art. 2220 of the Civil Code, breach of contract draws moral damages only where the defendant acted fraudulently or in bad faith. Under Art. 2217 of the Civil Code, moral anguish must be proximately tied to a wrongful manner and never to mere disappointment over consequence. Under the package award in Unsworth Transport International (Phils.), Inc. v. Court of Appeals (G.R. No. 166250, 2010), delay with interest and fees but without wilful injury carried no moral sum.
Here, the line delayed the bride three hours through plain mismanagement, apologized at once, and refunded the fare in full. The refund quenches the pecuniary part and the prompt apology negates the spite that moral requires. Her ruined photographs reflect genuine pain over consequence rather than Art. 2217 anguish proximately tied to a fraudulent or bad-faith manner. The counter-reading that deep disappointment alone opens moral fails because clean breach never does.
The claim therefore ends with the refunded fare and no moral award.

section: 3. Actual/Compensatory Damages; Attorney's Fees; Interests
stem: A carrier pays the fifty thousand pesos death indemnity but fights the one hundred thousand pesos moral award, arguing no fraud attended the accident. The death came from its own admittedly reckless overloading. What answers the carrier?
answer:
The carrier loses the fight, because the fifty thousand pesos indemnity stands beside the moral award and admitted recklessness opens exemplary correction as well.
Under Art. 2206 of the Civil Code, death gives moral damages to the spouse with descendants and ascendants for mental anguish by reason of the death alone, without separate fraud proof. Under Art. 2232 of the Civil Code, wanton, fraudulent, reckless, oppressive, or malevolent conduct opens exemplary damages in contract. Under Sps. Cruz v. Sun Holidays, Inc. (G.R. No. 186312, 2010), a package-tour drowning drew the indemnity with one hundred thousand pesos moral with one hundred thousand pesos exemplary on presumed recklessness.
Here, the carrier pays the fifty thousand pesos death indemnity but fights the one hundred thousand pesos moral award by arguing no fraud attended the accident. The death came from its own admittedly reckless overloading, and presumed fault stands unrebutted on these facts. The counter-reading that moral needs fraud fails because the Art. 2206 death door and the Art. 2232 recklessness door each open without fraud.
The indemnity therefore stands beside moral damages with exemplary correction on the recklessness shown.

section: 1. Civil Aviation Laws and Regulatory Perspectives; Civil Aviation; Aircraft Registration
stem: An investor buys a light aircraft abroad and starts selling seats on weekly Boracay runs without registering the aircraft and without any Board authority. A paying guest is hurt on landing and sues on carrier liability. How does the regulatory status affect the case?
answer:
The guest may hold the investor liable as a common carrier for the landing injury, and the lack of registration and Board authority does not negate that liability but exposes the operator to separate administrative and criminal sanctions.
Under Civil Code Art. 1732 with Arts. 1733, 1755 and 1756 and R.A. No. 776 of 1952 with R.A. No. 9497 of 2008, one who holds out carriage by air for compensation to the public is a common carrier bound to utmost diligence with presumed fault on injury, as confirmed in Sps. Cruz v. Sun Holidays, Inc. (G.R. No. 186312, June 29, 2010) and LRTA v. Navidad (G.R. No. 145804, February 6, 2003).
Here, the investor sells seats on weekly Boracay runs to paying guests for hire, which satisfies the holding-out and compensation test even without a permit or nationality marks, while the unregistered aircraft and unlicensed operation weaken documentary defenses and prove non-compliance that cannot excuse failure to observe extraordinary diligence.
Therefore the guest recovers upon proof of injury during carriage unless the operator proves utmost diligence, and the operator separately answers to the Civil Aeronautics Board and the Civil Aviation Authority of the Philippines for flying unregistered and unauthorized.

section: 2. Air Transportation in General; Persons Involved; Charter of Aircraft
stem: To celebrate her 70th birthday, A hired F Travel & Tours to arrange and facilitate her booking, ticketing, and accommodation for a two-week foreign tour, which included visits to Italy and Greece, for the total amount of PHP 145,000.00. On Wednesday, August 14, 2024, B, an employee of F Travel & Tours, went to A's house to deliver the travel documents and plane ticket. She told A to be at the Ninoy Aquino International Airport (NAIA) on Saturday, August 17, 2024 two hours before her flight schedule. Without checking her travel documents, A went to NAIA on Saturday, August 17, 2024. When she got there, she was informed that the flight she was supposed to take had already left the previous day. A demanded that F Travel & Tours refund her payment. She claimed that F Travel & Tours did not observe the standard of care required of a common carrier when its employee, B, informed her of the wrong flight schedule. Is F Travel & Tours liable as a common carrier? Reason(s).
answer:
F Travel & Tours is not liable as a common carrier, and A cannot invoke presumed fault and extraordinary diligence because the agency operated no carriage business, though it may answer for refund and damages under agency and fault rules if its negligence is proved.
Under Civil Code Art. 1732 with Arts. 1733 and 1755, only one engaged in carrying passengers or goods for compensation with service to the public is a common carrier, while a mere arranger of booking, ticketing and accommodation is an agent, as confirmed in Sps. Cruz v. Sun Holidays, Inc. (G.R. No. 186312, June 29, 2010) and British Airways v. Court of Appeals (G.R. No. 92288, February 9, 1993).
Here, F Travel & Tours for PHP 145,000.00 only arranged and facilitated booking, ticketing and accommodation for the Italy and Greece tour and operated no aircraft, and B as its employee merely delivered documents and gave the Saturday August 17 instruction that caused A to miss the Friday flight, which tests agency care in transmitting correct schedule information rather than carrier safety diligence.
Therefore the claim for breach of common-carrier diligence fails, and A recovers refund with damages only upon proving the agency contract and B's fault with actual loss within the scope of employment.

stem: To celebrate her 30th birthday party, socialite A chartered for her exclusive use the yacht usually utilized by XYZ Resort to ferry its guests from the public port to its private island. A brought her own private crew to operate the yacht and invited 30 guests to her yacht party. While in the middle of the ocean, a sudden storm caused the yacht to capsize. While all the guests survived thanks to the prompt rescue operations of XYZ Resort, A succumbed to her injuries after hitting her head on floating debris and drowning. B, A's father, sued XYZ Resorts for gross negligence, alleging that it failed to observe extraordinary diligence expected of common carriers. Is XYZ Resorts liable as a common carrier? Reason(s).
answer:
XYZ Resort is not liable as a common carrier for A's death, and B cannot invoke presumed fault and extraordinary diligence against it because the exclusive charter with A's own crew transferred command and made A the owner pro hac vice for that voyage.
Under Civil Code Art. 1732 with Arts. 1733, 1755 and 1756, carrier status turns on operating carriage for the public and control decides charter effects, so a demise transferring full possession, manning, victualling and navigation shifts liability while affreightment retains it with the owner, as confirmed in Planters Products v. Court of Appeals (G.R. No. 101503, September 15, 1993) and Sps. Cruz v. Sun Holidays, Inc. (G.R. No. 186312, June 29, 2010).
Here, socialite A chartered the XYZ yacht for her exclusive 30th birthday use with 30 guests, brought her own private crew to operate it from the public port to the private island, and sustained fatal head injury and drowning after a sudden storm capsized it mid-ocean despite XYZ rescue, so navigation and control lay with A and not with XYZ as mere owner-lessor.
Therefore B's common-carrier claim against XYZ fails, and any recovery must rest on a different proven fault outside carrier diligence, with the storm and control facts defeating the presumption B invokes.

section: 2. Air Transportation in General; Persons Involved; Charter of Aircraft
stem: A foreign flag carrier flies Taipei to Manila to Cebu and offers cheap Manila to Cebu seats to fill the domestic hop. The Board stops the sale while letting the through flight continue. Is the Board correct?
answer:
The Board is correct to stop the Manila to Cebu sale while allowing the Taipei to Manila to Cebu through flight to continue, because the domestic hop is reserved traffic that a foreign carrier may not sell without domestic authority.
Under the Chicago Convention of 1944 on sovereignty with R.A. No. 776 of 1952 on permits and R.A. No. 9497 of 2008 on regulation, every State owns the sky above its territory and scheduled commercial entry needs permission per freedom, with purely domestic carriage reserved to Philippine carriers.
Here, the foreign flag carrier operates Taipei to Manila to Cebu but offers cheap Manila to Cebu seats to local passengers to fill the hop, which is cabotage even though the aircraft is already flying the sector as part of an authorized through service, and the counter-reading that through-flight authority implies domestic-sale authority fails because transit and fifth-freedom rights never include the domestic leg.
Therefore the stop-sale order stands, the through carriage remains lawful, and the carrier may carry only through passengers on that sector unless it secures proper domestic authority.

section: 4. Extraordinary Diligence in Air; Tariff System; Baggage; Duty to Passenger; Denied Boarding; Air Passenger Bill of Rights; Inspection of Aircraft and Cargoes
stem: A confirmed economy passenger checks in on time and the airline bumps her without asking for volunteers because the flight is overbooked. She accepts the next-day rebooking and signs a compensation receipt. May she still sue for moral damages for wounded feelings?
answer:
The airline is liable for breaching the volunteer-first rule, but the passenger who accepted next-day rebooking and signed a compensation receipt cannot still recover moral damages for the same lost seat because the accepted package operates as liquidated damages closing that claim.
Under DOTC-DTI Joint Administrative Order No. 1, s. 2012 effective December 21, 2012 with Civil Code Arts. 1733, 1755 and 1756, a checked-in passenger with a confirmed reserved seat may board and may not be bumped for overbooking without consent until volunteers are called with rising amenities and compensation, as confirmed in British Airways v. Court of Appeals (G.R. No. 92288, February 9, 1993) and LRTA v. Navidad (G.R. No. 145804, February 6, 2003).
Here, the confirmed economy passenger checked in on time yet was bumped without any call for volunteers to free seats for standbys, which violates consent and escalation, but her acceptance of rebooking with a signed compensation receipt elects the liquidated remedy for the seat loss and the counter-reading that wounded feelings reopens it fails absent an independent actionable wrong outside the bargain.
Therefore the seat-loss claim is closed by the receipt, the carrier keeps the breach on record for regulatory purposes, and only separately proved injury beyond loss of the seat could still be pursued.
## 5. Montreal Convention 1999

section: 4. Extraordinary Diligence in Air; Tariff System; Baggage; Duty to Passenger; Denied Boarding; Air Passenger Bill of Rights; Inspection of Aircraft and Cargoes
stem: A Manila to Singapore passenger checks through with one ticket and her checked bag never arrives. She declares no higher value and writes a complaint on the tenth day after arrival. The bag is still missing on the twenty-fifth day. What may she collect and is her complaint timely?
answer:
She may recover up to 1,000 Special Drawing Rights for the checked bag and her tenth-day written complaint is timely as a delay and loss complaint, though it would have been late if framed as a damage complaint, with loss enforceable on the twenty-fifth day.
Under the Montreal Convention of 1999 Arts. 1, 17, 19, 22, 31 and 35, international carriage with one ticket from Manila to Singapore is covered, checked baggage pays on an event in carrier charge capped at 1,000 Special Drawing Rights absent higher declaration or intent or qualifying recklessness, with seven days for damage notice and twenty-one days for delay notice and loss enforceable after twenty-one days missing.
Here, she checked through with one ticket, declared no higher value and proved no cap-breaker so the 1,000 figure applies, and her tenth-day letter misses the seven-day damage window but falls inside the twenty-one-day delay window while the twenty-fifth-day continued absence triggers the admitted-or-twenty-one-day loss rule, defeating the counter-reading that any tenth-day letter is automatically barred.
Therefore she collects delay and loss value within the cap upon proving the contract and non-delivery with timely delay notice, and clean-receipt and fraud rules do not aid the carrier where no delivery occurred.

section: 4. Extraordinary Diligence in Air; Tariff System; Baggage; Duty to Passenger; Denied Boarding; Air Passenger Bill of Rights; Inspection of Aircraft and Cargoes
stem: Cargo flies Manila to Osaka and arrives water-damaged. The carrier proves the shipper packed the crate defectively and its own handlers did nothing wrong. The consignee sues on the third year after arrival. What is the outcome?
answer:
The consignee recovers nothing because the carrier proved the defective-packing defense and the suit filed in the third year is extinguished by the two-year limit, with domestic tort unable to revive the closed Convention claim.
Under the Montreal Convention of 1999 Arts. 18, 20, 22, 29 and 35, cargo pays only for an event during carriage by air subject to four exclusive escapes including defective packing by one other than the carrier or its servants or agents, capped at 17 Special Drawing Rights per kilogram absent higher declaration, with exclusivity channeling every action however founded through Convention conditions and with extinction after two years from arrival.
Here, the Manila to Osaka water damage was proved to come from the shipper's defective crate with no fault by the carrier's own handlers, satisfying the packing defense to its causal extent, and filing on the third year after arrival falls outside the two-year extinction that the forum computes but cannot extend, defeating the counter-reading that negligence pleading or domestic diligence reopens the case.
Therefore the defense and the time bar each independently defeat recovery, aggregate caps and exemplary-damage pleas do not arise, and dismissal with costs against the consignee follows.

section: 1. Maritime law defined with the vessel, the Philippine flag, registry, prescription, and co-owner rights
stem: A part owner of a merchant vessel sells his undivided share to a stranger without telling the other part owners, and the sale is recorded in the mercantile registry on June 1. On June 8 the remaining part owners tender the price and claim the share. Is their claim timely and what must they still do to perfect it?
answer:
Yes, the claim is timely, and the remaining part owners will take the share sold to the stranger if they deliver the price at once.
Under Code of Commerce Article 575, a sale of a part-owner share to a stranger triggers a nine-day right of option and withdrawal counted from record of the sale in the mercantile registry, perfected by immediate delivery of the price, a record-based trigger consistent with the registry system for vessels under Articles 573 to 585 and illustrated by Compañia Maritima v. Insurance Company of North America (G.R. No. L-18965, October 30, 1964) where legal effect turned on the formal commercial act rather than private notice.
Here, the sale was recorded on June 1 and the tender came on June 8, which is only seven days later and therefore inside the nine-day period, and the argument that time should run from knowledge or notice fails because the law names record as the sole starting point and demands prompt payment.
The remaining owners therefore succeed to the stranger share upon at-once payment, and the stranger buyer must yield despite having taken a conveyance that was valid between the parties.

section: 2. Real and hypothecary nature with maritime lien and the limited liability rule of no vessel, no liability
stem: Absolute Timber Co. (ATC) has been engaged in the logging business in Isabela. To secure one of its shipments of logs to be transported by Andok Shipping Co., ATC purchased a marine policy with an "all risks" provision. Because of a strong typhoon then hitting Northern Luzon, the vessel sank and the shipment of logs was totally lost. ATC filed its claim, but the insurer denied the claim on several grounds, namely: (1) the vessel had not been seaworthy; (2) the vessel's crew had lacked sufficient training; (3) the improper loading of the logs on only one side of the vessel had led to the tilting of the ship to that side during the stormy voyage; and (4) the extremely bad weather had been a fortuitous event. ATC now seeks your legal advice to know if its claim was sustainable. What is your advice? Explain your answer. (3%)
answer:
ATC recovers on the all-risks policy, and the insurer after payment is subrogated against Andok Shipping because none of the four defenses defeats liability for a loss caused by concurrent carrier fault.
Under Code of Commerce Articles 587 and 590 read with Civil Code Articles 1732 to 1739, the carrier bears extraordinary diligence from receipt to delivery and the real and hypothecary shield of abandonment protects only fault solely of the captain, as held in Phil-Am General Insurance Co., Inc. v. Court of Appeals (G.R. No. 116940, June 11, 1997) where deck stowage that destroyed stability was concurrent owner fault that barred abandonment.
Here, Andok sailed an unseaworthy vessel with an untrained crew and logs loaded on only one side so the vessel tilted, and the strong typhoon hitting Northern Luzon was an ordinary foreseeable weather event on that route rather than an irresistible fortuity, so the claim that bad weather alone sank the vessel fails because unseaworthiness, lack of training, and improper stowage concurred as proximate causes.
ATC therefore collects the total loss under the all-risks cover, and the insurer steps into ATC shoes to recover the full payment from Andok whose concurrent negligence leaves it without force majeure or limited-liability protection.

section: 3. Protests with admiralty jurisdiction, smuggling forfeiture, and marine pollution
stem: The captain limps into a strange Philippine port with a sprung mast and no ship agent in sight, fearing seizure by privateers reported along his course. What must he file within twenty-four hours and before whom, and what paper proves he complied?
answer:
He must make a sea protest within twenty-four hours before the maritime authority and obtain the vised certificate of arrival under stress.
Under Code of Commerce Article 612, the captain who makes a port in distress must present himself before twenty-four hours elapse and declare the vessel name, registry, port of departure, cargo, and reason for arrival, with the maritime authority in the Philippines or the Philippine consul abroad and the local authority only in their absence vising the declaration when acceptable, a timely-declaration rule likewise enforced for cargo claims through unfinished discharge in Regional Container Lines v. Netherlands Insurance Co. (Phils.), Inc. (G.R. No. 168151, September 4, 2009) where custody was held to continue until complete delivery.
Here, the captain entered a strange Philippine port with a sprung mast, no ship agent in sight, and reported privateers on his course, so the proper recipient is the maritime authority of that port within twenty-four hours from arrival and not the agent, the owner, or a later forum, and the fear-of-seizure plus sea-damage account must be stated for vising.
He therefore proves compliance only with the authority-vised certificate showing arrival under stress and its reasons, and without it the arrival cannot be treated as proper and the owner stays exposed to cargo and average consequences.
## 4. Cabotage and co-loading

section: 3. Protests with admiralty jurisdiction, smuggling forfeiture, and marine pollution
stem: A foreign vessel on a Singapore to Manila run loads Manila to Cebu boxes between foreign legs and files no transshipment manifest. May it carry them?
answer:
No, the foreign vessel may not carry the Manila to Cebu boxes, and it must keep only its Singapore to Manila foreign cargo with a proper manifest.
Under Republic Act No. 10668 Sections 4, 7, and 8 read with Republic Act No. 9295 of 2004, domestic cargo moving between Philippine ports is reserved to Philippine bottoms and a foreign vessel may co-load only foreign import or export cargo for transshipment through the four stated permissions, with compliant carriage declared not a public service and proved by a cargo manifest to the Port Authorities showing no domestic cargo aboard, a control-and-status approach consistent with National Steel Corporation v. Court of Appeals (G.R. No. 112287, December 12, 1997) where charter terms and vessel status fixed the applicable carriage regime.
Here, Manila to Cebu boxes are domestic cargo even though lifted between foreign legs of a Singapore to Manila run, and the operator filed no transshipment manifest and holds no Maritime Industry Authority special permit based on unavailability of domestic tonnage and public interest.
The boxes must therefore move on a Philippine vessel, and the foreign vessel that lifts them violates the cabotage reservation and faces customs and Maritime Industry Authority consequences.

section: 5. Persons in maritime commerce with ship agents, captains, and officers
stem: A ship agent without owner authority orders the vessel on a new voyage and insures her with an unsound underwriter. The venture fails. Who bears the loss?
answer:
The agent personally bears the failed venture, including subsidiary liability for the unsound insurer, while the owner answers only for authorized navigation needs proved to have benefited the vessel.
Under Code of Commerce Articles 586 to 588 and Articles 597 to 598, the ship agent may bind the ownership for repairs, equipment, provisioning, fuel, and freight but may not order a new voyage, make a new charter, or insure the vessel without owner or majority co-owner authority, with unauthorized insurance leaving the agent subsidiarily liable for the insurer solvency, a limit on who answers for whose undertaking likewise observed in Westwind Shipping Corp. v. UCPB General Insurance Co., Inc. (G.R. No. 200289, November 25, 2013) where the party that undertook delivery answered as carrier for that leg.
Here, the agent without owner authority ordered a new voyage and insured her with an unsound underwriter, so both acts fell outside repairs and navigation needs and the counter-reading that shore representation implies voyage authority fails because Article 598 expressly withholds new-voyage, new-charter, and insurance powers absent grant in the appointment.
The loss and the insurer shortfall therefore stay with the agent personally, and the owner is reached only to the extent a claimant proves an authorized outlay went to the vessel benefit.

section: 6. Special contracts with charter parties, bills of lading, and bottomry and respondentia
stem: Onassis Shipping, Inc. (Onassis) operated passenger vessels and cargo trucks, and offered its services to the general public. In line with its vision and mission to protect the environment, Go-Green Asia (Go-Green), an NGO affiliated with Greenpeace, entered into a contract with Onassis whereby Go-Green would operate with its own crew the MN Dolphin, an ocean-going passenger vessel of Onassis. While on its way to Palawan carrying Go-Green's invited guests who were international and local observers desirous of checking certain environmental concerns in the area, the MN Dolphin encountered high waves and strong winds caused by a typhoon in the West Philippine Sea. The rough seas led to serious physical injuries to some of the guests. Discuss the liabilities of Onassis and Go-Green to the passengers of the M/V Dolphin. Explain briefly your answer. (3%)
answer:
Go-Green answers as owner pro hac vice because it ran the vessel with its own crew and full command, and Onassis as bare owner does not answer for these injuries absent its own fault.
Under Code of Commerce Articles 586 to 588 on owner liability applied through the control test, a time or voyage charter keeps the owner as carrier but a demise that transfers command, possession, and navigation including master and crew makes the charterer answer as owner, as held in Planters Products v. Court of Appeals (G.R. No. 101503, September 15, 1993) and reinforced for private carriage under charter terms in National Steel Corporation v. Court of Appeals (G.R. No. 112287, December 12, 1997).
Here, Go-Green operated the MN Dolphin with its own crew on a Palawan voyage carrying its invited international and local observers, while Onassis collected only hire without navigating, so the argument that Onassis stays liable merely because it owned the vessel and offered services to the public fails because control, not title or prior public offering, decides carrier character on this voyage.
Go-Green must therefore meet extraordinary diligence and rebut presumed fault with seaworthiness and unavoidability of the West Philippine Sea typhoon, and Onassis pays nothing for these injuries unless its own fault is shown.

section: 6. Special contracts with charter parties, bills of lading, and bottomry and respondentia
stem: The master faces an imminent storm and deliberately jettisons hold bales to save ship and remaining cargo, then brings the venture safely to port. The shippers of the saved bales refuse to contribute, arguing that only the shipowner should pay for saving his own vessel. Who contributes and on what basis?
answer:
All saved interests contribute in general average, and the saved-bale shippers must pay their proportionate shares while the jettisoned hold bales are indemnified.
Under Code of Commerce Articles 809 to 812, general average comprises deliberate damage and expense to save vessel and cargo from a real and known common risk, with every interest in vessel and cargo at the time contributing, as distinguished in A. Magsaysay, Inc. v. Agan (G.R. No. L-6393, January 31, 1955) where accidental stranding without imminent common danger produced only particular average on the ship because voyage completion alone is not common sacrifice.
Here, the master deliberately jettisoned hold bales facing an imminent storm and saved ship and remaining cargo into port, so the objection that only the shipowner should pay for saving his own vessel fails because the peril threatened vessel and cargo together and the sacrifice was voluntary, successful, and for common safety.
The saved vessel, saved bales, and one-half of the freight therefore form the contributing capital pro rata, and the owner of the jettisoned bales recovers indemnity through adjustment.

section: 8. Ship Mortgage Decree 1978 (preferred mortgage meaning/requirements, preferred claims, executory contract doctrine, prescription/laches, necessaries liens, maritime tort, salvage lien, subrogation, mortgage with other properties, arrest/foreclosure)
stem: A bank records a whole-vessel mortgage with the good-faith affidavit and keeps its preference. On foreclosure the proceeds cannot pay everyone. Name in exact order the seven grades that beat the bank mortgage.
answer:
The bank is paid only after all seven preferred grades in exact Section 17 order, namely court costs and taxes, crew wages, general average, salvage including contract salvage, maritime liens prior in time to recordation, tort damages, and earlier recorded preferred mortgages.
Under Presidential Decree No. 1521 Sections 4 and 17, a whole-vessel mortgage recorded with a good-faith affidavit and without waiver takes preferred status as of recordation but remains subordinate to those seven grades in the order stated with sharing pro rata within the same grade, with general average as the third grade reflecting deliberate common sacrifice as explained in A. Magsaysay, Inc. v. Agan (G.R. No. L-6393, January 31, 1955) where the Court separated general contribution from particular average borne alone.
Here, the bank holds a whole-vessel mortgage with affidavit and retained preference yet faces insufficient proceeds, so the argument that recordation alone puts it first fails because seniority among preferred claims follows the statutory order and not mere recording date against these grades.
Each grade must therefore be satisfied in full before the next, and the bank takes only any remainder with later mortgages and ordinary claims behind it.

section: 9. Salvage Law (kinds, compensation, limit, excluded persons, jetsam/flotsam, rights/obligations)
stem: A fishing crew spots a burning yacht abandoned by its panic-stricken owner, and a passing tug that owes the yacht nothing tows her to port while the crew helps lash the line. Both claim salvage. Who earns and who is excluded?
answer:
The passing tug earns salvage and the fishing crew earns nothing for mere crew work, sharing only for accepted voluntary extra service beyond duty.
Under Act No. 2616 Sections 1, 8, 10, and 11 read with Presidential Decree No. 1521 Section 17, a stranger who voluntarily picks up and conveys to safety a vessel or cargo beyond crew control or abandoned, with success in whole or in part, earns court-measured reward capped at fifty percent of net proceeds secured by a fourth-grade salvage lien, while the crew of the vessel in danger, one who acts against captain opposition, or one who fails to deliver to customs earns nothing, a stranger-versus-duty distinction likewise preserved in carrier-custody cases such as Ganzon v. Court of Appeals (G.R. No. L-48757, May 30, 1988) where responsibility turned on who lawfully held the property.
Here, the burning yacht was abandoned by its panic-stricken owner in marine peril and the tug owed her nothing yet towed her to port successfully, while the fishing crew merely helped lash the line as hands already bound to the operation, so the claim that all helpers automatically share fails because only voluntary success beyond prior duty is rewarded.
The tug therefore collects the Section 10 reward with retention until paid, and the crew takes only if its extra help was voluntary and accepted for sharing.

section: 1. Public Utility Concept; Public Service under PSA
stem: A company owns no power plant and merely advances the building-wide Meralco bill while collecting each tenant's metered share. The tenants complain to the regulator that the company sells electricity without a franchise. Is the company a public service subject to regulation.
answer:
No. The company is not a public service and is not subject to regulation, so the complaint that it sells electricity without a franchise must be dismissed for lack of jurisdiction.
Under C.A. No. 146 Sec. 13(b) as amended, a public service must own, operate, manage, or control a covered service in the Philippines for hire or compensation for general business purposes, as applied in Cruz de Syquia v. Board of Power and Water Works (G.R. Nos. L-42783-85, November 29, 1976) where the Court held that a building administrator who merely advanced the compound-wide Meralco bill and recovered pro rata shares owned no plant and sold no electricity.
Here, the company owns no power plant, merely advances the building-wide Meralco bill, and collects each tenant's metered share while Meralco supplies electricity directly to the tenants as end users. The counter-reading that any collection for electricity is a sale for hire fails because there is no ownership, operation, management, or control of an electric service and no separate business of supplying power, only reimbursement of an advanced payment.
Therefore the company stays outside regulatory jurisdiction, the regulator must dismiss the complaint, and any dispute over the pro rata sharing is a purely civil lease controversy for the regular courts to decide.

section: 2. Regulatory Agencies; Bases of Regulation
stem: A bus operator with existing certificates applies for additional units and the regulator adds a twenty-five-year expiry to all its certificates without any hearing. The operator assails the whole statute as undue delegation. How should the challenge fail and the order fall.
answer:
The challenge to the statute fails while the challenge to the order succeeds, so the law stands but the twenty-five-year expiry imposed on all certificates without hearing must be set aside and remanded for hearing.
Under C.A. No. 146 Sec. 13(a) as amended by R.A. No. 11659 Secs. 3-4 and Constitution Art. XII Sec. 6, regulation of public services rests on police power over property affected with public interest, as sustained in Pangasinan Transportation v. PSC (G.R. No. 47065, June 26, 1940) where the Court upheld the Public Service Act because public interest is a sufficient standard for delegated certificate regulation within the fifty-year constitutional limit and a certificate is a mere privilege.
Here, the bus operator holds existing certificates, applies for additional units, and receives a new twenty-five-year expiry reaching all certificates without any notice or opportunity to present evidence. The counter-reading that privilege status allows summary amendment fails because the same decision requires prior notice and hearing before new conditions reach existing certificates.
Therefore the statute remains a valid police-power measure, the ex parte expiry is void for denial of procedural due process, and the regulator may reimpose conditions only after proper notice and hearing.

section: 3. Constitutional Provisions and Limitations
stem: TRUE or FALSE. Explain briefly your answer. (b) The term capital in relation to public utilities under Sec. 11, Art. XII of the 1987 Constitution refers to the total outstanding capital stock comprising both common and non-voting preferred shares. (2%)
answer:
FALSE. The statement misdefines capital because capital in Constitution Art. XII Sec. 11 means only shares entitled to vote in the election of directors with full beneficial ownership and never total outstanding stock including non-voting preferred shares.
Under Constitution Art. XII Sec. 11, only citizens of the Philippines or domestic corporations at least sixty per centum of whose capital is Filipino-owned may operate a public utility, as construed in Gamboa v. Teves (G.R. No. 176579, June 28, 2011) to mean voting shares and implemented through SEC Memorandum Circular No. 8, s. 2013 requiring sixty percent Filipino ownership of voting shares and of all outstanding shares, sustained in Roy III v. Herbosa (G.R. No. 207246, November 22, 2016).
Here, the proposition counts both common voting shares and non-voting preferred shares together as capital. The counter-reading that Filipino dominance of total stock cures foreign dominance of votes fails because control runs through electing directors, so a corporation whose foreigners hold sixty-four percent of voting common shares fails even when Filipinos hold all non-voting preferred shares.
Therefore the statement is FALSE, the sixty-forty test must be applied to voting shares with full beneficial ownership under the dual test, and a utility with foreign-held votes is non-compliant despite Filipino-held preferred stock.

section: 3. Constitutional Provisions and Limitations
stem: A water district charter provides that no other franchise for water service inside the district may issue without board consent. A cooperative seeks a franchise and the board refuses. Is the consent requirement valid.
answer:
No. The consent requirement is void and cannot bar the cooperative, so the cooperative may receive a franchise despite the board refusal.
Under Constitution Art. XII Sec. 11, no franchise, certificate, or any other form of authorization for the operation of a public utility shall be exclusive in character, as applied in RCPI v. NTC (G.R. No. L-68729, May 29, 1987) where the Court held that a prior franchisee has no insuperable right against later authority over the same area and a franchise can never block a newcomer granted for the public interest.
Here, the water district charter provides that no other franchise for water service inside the district may issue without board consent, the cooperative seeks a franchise, and the board refuses consent. The counter-reading that consent is mere regulation rather than exclusivity fails because a veto that lets one operator block all rivals creates indirect exclusivity prohibited in every case.
Therefore the consent veto is unconstitutional, the refusal has no legal effect, and the regulator may grant the cooperative franchise upon compliance with legal requirements.

section: 4. Foreign-Owned Enterprise; Critical Infrastructure
stem: A foreign state-owned enterprise proposes to acquire forty percent of a declared critical-infrastructure telecommunications operator after the effectivity of R.A. No. 11659. Its lawyers invoke the thirty percent sovereign wealth exception. May the acquisition proceed.
answer:
No. The proposed forty-percent acquisition cannot proceed and must be denied despite the sovereign wealth argument, so the state enterprise takes nothing.
Under R.A. No. 11659 Secs. 2(g), 24, and 25, an entity controlled by or acting on behalf of a foreign government or foreign state-owned enterprise is prohibited from owning capital in any public service classified as public utility or critical infrastructure, with only sovereign wealth funds and independent pension funds allowed to own up to thirty percent collectively, a police-power control of the kind sustained in Pangasinan Transportation v. PSC (G.R. No. 47065, June 26, 1940).
Here, a foreign state-owned enterprise itself proposes to acquire forty percent of a declared critical-infrastructure telecommunications operator after effectivity and invokes the thirty-percent sovereign wealth exception. The counter-reading that the fund allowance covers the state enterprise fails because the exception belongs solely to sovereign wealth funds and independent pension funds collectively and the forty-percent acquisition by the state enterprise itself exceeds that narrow allowance.
Therefore the acquisition remains prohibited, the regulator must deny approval, and only a qualifying fund within the thirty-percent collective cap could invest while the state enterprise itself cannot own any capital.

section: 1. Acts Requiring Approval; Legislative Franchise vs CPC; When Franchise Necessary; CPC; LGU Delegation
stem: A domestic airline with no congressional franchise applies to the CAB for a certificate while the statute lays down policy, citizenship, fitness, and procedure standards. An incumbent insists the Board must dismiss for want of jurisdiction. Must the Board dismiss.
answer:
No. The Board must deny the motion to dismiss for want of jurisdiction, retain jurisdiction over the domestic-airline application, and resolve after notice and hearing whether to issue a certificate or temporary permit on fitness and public convenience.
Under R.A. No. 776 Sections 4, 10, 12 and 21 in relation to C.A. No. 146 Section 15 as amended, as construed in PAL v. CAB (G.R. No. 119528, March 26, 1997), Congress may delegate licensing to the CAB through a law circumscribed by policy, citizenship, fitness and procedure standards, the Board is empowered to hear applications and to grant certificates and temporary permits, and want of a legislative franchise affects only the merits of issuance and never jurisdiction.
Here, the domestic airline holds no congressional franchise and applies for a CAB certificate while the statute lays down policy, citizenship, fitness and procedure standards, and the incumbent insists the Board must dismiss for want of jurisdiction, but that counter-reading confuses merits with power since absence of franchise goes only to whether the certificate should ultimately issue and the Board remains competent to receive evidence on capability and need.
Hence the dismissal does not lie, the Board proceeds to hearing to test promotion of the public interest in a proper and suitable manner, and it grants the certificate or temporary permit if the standards are met and denies it if they are not, with the incumbent free to oppose on the merits.

stem: A television operator holds a subsisting NTC permit but never obtained the congressional franchise that the radio law exacts. The NTC recalls its frequency after due hearing. Is the recall valid.
answer:
Yes. The recall of the frequency and the denial of renewal are valid, and the television operator may not stay on the air on an NTC permit alone.
Under Act No. 3846 Section 1 in relation to C.A. No. 146 Section 15 as amended, as construed in ACWS v. NTC (G.R. No. 144109, February 17, 2003), a congressional franchise remains a condition sine qua non for radio and television operation, neither P.D. No. 576-A nor E.O. No. 546 expressly or impliedly repealed that exaction, and franchise and certificate are distinct authorities that must concur, with recall sustained upon notice, hearing and substantial evidence.
Here, the television operator holds a subsisting NTC permit but never obtained the congressional franchise that the radio law exacts, the NTC recalls its frequency after due hearing, and the counter-reading that the later certificate power cures the missing franchise fails because a permit never dispenses with a required franchise and an erroneous permit never estops the government.
Therefore the recall stands, the operator must go off the air until it first secures a congressional franchise and then obtains the concurring NTC certificate upon the required public-interest finding.

stem: An applicant proves Filipino citizenship and financial capacity for a direct route that no incumbent serves, since the incumbents run full buses from farther north and skip the town. The incumbents invoke the prior operator rule. Must the grant fail.
answer:
No. The grant does not fail, the Commission may grant the newcomer the direct-route certificate, and the incumbents' opposition based solely on the prior operator rule must be denied.
Under C.A. No. 146 Section 16(a) as amended, as construed in Phil Rabbit v. Gabatin (G.R. No. L-24472, July 31, 1968), certificates issue only where the proposed operation will promote the public interest in a proper and suitable manner, findings on need and capability supported by substantial evidence are conclusive, and the prior operator rule protects only against needless or ruinous duplication and never applies automatically to bar a needed grant.
Here, the applicant proves Filipino citizenship and financial capacity for a direct route that no incumbent serves, since the incumbents run full buses from farther north and skip the town, and the incumbents invoke the prior operator rule and claim ruinous competition, but that counter-reading fails where substantial evidence shows unserved direct demand with a capable applicant because public service and public interest defeat incumbency.
Hence the opposition falls with the exclusivity claim, the Commission grants the newcomer upon the required public-interest finding, and the incumbents retain their existing certificates without a right to block the needed direct service.

stem: A carrier holds a provisional authority over two cities and claims exclusive rights there against a second applicant the regulator finds capable with a feasible plan. The first carrier cites the old one-carrier-per-area scheme. May the regulator authorize the second carrier.
answer:
Yes. The regulator may authorize the second carrier over the same two cities, the first carrier holds no exclusive territory, and the old one-carrier-per-area scheme does not tie the regulator.
Under Article XII, Section 11 of the Constitution and C.A. No. 146 Section 16(a) as amended in relation to R.A. No. 7925 Sections 4(f), 10 and 23, as construed in Eastern Telecom v. Intl Communication (G.R. No. 135992, July 23, 2004), no franchise, certificate or authorization is ever exclusive, later competition laws replaced the service area scheme with healthy competition, and a second provisional authority may issue on evidence of financial and technical capability with a feasible plan.
Here, the carrier holds a provisional authority over two cities and claims exclusive rights there against a second applicant the regulator finds capable with a feasible plan, and the first carrier cites the old one-carrier-per-area scheme, but that counter-reading fails because the scheme is at most one factor, provisional relief is temporary, limited, non-exclusive and revocable, and each provisional project carries its own duties.
Therefore the second authority stands, the incumbent keeps its own authority without monopoly and must improve service under competition, and the newcomer posts the separate escrow deposit and performance bond for its new project before operating.

stem: An incumbent telephone carrier refuses interconnection with a provisionally authorized cellular operator and claims a vested right to be spared competition. The regulator orders interconnection within ninety days. Is the order valid.
answer:
Yes. The order compelling interconnection within ninety days is valid, the refusal to interconnect is unlawful, and the claimed vested right to be spared competition must be rejected.
Under C.A. No. 146 Section 17(a) as amended in relation to R.A. No. 6849 and R.A. No. 7925 Sections 10 and 23, as construed in PLDT v. NTC (G.R. No. 88404, October 18, 1990), provisional authority issues on a prima facie showing of capability and urgent public need, interconnection to expand public access may be compelled under police power, and no utility owns a right to monopoly or to frustrate a newcomer through refusal to connect.
Here, the incumbent telephone carrier refuses interconnection with a provisionally authorized cellular operator and claims a vested right to be spared competition, while the regulator finds prima facie capability with urgent public need and orders interconnection within ninety days, and that counter-reading fails because agency construction of technical grants deserves respect and forfeiture or exclusivity cannot be raised collaterally to block access.
Hence the order stands, the incumbent must interconnect within ninety days on the regulator's terms while the main case continues, and the provisional grant remains temporary, limited, non-exclusive and revocable until final decision after full hearing.

stem: A bus company sells sixty percent of its subscribed capital to a single buyer in two connected deeds without Commission approval and books the transfer. The buyer demands recognition as stockholder. Must the company register the buyer.
answer:
No. The company must not register the buyer, must deny recognition as stockholder, and must treat the booked transfer as void and unregistrable until prior Commission approval is obtained.
Under C.A. No. 146 Section 20(h) as amended, as construed in PLDT v. NTC (G.R. No. 88404, October 18, 1990), no sale or book registration that vests more than forty per centum of subscribed capital in one transferee is lawful without prior Commission approval, connected previous sales are counted together toward the ceiling, and every violative transfer is void and of no effect and shall not be registered.
Here, the bus company sells sixty percent of its subscribed capital to a single buyer in two connected deeds without Commission approval and books the transfer, and the buyer demands recognition as stockholder, but that counter-reading fails because structuring in tranches never evades the ceiling and negotiation before approval is allowed while consummation without approval is void.
Therefore registration must be refused, the buyer holds nothing registrable and acquires no voting or dividend rights, and the parties must seek prior approval after notice and hearing upon just and reasonable grounds with no detriment to the public interest, facing sanction if the void booking is retained.

stem: A certificate holder disobeys service directives for eight years, cures nothing after inspection reports and hearings, and pleads protection of its investments against revocation. Must the Commission settle for a fine.
answer:
No. The Commission need not and must not settle for a fine alone, it may cancel and revoke the certificate with forfeiture of the franchise, and the plea for protection of investments must be denied.
Under C.A. No. 146 Sections 16(m) and 16(n) as amended, as construed in Rizal Light v. Morong (G.R. Nos. L-20993 and L-21221, September 28, 1968), a certificate is a mere privilege forfeited for breach, willful and contumacious refusal to obey orders, rules, regulations or certificate conditions warrants suspension or revocation after notice and hearing, and fines are cumulative and never bar revocation for an operator not of good standing.
Here, the certificate holder disobeys service directives for eight years, cures nothing after inspection reports and hearings, and pleads protection of its investments against revocation, but that counter-reading fails because the protection rule shields only operators of good standing and long neglect with substantial evidence of violation draws cancellation rather than a mere monetary penalty.
Hence the fine does not exhaust the remedy, the Commission revokes the certificate and forfeits the franchise on substantial evidence after due process, and service passes to a qualified operator upon the required public-interest finding.
