stem: A certificate holder disobeys voltage and metering directives for eight straight years, cures nothing after inspection reports and hearings, and pleads that the Commission must impose only the daily fine. Must the Commission settle for a fine.
answer:
No. The Commission is not limited to the daily fine and may revoke the certificate, because eight years of willful and contumacious disobedience of voltage and metering directives and certificate conditions warrants revocation and the Sec. 21 fine is only cumulative and additional and never bars any other remedy.
Under C.A. No. 146 Secs. 16(m), 16(n) and 21 as amended by R.A. No. 11659, approved March 21, 2022, the Commission may suspend or revoke after notice and hearing where the holder violated or willfully and contumaciously refused to obey any order, rule, regulation, or provision of law, with thirty-day pre-hearing suspension for good cause to avoid serious and irreparable damage, and the P5,000 to P2,000,000 daily fine leaves every other remedy intact, as confirmed in Rizal Light v. Morong (G.R. Nos. L-20993 and L-21221, September 28, 1968) where breach since 1954 drew revocation and investment protection shielded only operators of good standing.
Here, the holder disobeyed voltage and metering directives for eight straight years, ignored inspection reports and hearings, and cured nothing, which proves contumacious refusal and incapability rather than excusable interruption, so the plea that the Commission must settle for a fine misreads the cumulative-remedy sentence and asks the Court to substitute discretion where substantial evidence supports revocation.
The Commission therefore denies the fine-only plea and revokes the certificate with forfeiture on substantial evidence, with any accrued daily fine and enforcement available as cumulative and additional consequences.

section: 1. Due Process: Alternative Penalty, NTC Against Legislative Franchise, Hearing Rule
stem: The NTC cancels the CPC of a broadcast station that operates under a congressional franchise, and the station invokes free speech and prior restraint. May the NTC end the franchise by cancelling the certificate.
answer:
No. The NTC cannot end the legislative franchise by cancelling the certificate of public convenience, because the certificate withdraws regulatory permission to operate while the franchise itself survives as a congressional grant that only Congress may amend, alter, or repeal when the common good so requires.
Under Article XII, Section 11 of the Constitution and C.A. No. 146 Secs. 16(m) and 16(n) as amended by R.A. No. 11659, franchises are never exclusive, never exceed fifty years, and remain subject to congressional repeal, while the regulator may only amend, suspend, or revoke certificates for misrepresentation, material change, or willful violation, as confirmed in RCPI v. NTC (G.R. No. L-68729, May 29, 1987) where franchise and certificate were held distinct and the franchise never exempted the holder from NTC jurisdiction nor blocked newcomers, and in Albano v. Reyes (G.R. No. 83551, July 11, 1989) where delegated authorization was treated as a layer separate from the congressional grant.
Here, the broadcast station operates under both a congressional franchise and an NTC certificate, and the NTC act cancels only the certificate layer, so the argument that the franchise falls with the certificate merges two grants while the prior-restraint claim overstates the effect because fees, fines, conditions, and rule-making regulate without extinguishing the grant itself.
The NTC cancellation therefore operates only on the certificate upon due-process proof of violation, the legislative franchise survives until Congress repeals it, and the NTC retains fining, suspension, and rule-making powers subject to Supreme Court review.

section: 1. Due Process: Alternative Penalty, NTC Against Legislative Franchise, Hearing Rule
stem: The Commission suspended a certificate without prior hearing, the operator moved for reconsideration raising every merit and defense it would have raised at the original hearing, and the Commission granted partial relief after full argument. Was due process denied.
answer:
No. Due process was not denied, because the full hearing on motion for reconsideration that raised every merit and defense and won partial relief cured the earlier want of prior notice and hearing before suspension.
Under C.A. No. 146 Secs. 16(n), 29, 34 and 35 as amended by R.A. No. 11659, no certificate is suspended or revoked without prior notice and hearing except for thirty-day pre-hearing suspension for good cause to avoid serious and irreparable damage, and a procedural defect is cured where the operator actually adduced evidence, confronted the record, and argued through counsel, as confirmed in Rizal Light v. Morong (G.R. Nos. L-20993 and L-21221, September 28, 1968) where revocation stood on substantial inspection reports and protection shielded only operators of good standing who litigated the merits.
Here, the operator was suspended without prior hearing but then moved for reconsideration raising every merit and defense it would have raised at the original hearing and obtained partial relief after full argument, which shows actual opportunity to explain and be heard rather than ex parte deprivation, so the claim of incurable want of hearing misreads the curative effect of granted reconsideration.
The suspension therefore stands as a valid exercise of the Sec. 16(n) power within the thirty-day pre-hearing limit, with the reconsideration record supplying the due-process hearing and leaving review only for want of evidence, illegality, or want of jurisdiction.

section: 2. Rate Regulation: Police Power, Non-Delegation, Deregulation, Just Standard, Expenses, Provisional Increase, Collection
stem: The LTFRB authorizes provincial bus operators to collect the P0.37 per kilometer fare plus a floating band of fifteen percent over it at their own discretion, and a later increase compounds on the collected figure. Commuters challenge the band as surrender of rate power. Is the band valid.
answer:
No. The floating band is invalid, because authorizing provincial bus operators to collect fifteen percent over the P0.37 per kilometer fare at their own discretion lets each operator fix its own effective fare and surrenders the delegated rate power to the regulated party.
Under C.A. No. 146 Sec. 16(c) and Sec. 20(a) as amended by R.A. No. 11659, the regulator fixes only fair and reasonable rates that allow recovery of prudent and efficient costs with reasonable return and reasonable price without discrimination, upon reasonable notice with opportunity to be heard and burden of proof on the proponent, as confirmed in Pangasinan Transportation v. PSC (G.R. No. 47065, June 26, 1940) where rate regulation was sustained as police power over property devoted to public use and a certificate was held a mere privilege reachable by regulation under the public-interest standard.
Here, the LTFRB set a P0.37 base but left a fifteen-percent upward band plus compounding on the collected figure to operator discretion, which decides in advance that unknown future rates are just without evidence of prudent cost or reasonableness, so the defense that operators merely implement the authorization ignores that effectiveness without prior approval makes the operator the rate-maker.
The band therefore falls as an undue delegation and invalid subdelegation while the P0.37 base survives until lawfully changed after notice and hearing, with overcollection subject to refund in lieu of or in addition to the fine.

section: 2. Rate Regulation: Police Power, Non-Delegation, Deregulation, Just Standard, Expenses, Provisional Increase, Collection
stem: The regulator approves a provisional rate increase without hearing on urgent public need, publishes notice to affected parties, and opens the ratification hearing on the fifteenth day. The utility collects the provisional rate meanwhile. Was the procedure lawful.
answer:
Yes. The procedure was lawful and the utility may collect the provisional rate meanwhile, because provisional approval on urgent public need is temporary and adjustable and the fifteen-day ratification hearing preserves due process for the definitive rate.
Under C.A. No. 146 Sec. 16(c) as amended by R.A. No. 11659, the Commission may in its discretion approve rates provisionally without necessity of any hearing but shall call a hearing thereon within fifteen days thereafter upon publication and notice to affected parties in the territory affected to ratify, change, modify, or alter the rate on public interest, as confirmed in PLDT v. NTC (G.R. No. 88404, October 18, 1990) where provisional cellular authority with compelled interconnection was held temporary, limited, non-exclusive, and revocable with the merits reserved for final hearing, and in Eastern Telecom v. Intl Communication (G.R. No. 135992, July 23, 2004) where provisional entry by a second carrier was sustained under healthy competition.
Here, the regulator approved the increase without hearing on urgent need, published notice to affected parties, opened the ratification hearing on the fifteenth day, and collected only the provisional figure meanwhile, which tracks the statute exactly rather than making a final rate without hearing, so the objection that any collection needs prior hearing merges provisional relief with final adjudication.
The collections therefore stand pending the hearing outcome and fold into the definitive rate after final hearing, with refund or adjustment and cumulative fine remedies to follow any excess over the final lawful rate.

section: 2. Rate Regulation: Police Power, Non-Delegation, Deregulation, Just Standard, Expenses, Provisional Increase, Collection
stem: An electric utility books its income tax payments as operating expenses, asks a return on that item, and defends the entry as a cost of doing business. Consumers oppose the pass-through. Must the regulator allow the item.
answer:
No. The regulator must disallow the item and fix the rate without it, because income tax never forms part of operating expenses and its burden stays with the taxpayer alone and can never be shifted to consumers through rates.
Under C.A. No. 146 Sec. 16(c) and Sec. 20(a) as amended by R.A. No. 11659, rates must be fair and reasonable to allow recovery of prudent and efficient costs with reasonable return for viable and efficient operation at a reasonable and non-discriminatory price, with burden of proof on the proponent and approval only for prudent and efficient proposals, as confirmed in Pangasinan Transportation v. PSC (G.R. No. 47065, June 26, 1940) where regulation of fares and service was sustained as police power over business affected with public interest and reasonableness was left to regulator discretion on facts.
Here, the electric utility booked income tax payments as operating expense and asked a return on that item as a cost of doing business, which mischaracterizes an excise on the privilege of earning that benefits only the taxpayer and yields no service, so the claim that every booked cost earns a return ignores that only reasonable, recurring, and service-attributable costs enter prudent cost with depreciation and private-business profits under Sec. 16(c).
The regulator therefore disallows the income-tax entry and any return thereon, sets the fair and reasonable rate on service-related prudent costs alone, and leaves the tax burden with the utility.

stem: A bus company sells forty-five percent of its subscribed capital to a single buyer in two connected deeds without Commission approval and books the transfer. The buyer demands recognition as stockholder. Must the company register the buyer.
answer:
No. The company must not register the buyer, because the sale vesting forty-five percent of subscribed capital in a single buyer in connected deeds without prior Commission approval is void and of no effect and unregistrable in corporate books.
Under C.A. No. 146 Sec. 20(h) as amended by C.A. No. 454 and R.A. No. 11659, no public service may sell or register transfer of shares vesting more than forty per centum of subscribed capital in a transferee in itself or in connection with another previous sale without prior approval, and any violative transfer is void and unregistrable, as confirmed in PLDT v. NTC (G.R. No. 88404, October 18, 1990) where share sales were held to need only Commission approval while franchise assignment needs congressional sanction because stockholders own shares while the corporation owns the franchise.
Here, the bus company sold forty-five percent to one buyer in two connected deeds without approval and booked the transfer, which in itself and together exceeds the ceiling, so the demand for recognition as stockholder asks the corporation to book what the statute voids and the tranche structure fails because connected previous sales are counted together to prevent evasion.
The buyer therefore holds nothing registrable, the company must strike the entry and seek prior approval after notice and hearing on just and reasonable grounds without detriment to public interest, facing suspension or sanction if it keeps the void booking.

section: 3. Transfer of Properties and Shares; Unlawful Acts; Administrative Fines; Rule-Making and Quasi-Judicial Functions
stem: A utility sells ten percent of its stock to an alien and Filipino holdings fall to fifty-five percent of capital. The parties call the sale private and internal. What follows for the sale and the certificate.
answer:
The sale is void and of no effect and independently supplies sufficient cause for cancellation of the certificate, because Filipino holdings fell below the sixty-percent floor through an alien transfer that the law voids outright.
Under Article XII, Section 11 of the Constitution and C.A. No. 146 Sec. 20(i) as amended by C.A. No. 454 and R.A. No. 11659, no sale, alienation, or transfer to an alien that in itself or with another previous sale reduces Philippine citizens below sixty per centum of capital is valid, and every such transfer is void and sufficient cause for cancellation, as confirmed in RCPI v. NTC (G.R. No. L-68729, May 29, 1987) where franchise and certificate were held distinct and the regulator kept jurisdiction over every operator in the field, and in Pangasinan Transportation v. PSC (G.R. No. 47065, June 26, 1940) where police-power regulation of the privilege was sustained.
Here, the utility sold ten percent to an alien and Filipino holdings fell to fifty-five percent, which on its face breaches the floor whether viewed alone or with connected sales, so the characterization of the deal as private and internal cannot save it because citizenship compliance is a continuing grant condition and not an internal matter.
The Commission therefore strikes the transfer from the books, opens cancellation for the breach, and requires a compliant Filipino-majority structure with prior approval before any control-shifting transfer takes effect.

section: 3. Transfer of Properties and Shares; Unlawful Acts; Administrative Fines; Rule-Making and Quasi-Judicial Functions
stem: The NTC fines a broadcast station P100,000 per day for operating after its provisional authority lapsed, without any prior notice or hearing, and the station claims the fine needs a criminal case in court. Is the fine valid.
answer:
The fine as imposed is void for want of prior notice and hearing, though the NTC holds the fining power and no criminal case in court is needed, because the defect goes to procedure and not to jurisdiction over the violation.
Under C.A. No. 146 Sec. 21 as amended by R.A. No. 11659 and Sec. 28 as amended, any public service violating certificate terms faces P5,000 to P2,000,000 per day of continuing default after due notice and hearing, payable to the Government through the Commission with suspension until payment or refund compliance and court enforcement, as cumulative and additional remedies prescribing under Act No. 3326 as amended, as confirmed in RCPI v. NTC (G.R. No. L-68729, May 29, 1987) where the legislative franchise never exempted the holder from NTC jurisdiction over services and newcomers, and in Phil Rabbit v. Gabatin (G.R. No. L-24472, July 31, 1968) where Commission findings on substantial evidence were held binding on courts.
Here, the station operated after provisional authority lapsed and drew P100,000 per day, which is within the range and needs no criminal prosecution because Sec. 21 proceedings are administrative and regulatory rather than penal, yet the NTC imposed it without any prior notice or hearing, so the claim that expiry alone validates the fine ignores that Sec. 17 investigation needs no hearing while Sec. 21 fining always does.
The fine therefore falls as void while jurisdiction remains, the NTC must re-issue it only after proper notice and hearing, with consumer refund, suspension until payment, and court enforcement available as cumulative remedies.

section: 1. Competition and Importance; Constitutional Provisions; Policies and Rationale
stem: Congress deregulates the cement industry but keeps a prior-import-volume rule that only the two incumbent importers can meet, and no newcomer can sell a bag without five years of import records. A newcomer assails the rule as an entry barrier. Will the challenge prosper.
answer:
Yes, the challenge will prosper and the prior-import-volume rule will be declared void because it perpetuates the two incumbents' control and makes competitive entry by the newcomer impossible despite formal deregulation.
Under 1987 Constitution Article XII Section 19 and R.A. No. 10667 Section 2, approved July 21, 2015, the State must regulate or prohibit monopolies when the public interest so requires and must preserve open entry, as applied in Tatad v. Secretary of DOE (G.R. No. 124360, November 5, 1997) where the Court voided the Downstream Oil Industry Deregulation Act because its three percent crude and seven percent refined tariff differential, inventory burden, and predatory pricing rule entrenched Petron, Shell, and Caltex.
Here, the cement deregulation law retains a five-year prior-import-volume requirement that only the two incumbent importers can satisfy so that no newcomer can sell even one bag, which replicates the Tatad tariff and inventory walls in cement form and cannot be defended as ordinary regulation because it measures fitness by past incumbency rather than present ability to compete safely and efficiently.
The rule must therefore be struck down and entry opened on lawful and even terms, leaving the State free to impose neutral safety, quality, and capacity standards but powerless to condition market access on an incumbency history that newcomers by definition cannot possess.
authorities: Part IV-A Competition Foundations Scope Market.md :: 1. Competition and Importance; Constitutional Provisions; Policies and Rationale

section: 1. Competition and Importance; Constitutional Provisions; Policies and Rationale
stem: A mayor claims that the Constitution bans every monopoly so the city may seize the only ice plant in town without regulation. The owner answers that the plant charges fair prices and serves all buyers. May the city skip regulation and proceed to seizure.
answer:
No, the city may not skip regulation and proceed to seizure because the Constitution does not ban every monopoly and the fair-priced and fully serving lone ice plant presents no prohibited monopoly on these facts.
Under 1987 Constitution Article XII Section 19, the State shall regulate or prohibit monopolies only when the public interest so requires while no combinations in restraint of trade or unfair competition shall ever be allowed, as explained in Tatad v. Secretary of DOE (G.R. No. 124360, November 5, 1997) and confirmed in Gios-Samar v. DOTC (G.R. No. 217158, March 12, 2019) where exclusivity alone was held not to constitute a monopoly.
Here, the mayor treats the mere existence of the only ice plant in town as a constitutional violation warranting immediate seizure, while the owner shows fair prices and service to all buyers with no combination in restraint of trade or unfair competition, so the facts establish at most a factual monopoly that the public-interest test may tolerate and regulate rather than a prohibited monopoly that the Constitution condemns outright.
The city must therefore apply neutral regulation first and may prohibit or expropriate only upon a statute, due process, and payment of just compensation if the public interest so requires, so the attempted shortcut to seizure without that foundation must be denied.

section: 2. Methods to Deter Anti-competitive Conduct; Tools under the PCA
stem: All four refiners agree to fix pump prices and rotate winning bids for government fuel. The finance manager who signed the minutes seeks immunity and tells everything after the inquiry has started. The Department of Justice charges the presidents. Who goes to jail and what happens to the manager.
answer:
Yes, the presidents who knowingly and willfully joined the price-fixing and bid-rotation cartel face imprisonment and fine while the finance manager who disclosed only after the inquiry started cannot claim automatic immunity and keeps at best a chance at leniency.
Under R.A. No. 10667 Sections 14(a) and 14(b), Section 30, and Section 35, every per se price-fixing and bid-rigging agreement draws two to seven years imprisonment on responsible officers and a Fifty Million to Two Hundred Fifty Million Peso fine per violation, as the competition command explained in Tatad v. Secretary of DOE (G.R. No. 124360, November 5, 1997) condemns concerted closure of markets, while late disclosure earns only discretionary leniency for the first full and continuing cooperator.
Here, all four refiners fixed pump prices and rotated winning bids for government fuel through minutes the finance manager signed, so the agreement is complete upon concerted fixing and rotation without need to prove market effects, and the manager came only after the preliminary inquiry had started while the presidents acted knowingly and willfully, so belated candor cannot convert into pre-inquiry immunity that requires prompt exit and pre-inquiry reporting.
The presidents must therefore stand trial for the cartel with imprisonment and fine upon conviction for each violation, while the manager must seek leniency from the Commission and the Department of Justice on full cooperation without assurance, so prosecution proceeds against the leaders and mitigation alone remains for the late discloser.
authorities: Part IV-A Competition Foundations Scope Market.md :: 2. Methods to Deter Anti-competitive Conduct; Tools under the PCA

section: 2. Methods to Deter Anti-competitive Conduct; Tools under the PCA
stem: A consumer group proves a flour mill abused its dominant position and asks the Commission for P80,000,000 on first offense plus damages for every baker overcharged. The mill argues one forum must choose one remedy. Must the Commission stop at the fine.
answer:
No, the Commission need not stop at the fine because the administrative penalty for the State and the civil damages for the overcharged bakers are separate and cumulative remedies that proceed on different tracks after due process.
Under R.A. No. 10667 Section 29, Section 45, and Section 31, the Commission after notice and hearing may impose up to One Hundred Million Pesos on first offense guided by gravity and duration while any person directly injured may bring a separate civil action after the preliminary inquiry closes, a division confirmed in Gios-Samar v. DOTC (G.R. No. 217158, March 12, 2019) where the Court distinguished punishable abuse from mere position and demanded proof of ultimate facts.
Here, the consumer group proved abuse of dominant position by the flour mill and seeks Eighty Million Pesos within the first-offense ceiling plus full baker damages, while the mill wrongly reads singleness of forum into the law because the fine vindicates public competition and the civil suit repairs private overcharge, so one does not consume the other and triple fines apply if flour is a basic necessity under the pricing law.
The Commission must therefore impose the calibrated fine after notice and hearing and let the directly injured bakers file their independent damages action after the preliminary inquiry, so the mill pays the State for the violation and separately compensates victims for proven losses.

section: 3. Scope of the PCA; Relevant Market Rule; Single Economic Unit Rule
stem: Two shipping lines serve the same island route and charge identical fares. A new entrant proves passengers treat the two lines as fully swappable but proves freight from the rival port costs twice as much with twice the sailing time. The lines claim one national market while the entrant claims an island market. Which market controls.
answer:
Yes, the island market controls and the national-market claim fails because homogenous island conditions that differ materially from neighboring areas define a separate relevant geographic market even for an identical service.
Under R.A. No. 10667 Section 4(k) and Sections 24 to 27, the relevant market joins interchangeable products with a homogenous geography tested by substitution possibilities, distribution cost and time, user switching cost and probability, and access limits, as required in Gios-Samar v. DOTC (G.R. No. 217158, March 12, 2019) where the Court refused to find monopoly and restraint without pleaded and proven ultimate facts on market, position, and abuse.
Here, the two shipping lines serve the same island route with identical fares and passengers treat them as fully swappable so the product market is common, but freight from the rival port costs twice as much with twice the sailing time and users cannot practicably seek that distant port, so distribution cost, supply time, and switching probability split the geography and defeat the one-national-market reading.
The Commission must therefore define the island as the relevant geographic market and test dominance and abuse inside that boundary, so market share, power, and conduct are measured where competition actually occurs rather than diluted across a national area the island shipper cannot reach.

section: 3. Scope of the PCA; Relevant Market Rule; Single Economic Unit Rule
stem: 3. Ernest Bicycle Corporation (EBC) and Max Speed Corporation (MSC) are the leading manufacturers and sellers of electric bicycles in the country. EBC and MSC offer their bestselling models at PHP 25,000.00 per unit. In 2023, Gryffin Pedals, Inc. (GPI) entered the market and sold electric bicycles with features similar to EBC and MSC's bestselling models for only PHP 20,000.00. GPI has no physical stores and offers its products in digital marketplaces. After a year, GPI had 75% share of the market leaving EBC and MSC at 15% and 10% shares, respectively. EBC and MSC filed a complaint before the Philippine Competition Commission and alleged that GPI is fast monopolizing the electric bicycles market because of its dominant position. Will the complaint against GPI for violation of the competition laws prosper? Explain.
answer:
No, the complaint against Gryffin Pedals, Inc. will not prosper because its seventy-five percent share at most raises a rebuttable presumption of dominant position and the complainants prove no abusive conduct that substantially prevents, restricts, or lessens competition.
Under R.A. No. 10667 Section 27, Section 15, and Section 4(g), dominance at fifty percent share is only presumed and rebuttable while share won through superior skill, service, product, business acumen, or intellectual property is shielded and only abusive conduct is punished, as affirmed in Gios-Samar v. DOTC (G.R. No. 217158, March 12, 2019) where the Court held that position alone is never unlawful and that market, dominance, and abuse each require proof.
Here, Ernest Bicycle Corporation and Max Speed Corporation sold at Twenty-Five Thousand Pesos while Gryffin Pedals, Inc. sold similar-feature electric bicycles at Twenty Thousand Pesos through no-store digital marketplaces to reach seventy-five percent against fifteen and ten percent, which on these facts shows legitimate price rivalry and efficient distribution rather than below-cost predation or exclusion, so dominance even if presumed is explained by consumer choice and the high-share-equals-violation reading must be rejected.
The complaint must therefore be dismissed for failure to plead and prove the relevant product and geographic markets plus exclusionary abuse inside them, leaving Ernest and Max Speed free to refile only with ultimate facts of predatory or foreclosing conduct and leaving efficient low pricing that benefits consumers fully lawful.

section: 1. Anti-competitive Agreements
stem: All four refiners agree in a group chat to fix pump prices and rotate winning bids for municipal fuel. The finance manager who typed the minutes claims the deal was oral and informal so no agreement exists. Is the cartel per se prohibited.
answer:
Yes. The cartel is per se prohibited in both limbs, the pump-price fixing and the rotation of winning municipal-fuel bids, and the finance manager's oral-and-informal defense fails to negate agreement.
Under R.A. No. 10667 Sec. 14(a), approved July 21, 2015, restricting competition as to price and fixing price in any bidding including cover bidding, bid suppression, bid rotation and market allocation are per se prohibited between competitors without proof of market or outweighing efficiency, while Sec. 4(b) defines agreement to include every tacit, informal, explicit, oral or written concerted action, a rule reinforced for competition policy by Eastern Telecommunications v. ICC (G.R. No. 135992, July 23, 2004) where the Court sustained entry of a qualified rival because no operator is shielded from healthy competition.
Here, the four refiners fixed pump prices and rotated winning bids for municipal fuel in a group chat documented by the finance manager who typed the minutes, which squarely matches price restriction and bid rotation, and the claim that an oral and informal understanding is not an agreement collapses because Sec. 4(b) expressly captures informal, tacit and oral concerted action so no signed pact is required and no weighing of reasonableness is allowed for this track.
The cartel is therefore condemned per se without defining the relevant market or balancing harm against efficiency, and the operative consequence is prohibition of the arrangement with criminal exposure under Sec. 30 of two to seven years plus P50,000,000 to P250,000,000 for knowing participants.
authorities: Part IV-B Prohibited Conduct Mergers.md :: 1. Anti-competitive Agreements

section: 1. Anti-competitive Agreements
stem: Two cement makers divide towns by buyer with one taking north distributors and the other taking south distributors. A new entrant proves the division, and the makers answer that no price was ever fixed. Must the Commission still weigh effects before condemning the pact.
answer:
Yes. The Commission must still define the relevant market and weigh effects before condemning the pact, and the absence of any price fixing does not save the buyer-division because market sharing is tested under a different paragraph.
Under R.A. No. 10667 Sec. 14(b)(2), approved July 21, 2015, dividing or sharing the market by volume, territory, type of goods, buyers, sellers or any other means between competitors is prohibited only where it has the object or effect of substantially preventing, restricting or lessening competition, while Sec. 26 requires the Commission to define the relevant market and determine substantial adverse impact outweighing efficiency gains with a forward-looking totality review, a pro-rivalry approach confirmed in Eastern Telecommunications v. ICC (G.R. No. 135992, July 23, 2004) where the Court rejected any vested right to a fenced service area.
Here, the two cement makers divided towns by buyer with one taking north distributors and the other taking south distributors as proved by the new entrant, which fits market division by buyers and territory, and the counter-reading that no price was ever fixed misses the track because price fixing belongs to Sec. 14(a) per se while this buyer allocation lives under Sec. 14(b) where substantial lessening through object or effect is still required.
The pact is therefore condemned only after the Sec. 26 weighing finds substantial harm outweighing any proven efficiency, and the operative consequence is a Commission prohibition order against the division with the makers barred from enforcing the allocation.
authorities: Part IV-B Prohibited Conduct Mergers.md :: 1. Anti-competitive Agreements

section: 2. Abuse of Dominant Position
stem: A dominant flour mill sells below cost for six months with internal memos targeting the death of a new rival mill. A second dominant mill only matches the first mill price in good faith for comparable flour. Which mill abuses its position.
answer:
The first dominant mill abuses while the second dominant mill stays lawful, because destructive object is proved against the predator and good-faith matching shields the responder despite dominance on both sides.
Under R.A. No. 10667 Sec. 15(a), approved July 21, 2015, selling goods below cost with the object of driving competition out of the relevant market is prohibited as abuse of dominant position, while the same paragraph expressly saves a price established in good faith to meet or compete with a lower rival price for the same or comparable product of like quality, a conduct-focused test consistent with Tatad v. Secretary of DOE (G.R. No. 124360, November 5, 1997) where the Court struck down only entry-entrenching barriers and not size or entry itself.
Here, the first flour mill sold below cost for six months with internal memos targeting the death of the new rival mill, which establishes the prohibited destructive object beyond low price alone, while the second mill only matched the first mill price in good faith for comparable flour, which fits the statutory saving clause, and the counter-reading that dominance alone condemns both fails because dominance without abusive conduct is never punished.
The first mill is therefore liable for abuse with the operative consequence of a Commission cease-and-desist order plus fines and remedies against the predation, while the second mill is cleared because good-faith matching is lawful competition.
authorities: Part IV-B Prohibited Conduct Mergers.md :: 2. Abuse of Dominant Position

section: 2. Abuse of Dominant Position
stem: A dominant bottler charges provincial dealers a higher price than Manila dealers for identical drinks on identical terms, and the gap tracks no cost, volume, or rival-price difference. The bottler answers that price gaps are normal business. Is the differential permissible.
answer:
No. The differential is not permissible and constitutes abuse of dominant position because it unreasonably discriminates among contemporaneously trading dealers on similar terms with substantial lessening of competition and fits none of the four saving classes.
Under R.A. No. 10667 Sec. 15(d), approved July 21, 2015, setting prices that discriminate unreasonably between customers contemporaneously trading on similar terms where the effect may substantially lessen competition is prohibited, with only four permissible differentials for socialized pricing, cost-reflecting differences, responses to rival prices or facilities, and market-driven changes, a strict saving scheme consistent with Gios-Samar v. DOTC (G.R. No. 217158, March 12, 2019) where the Court required pleaded and proved ultimate facts on market, position and abuse rather than conclusions.
Here, the dominant bottler charged provincial dealers a higher price than Manila dealers for identical drinks on identical terms with the gap tracking no cost, volume, or rival-price difference, which establishes unreasonable discrimination on similar terms, and the counter-reading that price gaps are normal business fails because normalcy is irrelevant unless the gap reasonably reflects cost, answers rivalry, serves socialized pricing, or responds to market conditions.
The differential therefore falls outside every permissible class and is condemned as abuse, with the operative consequence of a Commission order to cease the discrimination, equalize terms or justify a saving differential, plus applicable fines.
authorities: Part IV-B Prohibited Conduct Mergers.md :: 2. Abuse of Dominant Position

section: 3. Mergers and Acquisitions Control
stem: Two beverage giants breach both operative thresholds and sign on June 1 with notice filed the same day. They close on June 11 before any decision. The giants claim the ten-day sprint harmed no one. What is the status of the closing.
answer:
The June 11 closing is void and both giants face an administrative fine of one percent to five percent of transaction value, with the thirty-day waiting period violated and the claim of no harm irrelevant to gun-jumping.
Under R.A. No. 10667 Sec. 17, approved July 21, 2015, parties breaching the operative thresholds under Sec. 19, currently Size of Party P9,100,000,000 with Size of Transaction P3,800,000,000 effective March 1, 2026, are prohibited from consummating until thirty days after notification with voidness plus one to five percent fine for breach, a waiting protection for rivalry consistent with Eastern Telecommunications v. ICC (G.R. No. 135992, July 23, 2004) where the Court privileged healthy competition over incumbency claims.
Here, the two beverage giants breached both operative thresholds and signed on June 1 with notice filed the same day yet closed on June 11 before any decision, which is only ten days into the thirty-day bar, and the counter-reading that the ten-day sprint harmed no one fails because Sec. 17 punishes the act of early closing itself without requiring proven market harm, leaving merits review still open.
The closing is therefore void ab initio with penalties accruing on transaction value, and the operative consequence is that the parties must unwind or re-notify and wait out the full clock with fines paid while the Commission retains power to prohibit or conditionally clear on merits.

section: 3. Mergers and Acquisitions Control
stem: A buyer takes control of a rival in four monthly slices within one year, with each slice below threshold but all four combined above it. The buyer files nothing and claims each slice stands alone. Must the buyer have notified.
answer:
Yes. The buyer was required to notify because the four slices aggregate into one transaction that breached the thresholds, and the claim that each slice stands alone fails against the creeping-transaction rule.
Under PCC IRR Rule 4 Sec. 3(e) implementing R.A. No. 10667 Secs. 17 and 19, approved July 21, 2015, successive transactions or part-acquisitions within one year between the same parties or their controlled entities count as one transaction for notification once the combined value breaches Size of Party P9,100,000,000 with Size of Transaction P3,800,000,000 effective March 1, 2026, an anti-circumvention rule consistent with Gios-Samar v. DOTC (G.R. No. 217158, March 12, 2019) where the Court looked past bundling form to ultimate market facts.
Here, the buyer took control of a rival in four monthly slices within one year with each slice below threshold but all four combined above it and filed nothing, which triggers aggregation from the step that pushes the total past the thresholds, and the counter-reading that each slice stands alone fails because the rule expressly reckons the one-year window as a single deal to prevent threshold evasion by slicing.
Notification was therefore due before consummating the breaching slice with the operative consequence that the closing without notice is void and draws one to five percent of transaction value, and splitting one takeover into small steps never defeats compulsory notification.
authorities: Part IV-B Prohibited Conduct Mergers.md :: 3. Mergers and Acquisitions Control

section: 1. Philippine Competition Commission
stem: The Secretary of Energy writes the Commission directing it to clear a refinery merger without review because the project is a presidential priority. The merging refiners invoke the letter and demand immediate clearance. Must the Commission obey the directive.
answer:
No. The Commission must disregard the directive and must independently review the refinery merger on the merits, and the merging refiners cannot compel immediate clearance by invoking the letter.
Under R.A. No. 10667 Sec. 5 creating the Commission as an independent quasi-judicial body attached only for administration to the Office of the President, Sec. 12 granting it original and primary jurisdiction over merger review, and Sec. 31 granting sole and exclusive authority to open and resolve inquiries, applied in Tatad v. Secretary of DOE (G.R. No. 124360, November 5, 1997) which struck down executive measures entrenching an oligopoly in violation of 1987 Constitution Art. XII Sec. 19, independence means adjudication turns only on evidence after due notice and hearing and never on political direction.
Here, the Secretary of Energy ordered clearance without review because the project is a presidential priority, and the merging refiners demand immediate clearance on that basis, but attachment to the Office of the President does not authorize direction of outcomes, and a cabinet letter invoking presidential priority is neither substantial evidence nor law that can displace notification and review, so the claim that administrative attachment equals obedience fails.
The Commission therefore disregards the letter, retains jurisdiction, conducts inquiry and merger review to prohibition or conditional clearance on the merits, and any clearance issued without that review would be void for lack of jurisdiction and due process.

section: 1. Philippine Competition Commission
stem: After due hearing the Commission finds a cement cartel and orders the members to sell two plants although a supervised price and supply commitment would restore rivalry. The cartel answers that divestiture is a listed remedy so the Commission may choose it freely. Is the divestiture order valid.
answer:
No. The divestiture order is invalid and must be set aside, and the Commission must instead impose the equally effective supervised price and supply commitment that restores rivalry with less intrusion.
Under R.A. No. 10667 Sec. 12(d) allowing stoppage or redress only upon substantial evidence after due notice and hearing through injunctions, divestment and disgorgement, and Sec. 12(h) permitting adjustment or divestiture orders only where no equally effective behavioral remedy exists or where any equally effective behavioral remedy would be more burdensome, proportionate only to lasting or repeated infringement risk rooted in structure, as enforced by an independent enforcer under Tatad v. Secretary of DOE (G.R. No. 124360, November 5, 1997) pursuant to 1987 Constitution Art. XII Sec. 19, mere listing of divestiture among remedies never makes it freely electable.
Here, the Commission found a cement cartel after due hearing but ordered members to sell two plants although it conceded a supervised price and supply commitment would restore rivalry, and the cartel wrongly reads mere listing of divestiture as free choice, but the admitted effectiveness of the behavioral commitment defeats the first statutory condition and shows the order punishes structure rather than curing conduct proportionately.
The Commission therefore vacates divestiture, substitutes the effective behavioral order with monitoring and retains disgorgement or fines if warranted, reserving divestiture for proof that conduct relief cannot work or burdens more than reorganization.
authorities: Part IV-C PCC Confidentiality Remedies.md :: 1. Philippine Competition Commission

section: 2. Composition, Term, Qualification; Confidentiality; Remedies of the Entity
stem: A business daily demands that the Commission publish the production costs and customer lists a cement maker filed during a cartel inquiry. The maker objects and withholds consent while no court orders disclosure. Must the Commission publish the data.
answer:
No. The Commission must deny publication, must keep the production costs and customer lists sealed, and must release only a redacted ruling that protects the sealed data.
Under R.A. No. 10667 Sec. 34 sealing confidential business information submitted in any inquiry or investigation and in any deliberation relating thereto against direct or indirect disclosure, publication, transfer, copying or dissemination, punishable by a fine of not less than P1,000,000.00 but not more than P5,000,000.00, with only three exits of notifying-entity consent, mandatory disclosure by law, or valid order of a court, government or regulatory agency including an exchange, consistent with Gios-Samar v. DOTC (G.R. No. 217158, March 12, 2019) which requires ultimate facts on market, dominance and abuse to be pleaded and proved in the proper forum first rather than aired as conclusions, inquiry filings stay inside the forum until a lawful exit opens.
Here, a business daily demands publication of the production costs and customer lists a cement maker filed during a cartel inquiry, the maker objects and withholds consent while no court orders disclosure, and no mandatory law is invoked, so press demand alone opens none of the three exits and the counter-reading that public interest or press request equals a valid order fails.
The Commission therefore keeps the data sealed, publishes only a ruling redacted to the extent possible, and any official who discloses faces the Sec. 34 fine of P1,000,000.00 to P5,000,000.00.

section: 2. Composition, Term, Qualification; Confidentiality; Remedies of the Entity
stem: A flour distributor directly injured by a price cartel files a civil damages suit in the Regional Trial Court while the Commission preliminary inquiry is still running. The cartel moves to dismiss as premature. Must the court dismiss the suit.
answer:
Yes. The court must dismiss the civil damages suit as premature without prejudice, and the flour distributor may refile only after the Commission completes its preliminary inquiry.
Under R.A. No. 10667 Sec. 45 allowing any person who suffers direct injury to institute a separate and independent civil action only after the Commission has completed the preliminary inquiry under Sec. 31, with Sec. 31 giving the Commission sole and exclusive authority to open fact-finding or preliminary inquiry to be completed within ninety days, and Sec. 44 giving the Regional Trial Court original and exclusive jurisdiction over the civil case once the gate opens, as applied in Gios-Samar v. DOTC (G.R. No. 217158, March 12, 2019) which dismissed competition claims pleaded as bare conclusions without ultimate facts on market, dominance and abuse, the inquiry first builds the facts that a court later tries.
Here, a flour distributor directly injured by a price cartel filed civil damages in the Regional Trial Court while the Commission preliminary inquiry is still running, and the cartel moves to dismiss as premature, but direct injury alone does not open the action because completion of the inquiry is a condition precedent, so the early filing jumps the administrative gate and the claim that separateness means immediacy fails.
The court therefore dismisses the suit as premature without prejudice to refiling once the Commission completes its inquiry, leaving the five-year Sec. 46 period from accrual and the later civil jurisdiction intact.
authorities: Part IV-C PCC Confidentiality Remedies.md :: 2. Composition, Term, Qualification; Confidentiality; Remedies of the Entity
